title: Jason Kenney stands for Canada in Alberta separatism surge
body: As separatist sentiment seems to strengthen in Alberta, former premier Jason Kenney is calling for more federal Conservatives to get on the front line of federalism. Kenney, who left office four years ago, has re-emerged on the public stage in recent weeks as one of the loudest voices speaking out against the patchwork of separatist groups who would see his province chart a path out of confederation. ""If this referendum goes ahead and goes forward with the most likely outcome, which is a 25 to 30 per cent 'yes' vote, the only big political winner is the Liberal party of Canada,"" Kenney told a Calgary audience Monday. A week after a separatist group said they'd collected more than 300,000 signatures in support of a referendum, he appeared alongside Corey Hogan - the lone Liberal MP elected in Calgary last year - for an event focused on the cross-aisle case for a united Canada. There has been a reluctance among right-of-centre federalists to speak out and ""create a five alarm fire"" before there is even an official referendum on the ballot, Kenney said. But continued silence from Conservatives risks creating a ""rally around the flag phenomenon"" among mainstream Albertans, worried about instability and keen to support a central government. Kenney's case for Canada appeared to take on personal stakes this week, when his home address was allegedly revealed to a group of separatist volunteers, as part of a massive breach of voter data now under investigation by both Elections Alberta and police. ""I used to say, 'I love being in the private sector. I've got freedom. I've got opportunity. I've got privacy. Well, at least I had that,' "" Kenney said Monday, prompting laughter from the crowd. Kenney, who was a federal minister before coming to Alberta to help forge the now-governing United Conservative Party, has also faced criticism that he helped fan the flames now blazing in the province. His government created the Citizen Initiative Act, the legislation now being used by separatists to push for a referendum, and he railed against what he argued was Ottawa's unfair treatment of Alberta. Like Smith, he also struggled to manage the far right faction of his party that was critical of the public health policies he enacted during COVID and that eventually played a role in removing him as premier. But on Monday, Kenney stressed the need for people across the spectrum to stop ""infantilizing"" the separatist movement and take the threat to Canadian confederation seriously. But for Conservatives in particular, he argues they stand to lose ground in what has historically been one of their biggest strongholds. Polling suggests separatist sentiment is entrenched among conservative voters, which has posed problems for its leadership. In Alberta, Danielle Smith has struggled to handle the increasingly vocal separatist faction of her party. In April 2025, her government significantly lowered the number of signatures needed for citizen-initiated referendums, in a move viewed by many as an attempt to appease them. But the pressure has also created an opportunity for conservative leadership to stand up and speak out, Kenney argued Monday. ""I would love to see a version of Mr. Poilievre this September that reminds some of us of Jean Charest in 1995,"" he said, referring to the then-leader of the federal Progressive Conservatives who became a key figure of the campaign to keep Quebec in Canada. ""I think that's possible,"" Kenney added.

title: Toronto World Cup tickets listed for $64,000 despite Ontario's new anti-scalping law
body: Hundreds of tickets for Canada's June 12 World Cup opener against Bosnia and Herzegovina are still up for sale at online reselling sites for more than ten times their original asking price - despite Ontario's new anti-scalping law. New amendments to the Ticket Sales Act make it illegal to resell tickets to any event in Ontario, including six Toronto games which are part of soccer's global showcase, for more than their face value. Monday evening, one pair of tickets with a face value of just over $3,000 a seat was listed at Stub Hub for $64,462 per seat. Another pair was going for $63,647. While those are a far cry from the $2 million a seat some prime tickets for the final in East Rutherford, N.J. are going for, it's just the type of mark-up the amendments - which went into effect April 23 - were supposed to eliminate. A spokesperson for Stephen Crawford, Ontario's minister of public and business service delivery, said the new law aims to keep fans from getting gouged. ""We...have no tolerance for bad actors trying to overcharge families,"" said Crawford spokesperson Giulia Paikin, who warned that companies who don't take down listings for tickets priced above their face value could be fined up to $250,000. Under questioning from NDP MPP Krisyn Wong-Tam in the Ontario legislature Monday, Crawford said the government is in touch with resale companies. ""Letters have been sent to all companies. We've been in discussions with every organization that is a reseller of tickets, and we will be continuing discussions with them and will be further enhancing enforcement in the very near future, if not in compliance."" In a written statement, a spokesperson for Stub Hub said the company is keeping a close eye on new listings to make sure they don't break the law. ""We...have implemented changes so newly-listed tickets comply with Bill 97 while we, and the entire industry, await further guidance,"" said the Stub Hub spokesperson. That ""guidance"" is coming in a technical briefing for the ticketing industry May 26 by staff from the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement, according to a ministry letter obtained by the Star. ""If you, your members, and/or your clients have questions about business obligations related to the purchase of event tickets, Consumer Protection Ontario would like to offer the opportunity to provide an informational webinar,"" the letter said. At Seatgeek.com, the handful of tickets still being sold for Canada's opener appeared to be much closer to their original prices, with the most expensive listed at $4,394, including a $3,765 for the ticket itself and a $628.92 ""ticket fee."" A Seatgeek executive blasted the new law, saying it will force eager fans to seek seats on social media or other sites which don't guarantee tickets are legitimate, unlike major reselling sites like Seat Geek, Stubhub and Vivid Seats. ""Price controls on resale don't lower what fans pay for World Cup tickets or any other event. What they do is push transactions off regulated platforms - like Seat Geek - to Kijiji and Facebook Marketplace, where there are no buyer protections and fraud rates are nearly four times higher,"" said Joe Freeman, Seat Geek's vice president of government affairs. ""Fans don't disappear when resale is restricted; they just lose their safety net."" After the new law came into effect, FIFA removed Toronto games from its own resale site. The changes caught the ticket resale industry off-guard, according to industry sources who said the Ontario government had invited companies to submit their comments on the proposed changes during a ""consultation period"" that wasn't scheduled to close until May 10th. Instead, the changes to the Ticket Sales Act were passed April 23 as part of an omnibus budget bill. If the pricey tickets do get taken down, however, that raises the risk of eager fans getting pushed to sites where they're at risk of getting scammed, warned veteran Toronto Police Service detective David Coffey. ""One of the groups that will definitely benefit from this law, and it's sad to say, will be the scammers because it will create more of a scarcity for the buyers. Whenever you have scarcity and high demand, that's the feeding ground for the fraudsters,"" said Coffey, who works for the Toronto Police Service's financial crimes unit. ""You're going to have buyers going to those illegitimate sites because there are going to be no other options, because there aren't going to be any tickets for sale on the legitimate sites."" For Coffey, the World Cup coming to town is a bit of deja vu from when Taylor Swift played six concerts of her Eras Tour in Toronto in 2024. Emotions, said Coffey, overcame judgment, and fans spent thousands of dollars on tickets that didn't exist. ""We really didn't know the extent of it until the day of the concert and people would show up to the stadium and suddenly be told 'sorry, this ticket has already been scanned nine times. You're out of luck,'"" said Coffey. In addition to keeping their emotions in check, fans should also be wary of claims that seem too good to be true when considering whether or not to buy tickets listed on social media or classified ad sites like Kijiji, Coffey added. ""You're basically throwing your money into this big pot with the expectations that this person that you're communicating with online, who you've never met, have no history with, that they're going to be true to their word,"" said Coffey. ""You ultimately just have to be very suspicious.""

title: Doug Ford cited abuse of OSAP as one reason for its overhaul. Here's what new data actually shows
body: Ontario data reveals that $13.1 million in financial aid over two years - a small fraction of total disbursements - was wrongly granted to students later found to be ineligible, with no cases referred to police, raising questions about the scale of alleged abuse Premier Doug Ford cited, in part, to justify overhauling OSAP. Last year, $8,332,363 in student assistance was wrongly issued due to ""false or invalid information, incorrect statuses, participation in non-bona fide studies or other discrepancies,"" according to records obtained by the Toronto Star through a freedom-of-information request. In 2024, the amount was $4,719,310. In the fiscal year 2024-25, the government spent $1.7 billion in OSAP grants and $301 million on loans, assisting 473,000 students. Based on these figures and the new data, the payments found to be ineligible represent less than one per cent of total disbursements and number of students affected. (The proportions of ineligible aid may in fact be overstated as the wrongly granted aid covers two whole years as opposed to one fiscal year.) ""Any inappropriate use of OSAP funding is unacceptable,"" Bianca Giacoboni, press secretary to Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn, told the Star on Monday. ""We have a robust framework in place to protect OSAP from fraudulent use, and we are implementing new technology and exploring other avenues to strengthen the program's integrity."" The records requested by the Star did not disclose how much of the funding has been recouped, noting that a ""standard OSAP repayment process"" applies. They note that while some cases may result in defaulted loans that proceed to collections, ""we do not have aggregate numbers based on investigations and do not track this data."" In February, the government, as part of its announcement of a $6.4 billion investment in post-secondary and the lifting of the tuition freeze, said it was revamping the Ontario Student Assistance Program, moving from a largely grant-based model to one where three-quarters of aid would be in the form of repayable loans. The ministry, which estimated the cost of OSAP could hit $4.1 billion by 2028-29, explained that the changes would strengthen the long-term sustainability of the program and bring it in line with other provinces. Days later, Premier Ford focused on allegations of misuse, saying he had received thousands of calls along with accounts of students using OSAP funds to purchase luxury items. ""I've heard some nightmare stories ... about kids going out there buying fancy watches and cologne and not needing it,"" he said. ""That doesn't fly with the taxpayers."" Quinn later told the Globe and Mail that over the past two years, the ministry has been investigating numerous cases of alleged fraud and misuse of OSAP funds, with 902 investigations last year, up from 862 the year before. At the time, the minister's office did not provide additional details on the outcomes of those investigations but provided the Globe with links to online videos and posts in which students appeared to claim using OSAP funds for Blue Jays tickets and Ray-Ban sunglasses. ""Any misuse of government funding through a program like OSAP is concerning because you want that financial assistance to go to students who need it the most,"" says New Democrat MPP Peggy Sattler, her party's critic for colleges and universities. But, she posited, ""Why is the premier making these suggestions that abuse of OSAP is rampant ... this data does not support that. ""They're using these allegations as a way to justify gutting the financial assistance that so many low and moderate-income students in Ontario rely on to be able to fund their post-secondary education."" Data obtained by the Star shows that there were 909 cases investigated by the province in 2025; 751 were closed and 151 remain open. In 2024, there were 879 investigations; 39 remain open. Over those two years, 530 cases were deemed the most egregious, and, according to the ministry, would have required immediate repayment of ineligible funds and restricted access to OSAP until the debt was repaid. Penalties in other cases vary depending on the seriousness and can include a hold on funding, a warning, an adjustment to entitlement and a requirement to repay overpayments. The ministry draws a clear line between misuse, misrepresentation, and fraud with only the latter constituting a criminal offence and the focus of police investigations, of which none were reported. The documents note that OSAP investigations are becoming increasingly complex, particularly in verifying the identity and eligibility of applicants with complicated immigration or residency status. They also point to challenges created by fully online applications and learning, along with the use of AI and other digital tools to alter or forge documents, as well as broader systemic pressures including comprehension barriers and predatory recruitment targeting vulnerable applicants. Giacoboni told the Star that the changes to the OSAP framework, which was ""no longer sustainable due to the federal government's decision to remove grant eligibility from students at private career colleges, coupled with increased program uptake,"" are intended to ensure the province can ""keep supporting our students' investment for many years to come."" However, Cyrielle Ngeleka, chairperson of the Canadian Federation of Students-Ontario, told the Star that regardless of the data, ""there is no situation that warrants sweeping cuts to grants and a broader shift towards loans, and it is very difficult to justify these changes as being about fraud prevention or misuse. ""What students are seeing is a government using a very limited number of cases to rationalize broader austerity measures in post-secondary education. The impact of these decisions are being felt by ordinary students who are now expected to graduate with deeper debt in a province where employment is not guaranteed. These policy changes place a heavy financial burden back onto students.""

title: New details emerge in allegations against Toronto city councillor Parthi Kandavel
body: A Toronto city councillor's dealings with developers appear to be the focus of the police investigation into allegations against him. The Ontario Provincial Police probe into Coun. Parthi Kandavel was prompted by a watchdog complaint from the owners of a development in his Scarborough Southwest ward, according to the company's lawyer, while sources allege he sought money in exchange for allowing a different project in the area to go ahead. In an email to the Star on Monday, John J. Pirie, a partner at Baker Mc Kenzie LLP, said a representative of his clients, Kennedy Road Holdings Ltd., made a complaint against the councillor to Toronto's integrity commissioner. According to Pirie, the commissioner then referred the matter to the Toronto police, without the input of his clients. The company owns a property at 708-712 Kennedy Road, and has been seeking permission to replace two midrise rental buildings at the site with a pair of highrises. Pirie declined to provide details of the complaint, but stressed that the company ""is not under investigation."" Integrity Commissioner Paul Muldoon couldn't immediately be reached for comment Monday. His office previously told the Star it ""does not routinely confirm or deny whether he has received a complaint."" Kandavel denies wrongdoing Meanwhile, a source with knowledge of another development in Scarborough Southwest said they were left with the impression that Kandavel wanted a significant financial payment from the proponents to allow the project to proceed. A second source confirmed hearing the same account. The OPP has reached out regarding the development, according to the first source. In a statement in response to the allegations, Kandavel said: ""There has been no wrongdoing on my part, which I'm confident the OPP investigation will conclude."" ""I am still learning about these allegations, and it is not lost on me that they've come during the election period. Regardless, my intention is to respect the process and let the OPP complete their work."" Councillor announced investigation on social media The councillor announced in a social media post on Sunday that he was under investigation by the OPP. He didn't provide details of the allegations, and said news of the investigation had taken him by surprise when he learned about it Friday afternoon. He wrote in the post that he had ""worked hard to earn the trust of the people of Scarborough Southwest, which I take seriously. I've strived to maintain the highest standards of ethics and integrity and will address any allegations that suggest otherwise."" The Toronto Police Service received the initial complaint about the councillor but referred it to the OPP ""to avoid any perceived conflict of interest,"" TPS spokesperson Stephanie Sayer said Monday. City councillors sit on the Toronto Police Service Board and vote on its annual budget. Neither the TPS nor OPP has said who filed the complaint, or detailed the allegations against Kandavel. The forces didn't immediately return a request for confirmation Monday night about who made the complaint. OPP sought information on Kennedy Road development The Star reported on Sunday that, according to one source, as part of its probe, the OPP had sought information about the development at 708-712 Kennedy Road. In 2022, the owners of the property submitted a request for a zoning bylaw amendment to demolish the existing 98 rental units at the site and redevelop it. A revised submission the company made in 2024 proposed two residential towers of 21 and 42 stories, for a total of 682 units, including 98 rental replacements. The owners appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal in May 2024 after council failed to make a decision within the required timelines. In June 2025, the owners submitted a settlement offer to resolve the OLT appeal, which reduced the height of the highest tower by four stories. That month, city solicitor Wendy Walberg submitted advice to council about the settlement. While the advice was confidential, according to one source with knowledge of her report, she recommended council accept the settlement, which included a concession from the owners to provide 1,500 square feet of non-residential uses. Kandavel moved a motion amending her advice however, requesting that the city approve the settlement but require 4,000 square feet. Kandavel motion amended settlement According to an October 2025 OLT decision, the city and the owners resolved most aspects of the appeal, but continued to disagree on the amount of non-residential space. The owner successfully convinced the tribunal it didn't need to include as much as Kandavel's motion requested, with the tribunal writing that the city hadn't provided evidence for ""why 4000 sq. ft. would be appropriate, how that precise number was good planning, or how exactly the development would have to be changed"" to accommodate it. Kandavel is a former elementary school teacher and Toronto District School Board trustee. He was elected to council in a November 2023 byelection, with about 27 per cent of the vote. Earlier this month his office told the Star he intends to run for re-election this year, but he has yet to sign up for the Oct. 26 contest. Nominations opened May 1. A spokesperson for Mayor Olivia Chow said Monday she wouldn't answer questions about an active investigation, but Toronto residents ""expect every councillor and the mayor to act with integrity."" With files from Mahdis Habibinia and Ben Cohen

title: Less than 1% of OSAP cases flagged as ineligible; Data casts doubt on Ford's claims of abuse as rationale for changes to student aid
body: Ontario data reveals that $13.1 million in financial aid over two years - a small fraction of total disbursements - was wrongly granted to students later found to be ineligible, with no cases referred to police, raising questions about the scale of alleged abuse Premier Doug Ford cited, in part, to justify overhauling OSAP. Last year, $8,332,363 in student assistance was wrongly issued due to ""false or invalid information, incorrect statuses, participation in non-bona fide studies or other discrepancies,"" according to records obtained by the Toronto Star through a freedom-of-information request. In 2024, the amount was $4,719,310. In the fiscal year 2024-25, the government spent $1.7 billion in OSAP grants and $301 million on loans, assisting 473,000 students. Based on these figures and the new data, the payments found to be ineligible represent less than one per cent of total disbursements and number of students affected. (The proportions of ineligible aid may in fact be overstated as the wrongly granted aid covers two whole years as opposed to one fiscal year.) ""Any inappropriate use of OSAP funding is unacceptable,"" Bianca Giacoboni, press secretary to Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn, told the Star on Monday. ""We have a robust framework in place to protect OSAP from fraudulent use, and we are implementing new technology and exploring other avenues to strengthen the program's integrity."" The records requested by the Star did not disclose how much of the funding has been recouped, noting that a ""standard OSAP repayment process"" applies. They note that while some cases may result in defaulted loans that proceed to collections, ""we do not have aggregate numbers based on investigations and do not track this data."" In February, the government, as part of its announcement of a $6.4-billion investment in post-secondary and the lifting of the tuition freeze, said it was revamping the Ontario Student Assistance Program, moving from a largely grant-based model to one where three-quarters of aid would be in the form of repayable loans. The ministry, which estimated the cost of OSAP could hit $4.1 billion by 2028-29, explained that the changes would strengthen the long-term sustainability of the program and bring it in line with other provinces. Days later, Premier Ford focused on allegations of misuse, saying he had received thousands of calls along with accounts of students using OSAP funds to purchase luxury items. ""I've heard some nightmare stories ... about kids going out there buying fancy watches and cologne and not needing it,"" he said. ""That doesn't fly with the taxpayers."" Quinn later told the Globe and Mail that over the past two years, the ministry has been investigating numerous cases of alleged fraud and misuse of OSAP funds, with 902 investigations last year, up from 862 the year before. At the time, the minister's office did not provide additional details on the outcomes of those investigations but provided the Globe with links to online videos and posts in which students appeared to claim using OSAP funds for Blue Jays tickets and Ray-Ban sunglasses. ""Any misuse of government funding through a program like OSAP is concerning because you want that financial assistance to go to students who need it the most,"" said New Democrat MPP Peggy Sattler, her party's critic for colleges and universities. But, she posited, ""Why is the premier making these suggestions that abuse of OSAP is rampant ... this data does not support that. ""They're using these allegations as a way to justify gutting the financial assistance that so many low- and moderate-income students in Ontario rely on to be able to fund their post-secondary education."" Data obtained by the Star shows there were 909 cases investigated by the province in 2025; 751 were closed and 151 remain open. In 2024, there were 879 investigations; 39 remain open. Over those two years, 530 cases were deemed the most egregious, and, according to the ministry, would have required immediate repayment of ineligible funds and restricted access to OSAP until the debt was repaid. Penalties in other cases vary depending on the seriousness and can include a hold on funding, a warning, an adjustment to entitlement and a requirement to repay overpayments. The ministry draws a clear line between misuse, misrepresentation and fraud with only the latter constituting a criminal offence and the focus of police investigations, of which none were reported. The documents note that OSAP investigations are becoming increasingly complex, particularly in verifying the identity and eligibility of applicants with complicated immigration or residency status. They also point to challenges created by fully online applications and learning, along with the use of AI and other digital tools to alter or forge documents, as well as broader systemic pressures including comprehension barriers and predatory recruitment targeting vulnerable applicants. Giacoboni told the Star that the changes to the OSAP framework, which was ""no longer sustainable due to the federal government's decision to remove grant eligibility from students at private career colleges, coupled with increased program uptake,"" are intended to ensure the province can ""keep supporting our students' investment for many years to come."" However, Cyrielle Ngeleka, chairperson of the Canadian Federation of Students-Ontario, told the Star that regardless of the data, ""there is no situation that warrants sweeping cuts to grants and a broader shift toward loans, and it is very difficult to justify these changes as being about fraud prevention or misuse. ""What students are seeing is a government using a very limited number of cases to rationalize broader austerity measures in post-secondary education. The impact of these decisions are being felt by ordinary students who are now expected to graduate with deeper debt in a province where employment is not guaranteed. These policy changes place a heavy financial burden back onto students.""

title: Councillor accused of asking developer for money; Kandavel denies wrongdoing as OPP probe interactions with local builder
body: A Toronto city councillor's dealings with developers appear to be the focus of the police investigation into allegations against him. The Ontario Provincial Police probe into Coun. Parthi Kandavel was prompted by a watchdog complaint from the owners of a development in his Scarborough Southwest ward, according to the company's lawyer, while sources allege he sought money in exchange for allowing a different project in the area to go ahead. In an email to the Star on Monday, John J. Pirie, a partner at Baker Mc Kenzie LLP, said a representative of his clients, Kennedy Road Holdings Ltd., made a complaintagainst the councillor to Toronto's integrity commissioner. According to Pirie, the commissioner then referred the matter to the Toronto police, without the input of his clients. The company owns a property at 708-712 Kennedy Road, and has been seeking permission to replace two midrise rental buildings at the site with a pair of highrises. Pirie declined to provide details of the complaint, but stressed that the company ""is not under investigation."" Integrity Commissioner Paul Muldoon couldn't immediately be reached for comment Monday. His office previously told the Star it ""does not routinely confirm or deny whether he has received a complaint."" Meanwhile, a source with knowledge of another development in Scarborough Southwest said they were left with the impression that Kandavel wanted a significant financial payment from the proponents to allow the project to proceed. A second source confirmed hearing the same account. The OPP has reached out regarding the development, according to the first source. In a statement in response to the allegations, Kandavel said: ""There has been no wrongdoing on my part, which I'm confident the OPP investigation will conclude."" ""I am still learning about these allegations, and it is not lost on me that they've come during the election period. Regardless, my intention is to respect the process and let the OPP complete their work."" The councillor announced in a social media post on Sunday that he was under investigation by the OPP. He didn't provide details of the allegations, and said news of the investigation had taken him by surprise when he learned about it Friday afternoon. He wrote in the post that he had ""worked hard to earn the trust of the people of Scarborough Southwest, which I take seriously. I've strived to maintain the highest standards of ethics and integrity and will address any allegations that suggest otherwise."" The Toronto Police Service received the initial complaint about the councillor but referred it to the OPP ""to avoid any perceived conflict of interest,"" TPS spokesperson Stephanie Sayer said Monday. City councillors sit on the Toronto Police Service Board and vote on its annual budget. Neither the TPS nor OPP has said who filed the complaint, or detailed the allegations against Kandavel. The forces didn't immediately return a request for confirmation Monday night about who made the complaint. The Star reported on Sunday that, according to one source, as part of its probe, the OPP had sought information about the development at 708-712 Kennedy Road. In 2022, the owners of the property submitted a request for a zoning bylaw amendment to demolish the existing 98 rental units at the site and redevelop it. A revised submission the company made in 2024 proposed two residential towers of 21 and 42 stories, for a total of 682 units, including 98 rental replacements. The owners appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal in May 2024 after council failed to make a decision within the required timelines. In June 2025, the owners submitted a settlement offer to resolve the OLT appeal, which reduced the height of the highest tower by four stories. That month, city solicitor Wendy Walberg submitted advice to council about the settlement. While the advice was confidential, according to one source with knowledge of her report, she recommended council accept the settlement, which included a concession from the owners to provide 1,500 square feet of non-residential uses. Kandavel moved a motion amending her advice however, requesting that the city approve the settlement but require 4,000 square feet. According to an October 2025 OLT decision, the city and the owners resolved most aspects of the appeal, but continued to disagree on the amount of non-residential space. The owner successfully convinced the tribunal it didn't need to include as much as Kandavel's motion requested, with the tribunal writing that the city hadn't provided evidence for ""why 4000 sq. ft. would be appropriate, how that precise number was good planning, or how exactly the development would have to be changed"" to accommodate it. Kandavel is a former elementary school teacher and Toronto District School Board trustee. He was elected to council in a November 2023 byelection, with about 27 per cent of the vote. Earlier this month his office told the Star he intends to run for re-election this year, but he has yet to sign up for the Oct. 26 contest. Nominations opened May 1. A spokesperson for Mayor Olivia Chow said Monday she wouldn't answer questions about an active investigation, but Toronto residents ""expect every councillor and the mayor to act with integrity."" With files from Mahdis Habibinia and Ben Cohen

title: Ohio man used social media to exploit 10-year-old in Manitoba, police say
body: A man in the United States has been charged with sexual exploitation and possessing child pornography in relation to a 10-year-old girl in Manitoba. RCMP say they received a report in December that the girl had been lured online and had been convinced to send explicit photos of herself via a social media platform. They say the male had also sent explicit photos to the girl. Authorities in the United States were alerted, searched a home in Wadsworth, Ohio, and in February arrested a 32-year-old suspect who remains in custody there. RCMP say it's important for parents to set rules for kids, such as limiting time spent online. Federal Culture Minister Marc Miller said last month the government is “very seriously” considering a social media ban for kids, and Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew has said his government will move on the idea for those under 16. This report by The Canadian Press was first published May 11, 2026

title: 'Numerous failure controls' and 'non-compliance' - what the audit of Conestoga College found that prompted the province to take it over
body: Conestoga College handed out pay raises with no justification, awarded contracts to higher bidders without explanation, allowed an executive to take part in recruiting their daughter into a management position, and had such poor oversight of procurements and purchase orders that one for $11,000 was recorded at $126 billion - and no one noticed. These are among the damning details contained in a recent, confidential two-part audit of the Kitchener-area college that rates the school as ""high"" risk, according to executive summaries obtained by the Star. The provincial auditors also recommend the college ""recalculate"" a controversial retirement package for former long-time president John Tibbits - estimated at around $4 million - and ""obtain legal advice to assess whether an overpayment occurred and determine appropriate remediation."" The auditors' findings, submitted to the government in January and April, prompted Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn last week to fire the board of governors and appoint a supervisor to run the school. While the college has rules around expenses and procurements, ""as well as a board of governors with defined roles ... our audit identified pervasive non-compliance with (public sector) requirements and Conestoga policies,"" one of the summaries states. "" ... Our audit identified numerous control failures that collectively diminish transparency to stakeholders, weaken the college's ability to demonstrate prudent stewardship and value for money, and increase the risk for fraud."" Phase two ""found that Conestoga has significant control weaknesses in executive compensation governance, hiring practices, and related oversight processes,"" and ""significant non-compliance"" with public sector salary laws, with auditors blaming the ""most significant issues"" on negligent oversight by senior leaders and the board of governors. Last Thursday, in a first for Ontario, the government sacked the college's board and appointed Linda Franklin, the former long-time president and CEO of Colleges Ontario, to be its administrator. Quinn has told reporters that Tibbits' 55 per cent salary increase over two years, hitting a high of $636,000 - making him the highest paid in the sector - was ""egregious"" and prompted the audit, which then uncovered numerous areas of concern. Conestoga had come under heavy criticism for its massive growth in international students in recent years, and was blamed in part for the federal government cutting back on its numbers; at one point, the college had the most foreign students of any post-secondary institution in the country. The audit notes that in 2023-24, the college had a surplus of $251 million, and a $121 million surplus in 2024-25 - but amid a 62 per cent drop in international students, it was projecting a deficit this school year, and it warns that colleges in general are grappling with reductions in revenue that could ""(create) potential fiscal exposure for the province."" Conestoga has also implemented the deepest job cuts out of all the Ontario colleges, with about 550 layoffs in the last year alone, and the local union estimates a total of 2,700 losses in the past couple of years. The auditors' findings touch on several areas, and they note lax controls over purchase orders, including one valued at $11,000 recorded as $126 billion and another valued at $15,000 recorded as $261 million. ""Both errors remained uncorrected and open at the time of our audit, indicating significant weaknesses in purchase order review and approval processes,"" one audit summary states. ""This deficiency increases the risk of overpayments to vendors, spending beyond approved limits,"" plus ""heightened exposure to fraud or misappropriations due to the lack of effective oversight."" (The orders were corrected after the provincial auditors pointed them out.) In procurements, the college provided ""no documented rationale for higher-priced vendor selection, as high was $57,240 compared to the lowest bid of $45,000,"" the auditors said, and in one case, work began before a contract was in place. As for travel and food expenses by senior staffers, pre-approvals were missing, ""inconsistent, retroactive and undocumented,"" along with ""selection of premium accommodations without required approvals and supporting documentation,"" including a $23,000 trip to Italy. They also found prohibited claims for alcohol, including a $1,300 dinner for Conestoga executives, where drinks comprised about half the bill. On the job front, they found candidates were sourced ""through informal referrals,"" an executive who didn't declare a conflict in their daughter's recruitment and eventual hiring, and urged the college to ""implement a formal recruitment process that includes public postings, structured evaluation criteria, and documented rationale for all selection decisions."" In some cases, lower-scoring applicants were hired without explanation. In its response, the college agreed to the auditors' recommendations in all areas, including tightening procurement and purchasing, and improving transparency and documentation around hirings, promotions and pay raises. ""Management acknowledges (government auditor) recommendations and has committed to the following action plans: Conestoga should enforce mandatory written pre-approvals, prohibit retroactive approvals, and strengthen documentation standards for travel and hospitality expenses ... and agrees that strengthening controls around travel and hospitality expenditures will enhance compliance, transparency, and financial stewardship,"" states the college's response. The auditors also found salary and termination payments went beyond what's allowed, and that executives were given pay hikes without proper proof that the extra pay was necessary, and estimated the college spent about $1 million over six years in raises for executives alone, despite a provincial freeze on wage hikes. As for Tibbits, auditors ""identified two postfreeze increases to the president's non-salary compensation terms, a retirement allowance from 12 to 24 months, and a vacation carry-forward from a 10-day maximum to 196 banked days."" Tibbits retired suddenly in January, and his package was voted on by the board despite members saying they were not provided any particulars; last week, the province said the former president's payout was equal to 83 times his monthly salary. While recommending seeking legal advice, the auditors said ""payments made under the president's retirement agreement at the end of employment exceeded the limits established in the executive compensation framework, and the college's calculation may have also overstated the retirement allowance. These conditions created significant compliance and financial exposure, including the potential for overpayments equal to at a minimum approximately five years of salary."" When asked if the college can recoup any of the payout, Quinn told reporters at Queen's Park last week that ""we're looking into all options to see if we can bring that money back where it should be with the students."" The minister has said he believes Conestoga is an outlier, though the auditors do say there are lessons to be learned for all public sector organizations ""to help reinforce expectations for strong governance and effective internal controls.""

title: Need a virtual health care provider? It’s one reason today’s CAA is newer, better
body: Personal finance and travel expert at moneywehave.com. He was previously affiliated with CAA and Bank of Montreal but currently has no relationship with either brand. The Canadian Automobile Association has a reputation for being the membership your parents relied on – maps in the glove box, guidebooks for road trips and a tow truck when you needed it. I haven’t been a CAA member for almost 20 years, thanks to free roadside coverage from one of my credit cards. But after taking another look, I was stunned at how much has changed. CAA has reinvented itself with benefits beyond towing, offering real-world value that most credit card issuers haven’t caught up to. Rather than offering airport lounge access, which has been the most popular and overrated credit card benefit for years, CAA has become more practical. While roadside assistance remains a core perk, all members also have access to doctors and nurses through Maple, a virtual health care provider that’s available 24/7. After creating an account, just open the Maple app, share your symptoms and within minutes, you’re talking to a health care professional. They can diagnose issues, write prescriptions, order tests and make referrals to specialists. Prescriptions can be sent to your pharmacy or delivered right to you. With an estimated six million Canadians lacking a family doctor – and many others waiting days or weeks for appointments with their regular doctor – virtual care isn’t a nice-tohave, it can be a lifeline. Getting quick access to a doctor means people can get the medication they need fast without dragging themselves into work sick, spreading germs or adding to already packed clinics and emergency rooms meant for urgent cases. CAA isn’t the only one recognizing the value of virtual care. The BMO Ascend World Elite Business Mastercard also includes five free Maple visits each year, with a $149 annual fee. When you stack up the costs, the value is more obvious. Maple’s unlimited family plan, which covers your spouse and dependants under age 18, costs $85 a month and can be paused at any time. CAA gives you access to the same virtual care at a fraction of the cost. A Premier Membership is $151 a year for unlimited Maple consults. That’s less than two months of Maple on its own. Plus Members ($121 a year) get five consults, while Basic ($77 a year) and Everyday ($30 a year) Members get one each. Even if you don’t drive and have no need for roadside assistance, there’s a clear case to be made that a membership is worth getting for the health care access alone, but that’s not the only innovative benefit of interest. All CAA Members get access to free cybersecurity education powered by cybercon IQ. This perk might not grab everyone’s attention, but with Canadians losing more than $700million to fraud last year, having this tool is more relevant than ever. Cybercon IQ starts out by personalizing your risk profile with a quick questionnaire. From there, it gives you tailored tips on avoiding scams, strengthening passwords and protecting your financial information based on the threats you’re most likely to fall for. Despite all the new perks, CAA hasn’t lost sight of its roots. Roadside assistance is still the backbone of the membership, but even that’s been refreshed with Bike Assist. If your bicycle breaks down and can’t be fixed on the spot, CAA will pick you and your bike up and get you to where you need to go. For years, travel cards have relied on the same predictable perks while consumer expectations have moved on. People want benefits that make their lives easier, not just their airport layovers. If credit card providers want to stay competitive, they need perks that deliver real, immediate value. CAA is already showing what that looks like. It’s taken a legacy benefit and layered on perks that solve everyday problems Canadians face right now. If you stepped away from the program, it might be time to take another look.

title: Conestoga audit raised red flags over 'significant non-compliance'

These are among the damning details contained in a recent, confidential two-part audit of the Kitchener-area college that rates the school as ""high"" risk, according to executive summaries obtained by the Star. The provincial auditors also recommend the college ""recalculate"" a controversial retirement package for former longtime president John Tibbits - estimated at around $4 million - and ""obtain legal advice to assess whether an overpayment occurred and determine appropriate remediation."" The auditors' findings, submitted to the government in January and April, prompted Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn last week to fire the board of governors and appoint a supervisor to run the school. While the college has rules around expenses and procurements, ""as well as a board of governors with defined roles ... our audit identified pervasive non-compliance with (public sector) requirements and Conestoga policies,"" one of the summaries states. "" ... Our audit identified numerous control failures that collectively diminish transparency to stakeholders, weaken the college's ability to demonstrate prudent stewardship and value for money, and increase the risk for fraud."" Phase two ""found that Conestoga has significant control weaknesses in executive compensation governance, hiring practices, and related oversight processes,"" and ""significant non-compliance"" with public sector salary laws, with auditors blaming the ""most significant issues"" on negligent oversight by senior leaders and the board of governors. Last Thursday, in a first for Ontario, the government sacked the college's board and appointed Linda Franklin, the former longtime president and CEO of Colleges Ontario, to be its administrator. Quinn has told reporters that Tibbits' 55 per cent salary increase over two years, hitting a high of $636,000 - making him the highest paid in the sector - was ""egregious"" and prompted the audit, which then uncovered numerous areas of concern. The auditors' findings touch on several areas, and they note lax controls over purchase orders, including one valued at $11,000 recorded as $126 billion and another valued at $15,000 recorded as $261 million. ""Both errors remained uncorrected and open at the time of our audit, indicating significant weaknesses in purchase order review and approval processes,"" one audit summary states. ""This deficiency increases the risk of overpayments to vendors, spending beyond approved limits,"" plus ""heightened exposure to fraud or misappropriations due to the lack of effective oversight."" (The orders were corrected after the provincial auditors pointed them out.) In procurements, the college provided ""no documented rationale for higher-priced vendor selection, as high was $57,240 compared to the lowest bid of $45,000,"" the auditors said, and in one case, work began before a contract was in place. While recommending seeking legal advice, the auditors said ""payments made under the president's retirement agreement at the end of employment exceeded the limits established in the executive compensation framework, and the college's calculation may have also overstated the retirement allowance. These conditions created significant compliance and financial exposure, including the potential for overpayments equal to at a minimum approximately five years of salary.""

title: Book excerpt: The complicated legacy of Otto Schaefer and Canada's Indigenous people
body: From the 1950s to the 1970s, a doctor educated under and possibly indoctrinated by the Nazis wielded tremendous authority over Canadian Indigenous people and their health care. ""Otto Schaefer had a very interesting history, which he tried very hard to cover up,"" the late writer Elaine Dewar observed. ""He studied under the leaders of Hitler's hygiene program, which was their science of race."" And he had a passion for studying the Inuit. What about caring for them? That, as her new posthumously published book ""Oblivious"" suggests, is a more complicated question. When he arrived in Aklavik, NWT., by plane in January 1953, dressed in European clothes that were next to useless in the -45 C weather, he ran to get out of the cold. He was a fast-moving small man, and the Inuit who saw him dash for cover gave him a nickname: shik shik - ground squirrel. Two years later, he and his family were posted to Pangnirtung, on the east side of Baffin Island, in what is now Nunavut. This was where he'd always wanted to be. Apparently, he and his wife absolutely loved their time there, though by then she had two children to care for, and he was often away with his guide and dog team taking care of people scattered around the island. Their little house was not up to the weather and frost would bloom all over the interior walls. Two years later he was posted to Whitehorse. He began to publish about the Indigenous people he cared for in 1957, after he left Pangnirtung. He referred to the Inuit as Eskimos, though he must have known that was not what they called themselves: he described how his Inuk guide refused to speak to him in English so he had to learn Inuktitut. He displayed the same combination of admiration and disgust I'd seen in earlier papers by other doctors who'd studied the Inuit and northern First Nations people. He described delivering babies in smoky tents without much more than an oil lamp for light. He wrote of a medicine woman who dealt with difficult deliveries involving recalcitrant placentas by reaching into the patient's uterus and scraping the placenta off the uterine wall with her bare hands. He described the fingernails on those hands as blackened with dirt, but the woman assured him she bit her nails off before reaching inside her patient. But he also described medical methods used by Indigenous people that worked better than the ones he employed. Using spruce gum to close a nasty wound, for example, worked better than his sutures. These early articles were rife with the racist tropes of the period and hinted that he'd bought into Hitler's version of race theory. Hitler had insisted that the original Aryans from whom Germans were said to descend, who invented all of civilization, were from somewhere in the far north and west - some place like Iceland or possibly the Eastern Arctic - that the ancients called Thule. Schaefer certainly believed in the existence of racial types. He also believed that civilization was destroying the noble savages of the North. After his time in Whitehorse, he went back to Edmonton and qualified as an internal medicine specialist. At the Charles Camsell Indian Hospital, he focused on the North, doing various experiments and studies. He sometimes worked on his own, sometimes with others such as Jack Hildes, a doctor whom he'd met on the medical survey ship C.D. Howe and asked for help getting the articles he wrote into publishable shape. By 1964 when Schaefer became director of Health and Welfare's Northern Research Medical Unit, he was convinced that the imposition of southern lifestyles was destroying the health of the Inuit. This was a theme he wrote about for years. By 1968 he was both a part of and the facilitator for the International Biological Program's Project D experiments on human adaptability in the North. Some 450 Inuit people of Igloolik and about 160 more from Hall Beach were roped into Project D as study subjects over the course of six years, everyone from babies to school children to the most elderly. From what I could tell from the papers and reports I reviewed, all the experiments done for Project D in Igloolik and Hall Beach were unethical: consent was not informed, nor was it given by individuals, and because the federal government which funded the project also provided housing, schooling, and medical care to the community, it was coercive. As I learned to my surprise working through his documents, Schaefer and Hildes had not published some important results of their research for the IBP in a timely way. As part of the medical survey they did of all the inhabitants of Igloolik, Schaefer and Hildes collected hair and blood samples and tested them for mercury and cadmium. Some contained high levels of both, which have serious neurological impacts. The deleterious impact of methylmercury was in the news at the time. The Indigenous population of Grassy Narrows First Nation and the Whitedog and Islington bands in Ontario were exposed to methylmercury in the English and Wabigoon River systems, dumped by a paper company in Dryden in 1962. The methylmercury bioaccumulated up the food chain into the fish they relied on, and some displayed early signs of Minamata disease, a severe neurological condition. Those facts had become public while the IBP experiments were conducted. My husband Stephen helped reveal them on CTV's ""W5,"" which is no doubt why Schaefer and Hildes collected the hair samples in Igloolik. Yet that information was not included in the first group of papers Schaefer and Hildes published on Project D. Letters show that Schaefer's colleagues at Health and Welfare at first thought the problem stemmed from industrial pollution drifting around the North. Then they came to believe that cadmium and mercury had bioaccumulated naturally in seal livers and trout. Some at Health and Welfare wanted to warn the Inuit to stop eating these foods. Schaefer argued against it: he feared that would exacerbate their already poor nutritional condition. The Inuit were very careful about how they ate animals with known parasites, like walrus and fish, he said. The internal argument continued for years. And it stayed internal. In 1977, Paul Grescoe reported on the disastrous health circumstances of Indigenous people. By then methylmercury poisoning had also been discovered in Cree people in northern Quebec. But it wasn't the governments of Canada or Quebec that informed the public. It was neurologist Dr André Barbeau, director of the Clinical Research Institute of Montreal. He told Grescoe that knowledge of methylmercury poisoning of Native people was treated by government ""as a state secret."" Telling the public through an academic journal that the Inuit in Igloolik had been exposed to mercury and cadmium - even if from a natural source - would have brought a lot of unwelcome media attention to the federal government. The Grassy Narrows situation caused a significant fuss, but federal politicians could brush it aside as a provincial environmental problem. But cadmium and mercury pollution in the North fell under federal responsibility and would have caused a ruckus that politicians would certainly have wanted to smother. In January 1977, for an article on the women's movement, I'd interviewed Marc Lalonde, who was then the minister of the status of women but also minister of health and welfare. After the interview, as I was packing up my notebooks to leave, his political assistant leaned in and whispered, ""The minister would like to have lunch with you."" ""I'm sorry,"" I said. ""Thank you for the invitation, but I have another appointment."" I walked from his inner office to the outer office. The outer office was jammed with reporters who wanted to ask the minister what he knew and when he knew that arsenic from the Giant Mine outside Yellowknife had contaminated Indigenous children and mine workers and infiltrated the sediments of Great Slave Lake. The National Indian Brotherhood and the steelworkers union had done independent tests, which showed the contamination was very significant. A government study in 1975 had also shown arsenic contamination in Indigenous children near the mine, but Lalonde downplayed those results to the point of suppression. I concluded I was asked to lunch to keep him out of the line of fire. In 1976, Schaefer, like Jack Hildes later was inducted into the Order of Canada. After reading his correspondence on mercury and cadmium, I began to wonder if Schaefer received the honour because he'd kept his mouth shut in public about what they found in the hair of people from Igloolik and Hall Beach. That March, Schaefer agitated to maintain the Camsell as a segregated treatment centre, even as the federal government took steps to shut it down . I found internal letters he wrote protesting the government's plan. It seemed to me clear evidence that Schaefer was worried that he'd lose access to a patient population he wanted to study. I read file after file of the reports he'd compiled from autopsies and from the studies he did on the northern Indigenous people in his care - files that frequently included names and details of the medical conditions his subjects suffered from. Some of the resulting papers, published in journals, included images of those patients' faces. He should not have used the medical information he gathered for those studies without getting informed consent from his patients. Even if he got it, those studies would still have been ethically dicey because he was working for the government that ran their lives. And yet I also read clippings of the many articles he wrote to local newspapers, advocating on behalf of Indigenous people who by the 1960s, he claimed, were suffering more from alcohol and accidents than from TB and other infectious diseases. In the 1980s he'd also written letters protesting the collapse of a clinical trial , to test a flu vaccine called Praxis . ""Otto Schaefer had a very interesting history, which he tried very hard to cover up,"" the late writer Elaine Dewar observed. ""He studied under the leaders of Hitler's hygiene program, which was their science of race."" And he had a passion for studying the Inuit. What about caring for them? When he arrived in Aklavik, NWT., by plane in January 1953, dressed in European clothes that were next to useless in the -45 C weather, he ran to get out of the cold. He was a fast-moving small man, and the Inuit who saw him dash for cover gave him a nickname: shik shik - ground squirrel. Two years later, he and his family were posted to Pangnirtung, on the east side of Baffin Island, in what is now Nunavut. This was where he'd always wanted to be. Apparently, he and his wife absolutely loved their time there, though by then she had two children to care for, and he was often away with his guide and dog team taking care of people scattered around the island. Their little house was not up to the weather and frost would bloom all over the interior walls. Two years later he was posted to Whitehorse. He began to publish about the Indigenous people he cared for in 1957, after he left Pangnirtung. He referred to the Inuit as Eskimos, though he must have known that was not what they called themselves: he described how his Inuk guide refused to speak to him in English so he had to learn Inuktitut. He displayed the same combination of admiration and disgust I'd seen in earlier papers by other doctors who'd studied the Inuit and northern First Nations people. He described delivering babies in smoky tents without much more than an oil lamp for light. He wrote of a medicine woman who dealt with difficult deliveries involving recalcitrant placentas by reaching into the patient's uterus and scraping the placenta off the uterine wall with her bare hands. He described the fingernails on those hands as blackened with dirt, but the woman assured him she bit her nails off before reaching inside her patient. But he also described medical methods used by Indigenous people that worked better than the ones he employed. Using spruce gum to close a nasty wound, for example, worked better than his sutures. These early articles were rife with the racist tropes of the period and hinted that he'd bought into Hitler's version of race theory. Hitler had insisted that the original Aryans from whom Germans were said to descend, who invented all of civilization, were from somewhere in the far north and west - some place like Iceland or possibly the Eastern Arctic - that the ancients called Thule. Schaefer certainly believed in the existence of racial types. He also believed that civilization was destroying the noble savages of the North. After his time in Whitehorse, he went back to Edmonton and qualified as an internal medicine specialist. At the Charles Camsell Indian Hospital, he focused on the North, doing various experiments and studies. He sometimes worked on his own, sometimes with others such as Jack Hildes, a doctor whom he'd met on the medical survey ship C.D. Howe and asked for help getting the articles he wrote into publishable shape. By 1964 when Schaefer became director of Health and Welfare's Northern Research Medical Unit, he was convinced that the imposition of southern lifestyles was destroying the health of the Inuit. This was a theme he wrote about for years. By 1968 he was both a part of and the facilitator for the International Biological Program's Project D experiments on human adaptability in the North. Some 450 Inuit people of Igloolik and about 160 more from Hall Beach were roped into Project D as study subjects over the course of six years, everyone from babies to school children to the most elderly. From what I could tell from the papers and reports I reviewed, all the experiments done for Project D in Igloolik and Hall Beach were unethical: consent was not informed, nor was it given by individuals, and because the federal government which funded the project also provided housing, schooling, and medical care to the community, it was coercive. As part of the medical survey they did of all the inhabitants of Igloolik, Schaefer and Hildes collected hair and blood samples and tested them for mercury and cadmium. Some contained high levels of both, which have serious neurological impacts. The deleterious impact of methylmercury was in the news at the time. The Indigenous population of Grassy Narrows First Nation and the Whitedog and Islington bands in Ontario were exposed to methylmercury in the English and Wabigoon River systems, dumped by a paper company in Dryden in 1962. The Inuit were very careful about how they ate animals with known parasites, like walrus and fish, he said. The internal argument continued for years. And it stayed internal. But it wasn't the governments of Canada or Quebec that informed the public. It was neurologist Dr André Barbeau, director of the Clinical Research Institute of Montreal. He told Grescoe that knowledge of methylmercury poisoning of Native people was treated by government ""as a state secret."" Telling the public through an academic journal that the Inuit in Igloolik had been exposed to mercury and cadmium - even if from a natural source - would have brought a lot of unwelcome media attention to the federal government. The Grassy Narrows situation caused a significant fuss, but federal politicians could brush it aside as a provincial environmental problem. But cadmium and mercury pollution in the North fell under federal responsibility and would have caused a ruckus that politicians would certainly have wanted to smother. title: Newcomer‑heavy Milton reacts to Canada’s tougher oversight of immigration consultants Shazia Nazir
body: Milton residents are reacting to the federal government’s latest move to tighten oversight of immigration and citizenship consultants, saying the changes could offer much‑needed protection for newcomers in one of Canada’s fastest‑growing communities. With thousands of new families arriving in Halton Region each year, many rely on consultants to navigate complex immigration pathways, sponsorship applications and citizenship processes. Some Milton residents say the new rules are overdue. “People in our community have been taken advantage of for years by unlicensed or dishonest consultants,” said Milton resident Sana Qureshi. “Newcomers trust these representatives with their future, so stronger oversight is absolutely necessary.” Others say the changes will help restore confidence in a system that has long struggled with inconsistent standards and limited accountability. The federal government announced this week that it is strengthening protections for people seeking immigration and citizenship advice by expanding the regulatory powers of the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants. The new regulations, unveiled by Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab, will take effect on July 15, 2026. Under the changes, the College will be able to impose stronger penalties on consultants who break the rules and will be required to publish more detailed information on its public register beginning in April 2027. The government says this will help applicants identify legitimate consultants and avoid unauthorized representatives who often operate without oversight. The regulations also introduce new reporting requirements for the College, clarify investigative procedures for misconduct cases and give the minister the authority to appoint someone to take over board duties if the College fails to meet its responsibilities. In addition, the government has established guidelines for the College’s compensation fund, which supports victims who suffer financial losses due to dishonest acts by consultants. Minister Diab said the changes reflect the government’s commitment to protecting people who rely on immigration and citizenship advice. “People looking to build their future in Canada deserve access to honest and reliable immigration and citizenship advice,” she said. “They need to have confidence that our government is taking effective steps to improve integrity. These changes reflect our commitment to protecting applicants from fraud and misconduct, and to supporting a system where consultants are held to high standards.” Kate Lamb, interim president and CEO of the College, said the new regulations will strengthen the tools available to the regulator and help ensure consultants continue to meet the highest professional standards. She said the College looks forward to finalizing supporting by‑laws and working with government partners to ensure the system remains transparent and accountable. In Milton, where immigration continues to drive population growth, residents say the changes could have a direct impact on families navigating the system. “I’ve seen neighbours lose thousands of dollars because they trusted someone who wasn’t even licensed,” said Milton resident Abdul Rahman. “If these rules prevent even one family from going through that, it’s a step in the right direction.” The federal government has been working to reform the sector for several years. The College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants was established in 2021 to regulate the profession, replacing the previous oversight body after widespread concerns about its effectiveness. The College operates independently and is funded entirely through fees paid by licensed consultants. The draft regulations were first published in the Canada Gazette in December 2024, giving consultants, advocacy groups and legal experts an opportunity to provide feedback before the final rules were approved. Advocates for newcomers say the new measures will not solve every issue but represent meaningful progress. They note that unauthorized consultants, often operating outside Canada, remain a challenge, and that public education is still needed to help applicants identify legitimate representatives. Still, many believe the strengthened regulatory framework will help reduce fraud, improve accountability and give newcomers greater confidence as they navigate the immigration system. With Milton continuing to welcome new families from around the world, residents say the timing of the reforms could not be more relevant.

title: Quebec begins digital health record rollout as projected cost climbs to $2.5B
body: Quebec’s provincewide effort to digitize health records officially began Saturday, and the cost is going to be at least a billion dollars more than expected. Initially estimated at $1.5 billion, the cost to deploy the system across all of Quebec is now evaluated at $2.5 billion. However, some experts warn that even these figures may be conservative. Samer Faraj, of Mc Gill University’s department of social studies of medicine, suggests the final tally could be much higher. “You’re looking at $5 billion of total cost, possibly more, rising quickly and at least a billion dollars of additional costs yearly,"" says Faraj. The Digital Health Record (DHR) rollout begins as a pilot project within two regional health authorities: the CIUSSS du Nord-de-l'Île-de-Montréal and the CIUSSS de la Mauricie-et-du-Centre-du-Québec. Santé Québec officials described Saturday morning’s launch as ""wonderful."" Erika Bially, the agency’s vice-president of information technology, said the system went live without any major technical failures. While Santé Québec had anticipated a higher volume of technical support requests, only 206 tickets had been filed by 2 p.m., more than 80 per cent of which had already been resolved. Administrators from the participating healthy agencies reported a sense of calm and mobilization on hospital floors, saying patient safety and continuity of care were maintained throughout the transition, according to Radio-Canada. The Cadillac of e-health records The digitization's high price tag is partly attributed to the platform the province has selected. Widely regarded as the Cadillac of electronic health records, the Epic system is known for its functionality and its premium price point. In a statement, Santé Québec defends the choice, noting the technology is already a global standard, currently used by over 500,000 doctors in 16 countries. Officials describe the system as a ""robust"" and ""proven"" solution despite the high cost. Beyond the initial setup, Santé Québec has revealed that operating the system in just the first two health authorities will cost $100 million per year, an amount that notably includes salaries for IT support staff, hosting and licensing costs. The public health agency announced the costs on its website Thursday. With 23 regional health authorities in total, the ultimate annual operating cost for the entire province remains unknown. The government is moving forward under the shadow of past IT bungles, such as the Dossier Santé Québec which was declared a failure by the Auditor General in 2011. Premier Christine Fréchette has been adamant that this project will not mirror the more recent auto insurance board transformation chaos. ""There might be bugs, but I assure you, we will not relive another SAAQclic,"" Fréchette stated recently. Digital health records needed, government says The government maintains that the investment in DHR is non-negotiable for a modern health-care system. ""It's a profound transformation of our way of doing things and above all, an improvement for patients and all the network's personnel,” the premier said. According to the government's official rollout plan, the primary benefit for patients is the end of information fragmentation. Once the system is fully operational, users will no longer need to repeat their medical history at every appointment, as clinical data will follow the patient automatically between different facilities. The government argues that the move will ultimately save money by eliminating paper-based inefficiencies and redundant systems, though for now, the focus remains on the massive upfront and recurring costs of the transition. Santé Québec issued a statement Thursday, claiming the DHR will generate at least $120 million in annual savings, mainly by eliminating several legacy systems and current licenses, as well as reducing costs related to archiving and managing paper files. ""In Quebec, within the health and social services network, there are currently more than 400 different systems and over 4,000 different applications,"" argued Health Minister Sonia Bélanger. ""As we integrate what we are doing, we will also divest ourselves of existing contracts, which will give us some breathing room."" WATCH | Some concerned about digital rollout: Click on link. Health-care workers have expressed concerns about the launch, and a Radio-Canada investigation revealed that cybersecurity measures will only be implemented after deployment. In a statement, Santé Québec leadership emphasized that teams, including hundreds of IT workers, are ""ready and mobilized on the ground"" with the agility to make rapid adjustments as bugs emerge. Bélanger admitted on Friday that she had been informed of the operating costs for a long time. Fréchette was also notified after taking office. Guillaume Cliche-Rivard of Québec Solidaire questioned the lack of transparency. ""It is unacceptable from the minister for a project of this scale,” he said. Liberal health critic Monsef Derraji said the situation “smells like a scandal.” He asked: “How much will the operating costs be if the government decides to go provincewide?”

title: UCP welcome back backbencher who was kicked out of caucus By LISA JOHNSON
body: A former backbench member of Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative caucus is back in the fold, a day after standing in the house to apologize for past actions and statements. The caucus, in a statement Thursday, welcomed Scott Sinclair back, more than a year after Mr. Sinclair was booted out for threatening to vote against the budget while accusing the government of not doing enough for his Lesser Slave Lake riding. “Sinclair has spent significant time reflecting on the responsibilities and expectations of government caucus MLAs,” government whip Justin Wright said in the statement. “Additionally, he expressed deep regret for his previous comments and actions and made clear they were the result of a misunderstanding of the Westminster Parliamentary system and misguided advice.” Under the Westminster system, a budget vote is critical business: if a government can’t pass a bill to spend money, it raises a larger question about its legitimacy and ability to govern. Ms. Smith, on social media, added, “I want to thank [Mr. Sinclair] for the sincere effort he has made to reconnect with caucus and rejoin our team.” After being booted out, the rookie legislature member sat on the other side of the aisle in the house as an Independent, refashioning himself into a fierce critic of his former caucus. But on Wednesday, in a prepared speech to the chamber, Mr. Sinclair said upon reflection, he was wrong. He compared politics to hockey, where emotions run high but the collective comes first. “No individual performance, regardless of passion and emotion, wins championships or experiences success like a strong team does,” he told the house. Mr. Sinclair said while he will always stand up for his constituents, he regrets how he did that “at times.” “With time and perspective I’ve come to better understand the responsibility that comes with those decisions in a Westminster system and the impact they have not just on the government but on the people we serve,” he said. “For that I’m sorry.” He also said that a year ago he failed to recognize that the government is making record investments for people, including his own constituents, in northern Alberta. NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said the United Conservatives forced Mr. Sinclair to publicly debase himself before being allowed back, calling it an instructive lesson in how Ms. Smith’s caucus treats people. “They made him give that grovelling apology to the premier today so that he can come back,” Mr. Nenshi told reporters Wednesday. “They have humiliated that guy.” Mr. Sinclair’s time in opposition was punctuated by a series of public statements, attacking the UCP. During that time, he attacked Ms. Smith and the UCP on everything from health care to separatism. He once told the House health care in his constituency was at “rock bottom” while Ms. Smith played “musical chairs” with the system. He called the UCP a “hostile” version of previous Alberta conservative parties and one that needs “to stop blaming Ottawa for everything.” He said the UCP had veered too far into the far right fringe and accused Ms. Smith of transforming it from a mainstream coalition into a “separatist party.” Along with fellow estranged UCP member Peter Guthrie, he sided with the NDP in the House to vote for a judge-led public inquiry into the allegations of corruption in health care spending. By rejoining the UCP, Mr. Sinclair brings the government majority in the house to 48 members. The Opposition NDP has 38 seats, and Peter Guthrie holds one as a Progressive Tory.
