title: Real problem for Ford was politics, not the plane Jaime Watt OPINION Jaime Watt is the Chair and Founder of Navigator Ltd. and a Conservative strategist.
body: Let me be clear: on the underlying question, Doug Ford was right. Every serious executive in this country, every CEO running a national operation, every big-city mayor, every premier who has to be in Thunder Bay in the morning and Windsor by dinner understands the same elementary truth. Time is the one resource you cannot manufacture. And that's why a plane is not a perk. It is a tool. The prime minister has one. The federal cabinet uses it. Major bank CEOs have access to one. Heads of government across the western world have one. The reason is not vanity. The reason is that a leader who spends 11 hours on a commercial flight with a layover at Pearson is not leading. Ontario is the economic engine of Confederation. Its premier runs a government larger, by GDP, than all but a handful of countries. Ford's own stated rationale: that the province is geographically vast, that single-prop aircraft are the grim alternative for northern travel, that a secure aircraft matters when you're flying into hostile Trump-era trade meetings, is not unreasonable. It is, in fact, precisely the case that should have been made to taxpayers before the purchase, not after it. That was the mistake. Not the plane. The ambush. But here's what's important: When Ford realized the politics had turned past the point of recovery, he did exactly the right thing. He killed the decision. The plane went back to Bombardier. The full $28.9 million came back to the province. No loss to the taxpayer. He apologized for how the transaction was rolled out, he refused to apologize for the underlying logic, and he moved on. Total elapsed time from announcement to reversal: two days. He ended the game. I've just written a book on crisis management, and if there is a single lesson drawn from decades of watching leaders either survive their bad days or be destroyed by them, it is this one. When a story turns, you have one job: compress the news cycle. Get ahead of it. Deny it oxygen. The single worst thing a political leader can do when a decision has gone sideways is to defend the indefensible one news day at a time, bleeding credibility in daily increments until the only remaining question is why it took so long to do what was obvious from the start. Think of the leaders who got this right. Think of the ones who didn't. Equifax waited a month to acknowledge its 2017 data breach. By the time executives spoke, the story had already hardened into ""cover-up,"" and they spent years in front of Congress paying for that hesitation. Ticketmaster, more recently, waited so long to disclose a massive hack that the hackers themselves broke the news. Buckingham Palace operated for decades under the ""never complain, never explain"" rule - right up until the former prince Andrew's behaviour around his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein curdled into something the Crown decided they could no longer tolerate as it had become something from which they could not recover. In every case, the leader or institution believed that holding the line was the safer play. In every case, they were dead wrong. The fact is that the modern news cycle does not reward stubbornness. It rewards clarity. A bad decision acknowledged quickly is a one-day story. A bad decision defended becomes a week. A bad decision defended badly becomes a referendum on your judgment itself. Ford, to his credit, saw where the story was going and changed course before the narrative could calcify. Over the weekend, the calls flooded his cellphone. The ""gravy plane"" label was already airborne. The auditor general was about to be asked to investigate. By Sunday, he had agreed to sell. By Wednesday, he confirmed the money was back in the treasury. The oxygen was cut. Make no mistake: There is a political cost to reversing course. Interim Liberal leader John Fraser is already calling him out of touch. Opposition Leader Marit Stiles is pushing for an audit anyway. The penguin line will get quoted for weeks. None of it matters much. The damage from a four-day climbdown is an order of magnitude smaller than the damage from a four-month defence. This is the thing most politicians never learn, and the thing Ford, despite the pundits eye-rolling about his style, has learned better than most of his peers. He governs with the same instinct he campaigns. Read the voter. Respect the voter. When you are offside the voter, stop being offside the voter. Don't explain. Don't litigate. Move. Here's the thing: the premier was right about the substance of the plane. He was wrong about the plane's politics and the communications around it. And when he figured out which of those things mattered more to the people who elected him, he acted on it in a weekend. That is not weakness. That is discipline. Other political leaders, watching from their capitals across the country, should take note. The premier who spent years being caricatured as impulsive just executed a textbook reversal - no money lost, no lingering contract, no dragged-out defence. The jet is back with Bombardier. The story is running out of runway. And the rest of Ontario's agenda, the one that actually matters to the people who elected him, gets to move forward. Doug Ford read the voter - then moved on. That's the story. Jaime Watt is the Chair and Founder of Navigator Ltd. and a Conservative strategist. He is a freelance columnist for the Star.

title: Reporter Carrie Tait named journalist of the year by National Newspaper Association
body: GLOBE STAFF Globe and Mail reporter Carrie Tait, whose dogged pursuit of a spending scandal in Alberta forced her to endure taunts by a cabinet minister and reputational attacks by a self-described political fixer, has been named journalist of the year by the National Newspaper Association. Ms. Tait also won in the politics category and as the lead reporter for a team entry in the investigation category. The Globe won eight categories at Friday night’s National Newspaper Awards, the most in total. Stories receiving recognition included a sustained series tracking how measles has made a comeback in Canada and for reporting from Syria. The Canadian Press won the second-most awards with four. “It was a thrilling evening and everyone at The Globe is delighted to have come out on top with a range of original and important work,” Globe editor-in-chief David Walmsley said. “Awarding Carrie Tait, deservedly, as journalist of the year, the judges rightly said Ms. Tait did not retreat in the face of a campaign of intimidation and threat. That determination, that the truth will come out, is the essence of The Globe and Mail. Brave, independent journalism that stands alone.” In citing Ms. Tait’s work, the NNA judges noted that her coverage of Alberta politics “stood apart as a model of investigative rigour and personal fortitude.” Her reporting did more than chronicle events: it altered the province’s political landscape, triggering real consequences and forcing accountability at the highest levels of government.” Ms. Tait, along with colleagues Tom Cardoso, Alanna Smith, Stephanie Chambers and others, have spent more than a year examining allegations of political interference tied to hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of contracts awarded by the Alberta government to an Edmonton businessman, Sam Mraiche. Premier Danielle Smith and her ministers have maintained that they did nothing wrong. The government dismissed a former health CEO, who first raised the allegations, as incompetent and suggested critics are simply opposed to health reform. The allegations have since prompted investigations by the RCMP – which executed search warrants last month, including at Mr. Mraiche’s company – and the Alberta Auditor-General. title: How international students became unwitting dupes for bank scams By ALEXANDRA POSADZKI
body: The scam started as many scams do, with a phone call from someone impersonating a bank employee. It ended with nearly 300,000 Australian dollars (about $288,000) being transferred out of a Melbourne woman’s bank account and withdrawn from automated banking machines. Australia’s financial intelligence agency included the incident in a 2024 report to highlight a growing problem. After gaining access to the victim’s funds, the scammers transferred the money to 11 different bank accounts, most of which had been opened by international students from India. At the time when the cash was being withdrawn, the students had already returned home – which meant someone else was controlling their bank accounts, the Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre said. The students had, wittingly or unwittingly, become what are known as “money mules” – individuals who move illegally acquired funds on behalf of someone else. Illegally acquired access to bank accounts is becoming a growing problem around the world, as criminal organizations look to move money they have stolen through increasingly pervasive scams. Last November, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) launched a campaign, called “Your Name. Your Responsibility,” to bring awareness to the global phenomenon. Members of organized crime groups have been approaching international students through social-media platforms, messaging apps or in real life, offering between 200 to 500 Australian dollars for the use of their bank accounts, the police agency said. Sometimes the students receive a commission of around 10 per cent of the funds that flow through the account, as well. For cash-strapped students who are studying in expensive countries, it can sound like an easy way to make some money – especially if they’re heading home and not planning to return. Many of them don’t realize they’re laundering money for cross-border scam operations. “We see evidence that that is a persistent risk in our environment as well,” said Aaron Mc Allister, vice-president of fraud threat management at Bank of Nova Scotia. “It can be somebody who’s entirely unwitting, where they believe that they’ve just got this great new work-from-home job, and all they have to do is process payments. But they’re told that as part of the job, they’re processing those payments on their own account, or an account that they’ve been instructed to open,” Mr. Mc Allister said. The RCMP said it has encountered instances in which criminals have influenced international students to open accounts at Canadian banks, then used the accounts to facilitate moneylaundering and fraud. “Students are often targets for money mule recruitment,” Robin Percival, a spokesperson for the RCMP, said in a statement. Sometimes, bank accounts are bought and sold online, in what amounts to a black market. Montreal-based cybercrime research firm Flare Systems Inc. said it identified 4,337 posts offering or requesting verified Canadian accounts during a recent 12-month period. (Verified accounts are those that have had their ownership confirmed, making them less likely to get frozen by the bank than an account that has been stolen.) The vast majority of those posts – 3,828 of them – were on the messaging app Telegram. “It’s increasing year on year,” said Adrian Cheek, a senior cybercrime researcher at Flare. “It’s not just the students who are leaving. It’s also a lucrative market for students who are here to generate extra income.” Stuart Davis, a financial crimes expert who has held roles at three of Canada’s Big Five banks, said the rising prevalence of scams and fraud is driving a growing need for mule accounts. Fraud victims reported more than $704-million in losses to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre last year. Those losses, which are believed to represent just 5 per cent to 10 per cent of all fraud, surpassed the $645-million reported to the agency in 2024. “The mule account business is a revolving-door business, because very seldom can you reuse the same account more than a few times,” said Mr. Davis, president of Surpass Insights Inc., an advisory firm that is focused on anti-money-laundering, fintech and artificial intelligence. “They’re always having to harvest new mule accounts. So, that’s why they prey on the students; that’s why they prey on the vulnerable.” In 2019, a sergeant from the RCMP’s Greater Toronto Area financial crime unit wrote a report that addressed the operations of telephone and cyberenabled scams. The report, which was cited in a 2024 Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada ruling, noted that the masterminds of a “tech scam” that originated from call centres in India often used international students as mules to move fraudulently obtained money. International students are not the only targets for money mule recruitment, which happens on campuses, through social media and even on dating apps. But they are often in need of cash, which can make the offer appealing, and they are sometimes tricked into moving money by fake job ads or promises of immigration assistance. “English is probably the second language. They’re isolated from their support network at home. Australia is a very expensive country and the syndicates are very acutely aware of how young people communicate, so they have very realistic socialmedia advertising,” said acting Superintendent Chris Jessop, who is in charge of the Joint Policing Cybercrime Coordination Centre for the AFP. Jatin Chahal, an Indian citizen studying in Canada who was accused of acting as a money mule in a scam centred around the Canada Revenue Agency in 2020, said he didn’t realize he was involved in criminal activity. “I was in need of money and … I got misleaded,” Mr. Chahal testified, according to a 2021 decision by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada. Mr. Chahal said he believed he was doing a job for a man named Samir. The job involved receiving packages of cash and either handing them off to another individual or transferring them into a U.S. bank account. The tribunal determined that there were reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Chahal was a member of a criminal organization, and issued a deportation order against him. But it said there was insufficient evidence that he’d engaged in the crime of money-laundering. Another student from India, Ravi Shah, said he was seeking job opportunities and permanent residency in Canada when he placed his personal documents inside a package he’d received and mailed it to what he thought was a lawyer’s address in Brampton, Ont. Mr. Shah, who came to Canada in 2019 to study at Fanshawe College in London, Ont., testified that he didn’t look inside the package, which contained $15,000 from a victim of a scam based on Microsoft Corp. technology. He believed the envelope contained sensitive information about other candidates, according to a 2024 decision by the immigration board. “I was told it was confidential, not to open it,” said Mr. Shah, who has been accused of acting as a money mule in the scam. Organized crime groups may use mules to mail cash to various addresses as a way of obfuscating the original source of the funds. The tribunal decided not to deport Mr. Shah, finding that the Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness had “failed to establish on reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Shah is a member of an organized crime group.” Regardless of whether mules are knowingly participating in criminal activity or not, identifying and shutting down their accounts poses a continuing challenge for banks. “It’s pretty persistent and common,” Mr. Davis said. AI may be able to help. The technology has been blamed for enabling fraud, for instance by creating increasingly realistic deep fakes, but it’s also helping financial institutions tackle scams. At Scotiabank, AI is being deployed to detect fraudulent activity, including to identify mule accounts, Mr. Mc Allister said. “We’ve got an in-house team of data scientists that work on developing these types of models to make sure that we’re identifying fraud when it happens,” Mr. Mc Allister said. Scotiabank uses tools such as graph-based machine learning to identify and take down networks of mule accounts, and the bank monitors changes in behaviour that could indicate an account has been co-opted by criminals. The moment when an account goes from making ordinary transactions, such as paying rent or buying groceries, to quickly sending and receiving large sums of money is referred to as a bustout, according to Mark Hines, head of product, fraud at Interac Corp. The financial services industry has been working with predictive modeling to try to spot accounts that are at risk of pivoting to criminal activity, Mr. Hines said. “Trying to find the data that gives you the warning signal, that’s sort of the magic sauce that everyone is looking for right now,” he said. Other banks have systems in place, too. Mathieu Genest, a spokesperson for Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, said the bank has “sophisticated layers of security and monitoring that work effectively to help prevent the fraudulent use of accounts.” The other three Big Five Canadian banks declined to comment. In Australia, there are two cases currently before the courts involving money mules, Supt. Jessop said. In one of those cases, six out of the seven people accused of recruiting international students, primarily from China, to move dirty money have pled guilty. The alleged head of the syndicate has pled not guilty and is going to trial, Supt. Jessop said. It’s difficult to quantify the effectiveness of the AFP’s awareness campaign. “We can’t put metrics behind it, but we think it’s having a good effect,” Supt. Jessop said. “If we’re getting the message out there and we’re preventing people from becoming victims, that’s where we want to be.”

title: Woman gets house arrest for defrauding her mother; Ontario Jane Sims; Postmedia News
body: A judge has ruled a months-long delay in completing a Gladue pre-sentence report for a woman convicted of defrauding her mother of $150,000 in residential school settlement money violated her constitutional rights. However, even though Ursula Doxtator won her Charter challenge, she must still serve 15 months of house arrest with a GPS monitor, followed by two years of probation for fraud over $5,000 and forgery. Doxtator, 56, a former Oneida band councillor and Oneida language instructor, was found guilty more than 11 months ago for depositing a $150,000 cheque into her personal bank account that had been made out to her mother, Carol, in a classaction settlement for residential school survivors. Doxtator had been given power of attorney over her mother's affairs. Her mother lives in the United States and, with her blessing, Doxtator applied for the residential school settlement. In 2023, the mother and daughter opened a joint bank account at a London bank in anticipation of the cheque's arrival. What her mother did not know was that Doxtator already had the cheque. The same day the joint account was opened, she forged her mother's name on the endorsement and deposited it into her own account. Two months later, Doxtator told her mother the cheque's arrival was imminent and would be $50,000. Her mother went to the bank later that month and discovered the amount was triple what her daughter had told her, it had already been deposited and the money was almost gone. On May 13, 2025, Ontario Court Justice Kevin Mc Hugh convicted Doxtator and ordered a Gladue report, which addresses over-representation of Indigenous offenders in the criminal justice system. London courts have been told routinely that it could take eight months to get a report finished. By November, Doxtator's report still hadn't been started, and Doxtator's lawyer signalled she would be making a Charter challenge. Defence lawyer Karen Simpson had argued the sentence should be set aside, or that Doxtator be given a oneyear conditional sentence if there was a Charter violation. Assistant Crown Jeremy Carnegie had argued for a two-year prison sentence, or a conditional sentence if the breach was found. Mc Hugh said the offences were serious and staying the sentence ""would result in an unjustified and unwarranted loophole for the accused."" ""The offence here is serious and a proportionate sentence should be imposed, keeping in mind some enhanced mitigation for delay needs to be addressed."" Doxtator's mother will be compensated for the full amount, and the bank was able to retrieve some losses. Doxtator was ordered to pay $88,624.89 in restitution to the bank.

title: Ticketmaster delists Ontario resale tickets after new law caps prices
body: Ticketmaster has begun delisting resale tickets for Ontario events to comply with a new provincial law that caps the price of such tickets at face value. The platform's spokesperson, Shabnum Durrani, said customers will be able to relist their tickets next week when it will have updated its resale marketplace. ""We remain committed to creating a fair and secure ticket marketplace for everyone in compliance with all applicable laws and regulations,"" Durrani said, adding that Ticketmaster has been notifying customers of the changes. The move comes after the Ontario government passed its budget bill, which included the resale ticket price cap. The bill received royal assent on Friday. The price cap follows consumer complaints about tickets to popular events, such as last year's World Series and Taylor Swift's Eras tour, being scooped up by resellers who posted them for several times their face value. WATCH | Province capping resale ticket prices: Click on link. Amendments to the 2017 Ticket Sales Act were announced by the government last month and followed the premier's vow last year to review legislation due to sky-high World Series resale tickets in Toronto. That promise was a marked change in stance by Premier Doug Ford after his government scrapped part of an anti-scalping law in 2019 that would have capped ticket resale prices at 50 per cent above the original face value. While tickets to FIFA World Cup events in Toronto this summer were expected to be exempt from the resale cap, a spokesperson for the minister of public and business service delivery and procurement said the cap would in fact apply to the sporting event as well. ""FIFA will be subject to the cap, no exemptions,"" said Giulia Paikin, press secretary for Stephen Crawford. Crawford told reporters on Friday the recap rule takes effect immediately and that his government would be in communication with ticket-selling companies. Stub Hub, Seat Geek opposed change A spokesperson for Stub Hub told CBC News that the resale platform intends to comply with the law — and is looking for more guidance from the province — despite its opposition to the cap. ""Price caps expose fans to a massive increase in ticket fraud, but don’t bring costs down. We will continue to work with Ontario through the implementation process and remind the Government that they were right when they found price caps 'unenforceable' just a few years ago,"" a Stub Hub spokesperson said in an email. Joe Freeman, vice-president of government relations at Seat Geek, did not say how his company plans to comply. But he said Seat Geek is reviewing the legislation and would continue to ""advocate for the best outcome for fans."" WATCH | U.K. government to ban ticket resales above face value: Click on link. Freeman argued that price caps will hurt fans, rather than improve the ticket market. ""Price controls on resale don’t lower what fans pay. They push transactions and fans off regulated platforms to sites like Kijiji and Facebook Marketplace, where there are no buyer protections and fraud rates are nearly four times higher,"" he said. Seat Geek sent an email to some of its customers on Thursday, saying the change could impact fans' ability to buy, sell and access live events. The email, viewed by CBC News, encouraged users to comment on the proposal on the Ontario government website and asked them to take a survey about the resale cap, the results of which would be shared with the government. Gametime declined to comment, as they said they were awaiting clarity on the rule. title: Bluewater trustees debate funding motion ahead of Ministry of Education’s announcement Emily Bowen
body: CHESLEY - Trustees with the Bluewater District School Board (BWDSB) debated a motion on professional development funding, just before the province revealed a legislation aimed at tightening school board governance and oversight. The board’s meeting, which began at 1 p.m. on April 13, coincided closely with a major announcement from Minister of Education Paul Calandra around 1:30 p.m., when he introduced the Putting Student Achievement First Act, 2026. Trustees were unable to adjust their agenda in response to the announcement due to a deadline imposed by the Ontario Public School Boards' Association (OPSBA), but discussion at the local level reflected many of the same concerns raised provincially about governance, accountability and the use of public funds. At the centre of the Bluewater discussion was a notice of motion brought forward by Vice-Chair Jan Johnstone during an April 7 Governance Standing Committee meeting. The motion addressed a potential gap affecting trustees serving on boards placed under provincial supervision, particularly in relation to access to professional development funding. “I am very pleased to bring this resolution forward because it addresses an emerging governing gap that could affect boards of trustees across Ontario - and it’s just, in particular, to the Ontario Public School Boards. It’s exclusive of anything else,” said Johnstone. The motion describes the concerns about the Supporting Children and Students Act, 2025, which expanded the province’s authority to place school boards under supervision where it is deemed to be in the public interest. Under such supervision, trustees may lose access to funding typically used for professional development, even as expectations for governance and oversight remain. The proposal calls on the OPSBA to explore creating an education support fund. This fund would assist trustees from supervised boards by partially covering costs associated with attending professional learning opportunities, including the Public Education Symposium, the Labour Relations Symposium and the association’s annual general meeting. The motion further recommends that OPSBA consult with regional councils to establish eligibility criteria and parameters for the funding, ensuring alignment with principles of accessibility and equity. Any proposed framework would ultimately be presented to member board delegates for consideration at a special meeting. Trustees at BWDSB debated the implications of such a fund. “We all know that there have been some trustees who have been quite fiscally naughty, but It’s not fair for all the other goods boards to be able to fall short of the optics that this might create,” said trustee Wayne Peters. “We don’t want the magnifying glass to be drawn over to Bluewater because we have somehow provided the keys to ‘unlock the handcuffs’ of some of these trustees. That’s just my concern.” Trustee Tracy Lynn Atkinson agreed with Peters, saying she didn’t “feel the funds that Bluewater sends to OPSBA as its dues are fair to use for things other than what they’re allotted for.” The timing of the discussion placed it alongside the announcement of a provincial initiative targeting similar issues. Calandra announced legislation the same afternoon that was designed to address what the government describes as ongoing governance breakdowns and financial mismanagement within Ontario’s school boards. “Almost one year ago, I announced that several school boards facing serious governance challenges would be placed under ministry supervision. I made it clear that any board failing to put students, parents and teachers first could face the same consequences. What we have uncovered since then is deeply concerning,” said Calandra. “In some cases boards have spent millions of dollars fighting internal battles, ignoring best practices and conflict of interest rules.” The proposed Putting Student Achievement First Act, 2026 seeks to strengthen oversight, standardize governance structures and ensure more consistent educational experiences for students across the province. The government says the legislation is intended to move Ontario toward a more accountable and modern model of public education. “Students, parents and teachers have been clear; They expect more from a ministry of education that invests over $43 billion annually. And that is why earlier today I introduced the putting student achievement first act in the legislature,” said Calandra. “This legislation is an important step forward… but it is not the final step. There is more work that still needs to be done.” Among the proposed changes are new limits on trustee discretionary expenses and honoraria, along with a cap of 12 elected trustees per board. Trustees would also be required to pay out-of-pocket for certain external organization membership fees, including some associated with professional associations. The legislation proposes restructuring leadership roles within school boards by renaming the Director of Education as Chief Executive Officer (CEO), responsible for financial and operational oversight, and introducing a CEO focused on student achievement. Additional measures would allegedly strengthen budget oversight, including provisions allowing the Minister of Education to intervene when trustees cannot reach agreement on budgets. The province has pointed to multiple examples of financial mismanagement to justify the reforms. According to government data, several boards have incurred significant expenses unrelated to core educational priorities, including travel, personal electronics and internal legal disputes. BWDSB itself is listed as having spent more than $52,000 in legal fees tied to internal conflicts. The broader context includes eight school boards currently under provincial supervision due to concerns such as depleted reserves and governance issues. The government maintains that despite record levels of funding - including $30.3 billion in core education funding for the 2025–26 school year - some boards have failed to direct resources toward student outcomes. In addition to governance reforms, the legislation proposes changes aimed at standardizing learning experiences across Ontario. These include mandating the use of ministry-approved learning resources, introducing mandatory written exams for Grades 9 through 12, and incorporating attendance and participation into final grades. The province also plans to establish Student and Family Support Offices within all school boards by September 2026, providing a formal avenue for parents and guardians to address concerns about their child’s education. At the local level, the Bluewater motion reflects a narrower but related concern: how trustees can continue to access professional development opportunities in a system where increased oversight may restrict funding in certain circumstances. Supporters of the motion argue that access to training and professional learning is essential for trustees to effectively fulfill their governance responsibilities, particularly in an environment of evolving legislation and heightened accountability expectations. The motion explains that taking part in OPSBA events is intended to help trustees do their jobs and supports equity, diversity and inclusion in public education governance. However, as the discussion at the April 13 BWDSB special meeting demonstrated, questions remain about how such initiatives should be funded and whether they risk undermining efforts to tighten financial controls. As the proposition moves through the legislative process, school boards across the province - including the BWDSB - will be required to align with new provincial requirements related to governance, accountability and oversight.

title: Doug Ford's government is officially keeping secrets + Carney slams U.S. trade 'violations'
body: Good morning. This is the Friday, April 24 edition of First Up, the Star's daily morning digest. Sign up to get it earlier each day, in your inbox. ?? If you didn't have the patience to sit through the entire City Council debate yesterday, you might have missed a motion introduced by Councillor Gord Perks during the debate on the Billy Bishop Airport plan: ""That City Council request the City Manager to create a waterfront colouring book and provide a copy to the premier of Ontario."" His logic was that Ford could draw his big ideas in the book instead of imposing them on the city of Toronto. The motion was ruled out of order. Here are six things you should know to start your day: It's on: the Ford government formally moved to expropriate the island airport, while city council voted to explore legal options to oppose them.Police seized an ""SMS Blaster"" from a fraud operation that attacked phones through fake data network connections.Mark Carney took issue with American complaints about ""trade irritants"" like Canadian dairy quotas.Pierre Poilievre is asking Carney to put more Conservatives in the Senate.New home taxes and fees were slashed to make housing more affordable. So far, most prices aren't moving.Raptors vs. Cavaliers: Scottie Barnes dragged Toronto back into first-round series, writes Bruce Arthur. ?? Before we get into it, the homegrown TV sensation ""Heated Rivalry,"" has won a prestigious Peabody Award. Its citation lauded the gay hockey romance for making ""the biggest cultural impact in television."" The jury did not cite the show's broader educational contribution, popularizing knowledge of the ""stupid Canadian wolf bird"" (you know, the one pictured on our dollar coin). On with the show. DON'T MISSFord's government passed a law to shield politicians from public scrutiny The Ontario government retroactively gutted freedom-of-information laws, prompting criticisms that Premier Doug Ford's aim is to conceal things from the public - allegations he angrily brushed aside. Opposition parties accused the Progressive Conservative government of rushing passage without public hearings. Ford's government has said the law is necessary to protect cabinet confidentiality and strengthen cybersecurity in the modern era. Ontario tabled its bill to take over Billy Bishop despite Toronto's opposition Doug Ford is seizing the city's role in Billy Bishop airport despite Mayor Olivia Chow's opposition to the premier's ""land grab."" The provincial government formalized its usurping of the city's responsibilities in the tripartite agreement that governs the island airport. The 13-page legislation also takes ownership of city-owned lands at the airport - a move that helps clear the way for a runway extension that would allow jets to land there. Fighting back: On Thursday, Toronto council weighed the city's legal options to oppose Ford's move to take over the island airport.Mark Carney blasted the U.S. over 'violations of our trade deal' The prime minister blasted the United States for ongoing complaints about ""trade irritants"" like Canadian dairy quotas, saying it is the U.S. that breached the free trade pact. ""Look, you know what's an irritant,"" said Carney. ""Fifty per cent tariff on steel, 50 per cent tariff on aluminum, 25 per cent tariff on automobiles, all the tariffs on forest products."" Carney also distanced himself from but defended provincial bans on U.S. booze. Chiming in: Former prime minister Justin Trudeau warned American tariffs threaten to drive Canada closer to China.New destinations: Canadian travel to the U.S. declined for the 14th consecutive month. But, overseas travel jumped.WHAT ELSE Parliamentary record contradicted Michael Ma's defence of his comments on forced labour in China.A preliminary report about the La Guardia crash confirmed the fire truck involved did not have a transponder.Alberta's government introduced a bill that would see the province remain on daylight time year-round.Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is set to head to the International Space Station on NASA's Space X mission.Three Canadians made it onto Spotify's list of the 10 most streamed artists of all time. Here's who.Warner Bros shareholders approved Paramount's $81 billion takeover of the company.The seats Drake froze at Scotiabank Arena to promote his album smelled so bad they had to be removed.Meet a few of the 89 musicians who cheer people up by performing across the TTC's 29 subway stations.AI has come for your kids' brains - and your kids are fighting back, writes columnist Elizabeth Renzetti.Mike Wilner: Deep Left Field looks back at the Jays' three-game winning streak and the closer controversy.POV Justin Ling: Carney can't stickhandle a new world order alone. He'll need help from his hockey buddy THE CONVERSATION SECRETS, OFFICIAL: We are unlikely to ever find out what kind of deliberations happened among Doug Ford's staff and cabinet before they agreed to buy a private jet, and then unceremoniously decided to sell it mere days after taking possession. No doubt it would be enlightening to understand the thought process of the flip and then the flop. It could even instil confidence. But we'll never know. The legislation that retroactively shields the premier and his cabinet from freedom of information requests has now passed with the provincial budget, sped through the legislature without hearings. In addition to any deliberations on the ""gravy plane,"" this also puts an end to requests already in progress about Ford's cellphone records (which courts had previously ruled he had to fulfil). We've already covered the stories that would have remained secret if this shield had been in place earlier. To many journalists, this will look like another giant step in an evolution of communications strategy by governments to be ever-less transparent and more tightly controlling of messages. To a lot of the public, it will look like another heavy-handed step from the premier. I know a lot of you have strong feelings about this. I'm inviting you to share your feelings about the new ban on FOI requests on the premier and cabinet in the comments here. Ford says other provinces and the federal government already have similar laws - is that good enough for you? Are you worried about what won't get reported? About the chipping away of transparency in government? Let us know. ICYMI: The other day, I invited you to join me for a Q&A with Queen's Park Bureau Chief Robert Benzie about the ""gravy plane"" situation. Here are some highlights of that chat.Live event: If you're hoping to score tickets to the April 28 live conversation between Star editor-in-chief Nicole Mac Intyre and reporter and author Moira Welsh about ""The Astonishing Lives of Older Women,"" tell them First Up sent you by entering the promo code STAR5 to get a $5 discount. ? Before you go: if you're planning on trying to get anywhere in Toronto this weekend, please know that the Gardiner Expressway is going to be closed from the Humber River to Spadina from Friday night until Monday morning. And the TTC is closing the western end of Line 2 from Kipling to Jane on Saturday. A good weekend to stay home and cheer on the Toronto Sceptres as they battle for their playoff lives. Thank you for reading. The Star's Sima Shakeri and Nikhil Kanekal contributed to today's digest. ?? We'll be making changes to First Up over the next little while. Tell us what you think. Email us at firstup@thestar.ca. Sign up here to get this newsletter in your inbox.

title: PMs should have to sell assets, ethics committee recommends By MARIE WOOLF
body: Liberal members dissent from report, claim it appeared to be designed to target Carney The House of Commons ethics committee has recommended that prime ministers should be required to sell their assets, rather than placing them in a blind trust, within two months of taking office, and should have to divest fully from tax havens. A report published Thursday also suggests that the ethics watchdog be able to impose a sliding scale of penalties on public office holders who breach ethics rules, tied to their level of authority and the seriousness of the breach. The report follows a review by the cross-party Commons ethics committee of the 2007 Conflict of Interest Act. The law applies to the prime minister, ministers and parliamentary secretaries, as well as some unelected individuals including deputy ministers, ministerial staff and advisers. The committee recommended the act be strengthened and also apply to leaders of political parties who are not MPs, such as the new NDP Leader Avi Lewis. The four Liberals on the committee dissented from the report, which was passed with Conservative and Bloc Québécois support and the casting vote of the Tory committee chair John Brassard. Liberals said they could not support it because it appeared to be designed to target Mark Carney. In a dissenting report published Thursday, Liberal MPs on the committee said a number of the recommendations “appear to have been crafted with one individual in mind, rather than in pursuit of sound, durable public policy.” Mr. Carney placed all of his financial assets, other than personal real estate, into a blind trust after taking office. But he has faced concerted criticism from Conservatives over his blind trust and the apparent use of tax havens by his previous employer Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. In a blind trust, an individual’s assets such as stocks and bonds are managed by an arm’s-length third party who makes trades, sales and purchases without the beneficiary’s knowledge. The ethics committee had heard from some witnesses that blind trusts are not truly blind because the person who sets them up knows what was put in there. The majority committee report recommended that a prime minister, rather than using a blind trust, should have to sell all controlled assets, including publicly traded securities. Controlled assets are defined under the act as those whose value could be directly or indirectly affected by government decisions or policy. In their dissenting report, the Liberals said the recommendation “is a rule built around one individual.” It contended that the final report did not reflect evidence heard by the committee that blind trusts work, and that the Prime Minister would no longer know what is in the trust or how it is being managed. The committee of MPs also recommended that the Conflict of Interest Act be updated to prohibit public office holders from investing in companies that use tax havens. Before taking office, Mr. Carney chaired Brookfield Asset Management. Last year, Radio Canada reported that while at Brookfield, Mr. Carney co-chaired two investment funds worth about $25-billion registered in Bermuda, a tax haven. Mr. Carney has said the structure is designed to benefit the Canadian pension funds that invest in them. He said taxes are paid in Canada, because the “flow through” of the funds goes to Canadian entities who pay taxes properly. Mr. Brassard, said at a press conference Thursday that reviewing the Conflict of Interest Act gave the committee the chance to “shed further light on its application to Prime Minister Mark Carney ... but more importantly, to the position of prime minister itself, now and into the future.” “The Prime Minister very clearly knows what’s in his blind trust, and the way to assure confidence for Canadians is for complete divestment,” Mr. Brassard added. Duff Conacher, co-founder of the non-profit advocacy group Democracy Watch, appeared before the committee during its review. He said if the report’s recommendations were to be enacted, Mr. Carney and several cabinet ministers and top government officials would have to sell investments “in businesses that cause conflicts.” Public office holders should also arrange their affairs to prevent both a real or apparent conflict of interest, the committee said. The government has 120 days to respond to the report’s 20 recommendations. But the Liberals on the committee urged caution to ensure any changes to the act are “principled, workable, and designed to serve all Canadians – not to target any one individual.” The report was written at a time when opposition parties still held a combined majority. After securing its majority, the government announced plans this week to change House of Commons rules so that it has a majority in committees. The ethics committee last conducted a review of the Conflict of Interest Act in 2013, presenting its report in February, 2014. It did not result in any reforms.

title: P.E.I. cabinet minister resigns, says conflict over lobster licence was 'a huge distraction'
body: Prince Edward Island cabinet minister Sidney Mac Ewen has resigned from his role on executive council, the province said in a news release Thursday afternoon. The move follows a decision by Fisheries and Oceans Canada to deny his request to name a substitute operator for his lobster fishing fleet. That denial increased pressure on the transportation, infrastructure and energy minister and the Progressive Conservative government to ensure Mac Ewen is in compliance with P.E.I.'s Conflict of Interest Act. The act states ministers must place their business assets into a blind trust during their time in cabinet, but DFO's owner-operator policy requires Mac Ewen's lobster licence to stay in his name. There are only rare exemptions to that policy for things like a death in the family. In response, the PCs introduced Bill 102 last week to amend the act to allow Mac Ewen to maintain his fishing licence. It has passed first reading, but the legislation would need to move through the House and become law by the end of Thursday in order to bring Mac Ewen into compliance with the act by the deadline set out in the legislation. That's not going to happen. ""The conflict of interest commissioner established a timeline for compliance under the existing legislation. As work continues through the legislative assembly to address this matter, it has not been possible to complete those changes within that timeframe,"" reads the release from the province. Mac Ewen will continue to serve as the MLA for Morell-Donagh. P.E.I. Premier Rob Lantz is now acting minister of transportation, infrastructure and energy. ""Work will continue to make the necessary amendments to the Conflict of Interest Act to fix the gap that is keeping a whole sector from serving our province in executive council,"" reads the release. WATCH | P.E.I.'s newest cabinet minister says conflict of interest rules unfair to lobster fishermen: Click on link. Speaking with reporters Thursday outside the P.E.I. Legislature, Mac Ewen said he is disappointed that he had to resign but that he wanted to be compliant with the act. He said changes to the act have been discussed in the past and he has spoken with the province's conflict of interest commissioner about what amendments could be made. ""It's never been able to be done before. Someone had to take it on, someone had to do it. So I'm thankful for the premier for trying to make this happen,"" Mac Ewen said. ""I don't regret trying to make it happen. Hopefully, it still will happen at some point."" The discussion around changing the legislation ""went off the rails"" and became ""a huge distraction,"" Mac Ewen said. He said opposition MLAs have expressed support in the past for allowing fishers to become cabinet ministers — but when the topic becomes ""politically convenient ... it gets chastised."" ""It didn't happen in this tight timeline. If we had've been given more time, maybe changes could have happened, and maybe they can happen in future,"" Mac Ewen said. ""I've worked hard to represent the district and I hope to continue to."" Lantz called Mac Ewen ""eminently qualified to be in cabinet,"" and said opposition parties have privately recognized that fishers being blocked from serving on executive council is an issue. View image. P.E.I. Premier Rob Lantz says he intends to continue toward amending the Conflict of Interest Act to allow fishers to serve on executive council. (Rick Gibbs/CBC) ""In fact, privately, many of them congratulated [Mac Ewen] when he was appointed and that it was well deserved,"" Lantz said outside the legislature. ""Many of them said that they would co-operate in … making this possible. I think politics got in the way here."" Lantz said he still intends to work toward changing the act to allow fishers to serve in executive council but, for now, Mac Ewen will sit in the backbenches. ""We have a proposed bill — there's no reason why we can't amend that. But we have some time now,"" the premier said. ""I had no illusions this would be easy. Oppositions will take any chance to score political points and that's what they're doing here publicly. But, as I said, the attitude was certainly different privately."" 'He needs to make up his mind' P.E.I. Liberal Leader Robert Mitchell told reporters that an amendment to the Conflict of Interest Act could weaken the legislation. He pointed to former MLAs Charlie Mc Geoghegan, Allan Campbell and Buck Watts as members who understood the rule surrounding lobster fishers. View image. P.E.I. Liberal Leader Robert Mitchell says his party will continue to ensure any changes to the Conflict of Interest Act aren't being made to accommodate just one MLA. (Rick Gibbs/CBC) ""[Mac Ewen] chose to fish and that's what he's going to do,"" Mitchell said. ""And he will do that from the backbench, as he should."" Mitchell said Liberal MLAs will continue to ensure any changes to the Conflict of Interest Act aren't being made to accommodate just one person. ""Sidney's a great guy, he's a great MLA and I know he'll work hard for his district out there,"" Mitchell said. ""But he needs to make up his mind and make his decisions. Does he want to be in cabinet or does he want to be in his fishing boat?""

title: Prime minister should be required to divest assets, says committee
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney and other Canadian prime ministers should be required to divest their investment portfolios when they assume office, not just put them in a blind trust, the House of Commons ethics committee recommends in a new report. In its report made public Thursday morning, the committee said putting assets in a blind trust isn’t good enough, recommending instead ""that the Government of Canada amend the Conflict of Interest Act that, for the application of subsection 27(1) the prime minister, as a reporting public office holder, is fully divested from their controlled assets through sale, since placement in a blind trust does not constitute true divestment."" The committee also wants the law amended to require public disclosure of ""high-level holdings categories placed in a blind trust by reporting public office holders (sector/asset class, and whether the holdings are Canadian-market concentrated),"" a recommendation that could shed new light on the financial interests of a number of top officials and cabinet ministers. The report to Parliament is not binding on the government. However, it could reignite debate about Carney’s interests in companies like Brookfield Asset Management and Stripe, which he placed in a blind trust last year. Carney also has a conflict of interest screen designed to prevent him from being involved in any decisions that could affect Brookfield Asset Management, Brookfield Corporation and Stripe. While opposition parties on the committee endorsed the recommendation, Liberal members of the committee issued a dissenting report, saying experts testified that blind trusts were effective. The debate over blind trusts How the assets of Canada’s top political and government leaders should be handled has long been a matter of debate. Some have expressed concern that the personal holdings of public officials risk influencing their decisions, and that a blind trust isn’t truly blind because a public office holder like Carney knows what they put into it before they turn it over to a trustee. Others argue that blind trusts are effective. They say requiring an official to sell off their investments when they assume office — potentially saddling them with capital gains taxes or investment losses — could dissuade people who have been successful in their careers from serving in government. The Conservatives often raised the issue during the last election, suggesting that Carney’s role with Brookfield and his investments in the company would place him in a conflict of interest. In the 79-page report and dissenting report tabled in Parliament on Thursday, the standing committee on access to information, privacy and ethics proposes a series of changes to the Canada’s Conflict of Interest Act, which governs ministers, parliamentary secretaries and hundreds of other public office holders who are required to file reports with the ethics commissioner’s office. The report says there should be special rules when it comes to Canada’s prime minister, such as a requirement to sell all controlled assets within 60 days of assuming office. ""The committee considers that the act should be amended to establish separate rules for the position of prime minister, because individuals with greater decision-making authority should be held and must be held to a higher standard,"" Committee chair John Brassard told reporters during a news conference. The prime minister isn’t the only one singled out in the report. It also recommends that political party leaders — including those who don't have a seat in the House of Commons like NDP Leader Avi Lewis — be subject to the Conflict of Interest Act and disclose their assets to the ethics commissioner within 30 days of becoming party leader. The report also calls for party leaders and cabinet ministers to divest fully from tax havens, and to prohibit them from investing in companies that use tax havens ""in order to avoid eroding public trust by creating the impression that they are not respecting their share of the fiscal social contract."" Tightening conflict of interest rules The report also recommends tightening the rules when it comes to conflict of interest screens for the prime minister and cabinet ministers. Critics have pointed out that the people charged with separating elected officials from companies or individuals that could constitute a conflict of interest are often political staff members who are beholden to the politicians. The report calls for a written log showing when the screen has been employed and for non-partisan public servants to administer it, as well as mandatory public reporting of the scope of the screen and where it was applied. The report includes one recommendation that would soften the rules for those subject to the Conflict of Interest Act. Currently, public office holders face restrictions if they want to take part in outside activities such as teaching or working with a charity. The report recommends giving the ethics commissioner discretion to allow them to take part in those kinds of activities if it's determined it would not create a conflict of interest. In their dissenting nine-page report, Liberal members of the committee took exception with a number of recommendations and accused opposition members of the committee of targeting Carney. ""Throughout these proceedings, it became clear that many of the majority’s recommendations were animated not by a desire to improve the Act for all Canadians, but by a desire to impose specific constraints on the current Prime Minister,"" the Liberal members wrote. ""Several recommendations explicitly single out the prime minister for separate, more onerous treatment, such as mandatory sale of assets, prohibition on blind trusts, separate rules, without adequate justification in the evidence."" The Liberals also questioned recommendations calling for more transparency. ""We are concerned that the majority’s approach to disclosure risks crossing the line from accountability into punitive transparency, and serves as an approach that would deter accomplished Canadians from public service, undermine the role of the Commissioner, and disregard the considered views of the Federal Court of Appeal,"" they wrote. Poilievre 'stunned' at lack of scrutiny The report comes as the Carney government has served notice of plans to change the composition of committees now that it has a majority — changes that could soon give Liberal MPs the majority on committees including the ethics committee. Currently, the committee is composed of four Conservative MPs, four Liberal MPs and one member of the Bloc Québécois. The report also comes as the ethics disclosure process for many members of Parliament, including Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty and Northern and Arctic Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand, has yet to be completed. According to a report from the ethics commissioner’s office, one year after the election, 281 MPs have completed the process, but in 36 cases the process is incomplete because of delays or missing information from MPs, while 23 more are outstanding because of the ethics commissioner’s office. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre welcomed the committee's report and the prospect of more checks on the prime minister’s assets and potential conflicts of interest. ""I am stunned by how little scrutiny there has been of his personal financial interests and how they run in direct opposition to the national interests of this country,"" Poilievre told reporters during a news conference Thursday. ""I’m also stunned that the prime minister has used legalese to try and keep profiting himself at the expense of the public interest, rather than doing the honourable thing, which is to divest himself completely, sell all of his assets and put it into a blind — fully blind — trust."" Duff Conacher, co-founder of ethics watchdog group Democracy Watch, welcomed the committee’s report and called on Parliament to adopt its recommendations. ""The committee's report should be applauded and acted on by the Liberal majority government as it calls for most of the changes needed to close huge loopholes in the ethics law, and to make the ethics commissioner more independent and enforcement more transparent, and to ensure violators of the law are penalized,"" he said. Conacher predicted it could also mean big changes for Carney and a lot of top officials. ""If the committee's recommendations are enacted, Prime Minister Mark Carney would essentially be required to sell his investments in Brookfield and other companies that cause a serious, ongoing financial conflicts of interest for him, and several cabinet ministers and top government officials would also have to sell their investments in businesses that cause conflicts, which would be important steps forward to reduce their many serious conflicts.""

title: Checking out the political optics of Bell's AI data centre near Regina
body: An AI data centre that will cost $1.7 billion and was endorsed by Premier Scott Moe received unanimous support from the council of a rural municipality where a majority of members were appointed recently by the provincial government. When the Rural Municipality of Sherwood's council held a vote approving the project, heavy equipment was already waiting on the parcel of land where construction is set to begin. For opponents of the project protesting outside the RM's office this week, the converging details are proof that it did not matter how vocal they were — construction of Canada's largest AI data centre would go ahead no matter what. Tom Mc Intosh, a professor of politics at the University of Regina, said that feeling is an unfortunate reality when people feel a process has not been transparent. ""This is the kind of stuff around which we make conspiracy theories, right?"" Mc Intosh said. The appointment of new councillors by the province and the vote on the project's development were all in line with the appropriate legislation, he added. The Government of Saskatchewan also highlighted that point when asked for comment. But Mc Intosh said that doesn't stop the AI data centre from becoming an issue of political optics for everyone involved. ""The less transparency, the more there are these kinds of questions, the more people are going to say something was cooked, something smells, something is fishy here,"" he said. View image. (Alexander Quon/CBC) The information gap In February, CBC News broke the story that Bell Canada was planning to build an AI data centre near Regina. Although CBC reached out to Bell before publication and continued to do so as we published follow-up stories, the company either failed to respond or declined to comment, saying it had ""no announcement to make at this time."" WATCH | The fraught political optics of Bell Canada's new AI data centre: Click on link. It wasn't until March 16 that Bell finally confirmed it was behind the project. That's when Bell Canada CEO Mirko Bibic, visiting Regina and flanked by the premier, announced that the telecom giant would spend $1.7 billion to construct a new data centre. ""We're a 145-year-old company and this will be our largest ever investment in this province,"" Bibic said. WATCH | RM of Sherwood council approves Bell Canada AI data centre near Regina : Click on link. The month that elapsed between CBC's reporting and Bell's official confirmation meant residents only had the sparse details contained in the RM of Sherwood's council agenda to understand the proposed project. Many people turned to existing reporting on concerns about data centres being built in other regions, including the United States. Even though Bell has indicated that its data centre won't be anywhere close to the water-guzzling projects found in other markets, the lack of details allowed an ocean of misinformation to fill the gap. Could providing more information have stopped people from opposing the project? It's not very likely. There are established camps ""for"" and ""against"" AI-related projects. Outside of those two camps there is a much larger ""middle"" which could otherwise be ambivalent to the project, Mc Intosh said. ""Those people in the middle, when they see what might be interpreted as shenanigans of some kind going on, that tends to push them one way or the other."" One of those potential issues is the vote by the RM's council earlier this week. Its seven members unanimously approved the data centre's development plan. Only three of them were elected and live in the RM. The remaining four — three councillors and the reeve — were appointed by the provincial government until elections are held in November. That can be a big problem when it's a decision on something as big and controversial as this decision. ""This is a really substantive, important vote. And so there are questions of the optics when a majority of that council is actually not elected,"" Mc Intosh said. Ray Orb, the former president of the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, was appointed to serve as the reeve. In an interview with CBC's The 306, Orb insisted he was not questioned about his position on the AI data centre before he was appointed. In a statement, the provincial government said it contacts potential candidates based on experience and proximity to the municipality and is mindful to whether or not they have business or personal interests in the municipality that would put them in a conflict of interest. Although he admitted the optics of unelected councillors making such an important decision may not be great, Orb said he did his own research and that the council had the information necessary to make a decision. ""The province announced it quite awhile ago that this project was going ahead, and so I think that's why they brought us in, to keep this project going,"" he said. Bell Canada insists that it has been transparent and the project ""will bring significant benefits, employment opportunities and tax revenues to the community and to Saskatchewan."" The company said it's committed to addressing the questions and concerns prompted by a project of this scale. ""Throughout the development process, we have engaged continuously with residents and other stakeholders and adapted our plans based on feedback we have received,"" Bell said in a prepared statement. View image. (Alexander Quon/CBC) It said that feedback resulted in some additional commitments laid out in the development agreement approved this week. The company pointed to a new website it believes will help people find answers to most questions about the project. Government responds The provincial government did not directly address a question on the concerns about optics. Instead, in a statement, it highlighted that the project ""proceeded to a significant degree under the previous council,"" referencing a special meeting held by the RM in February. ""The Ministry of Government Relations can confirm the RM of Sherwood rezoned the land to facilitate the proposed development in February 2026, following a public hearing,"" the government's statement said. Minutes from the Feb. 9 special meeting indicate that the public hearing and second and third reading of the bylaw to rezone the 160-acre parcel of land to allow for a data centre took less than an hour. That meeting was also the first time the rezoning bylaw publicly referenced an AI data centre project. The agenda for the Jan. 19 council meeting made no mention of an AI data centre, only saying it was a rezoning application to change the parcel from agricultural to light industrial use. The first reading of the rezoning bylaw was passed by the RM's council unanimously.

title: Retired senator ready to fight for expenses; Conservative says Ottawa will have to take him to court if they want him to pay
body: At least one retired senator says the Senate will have to go to court if it wants him to repay travel and other expenses the auditor general said he claimed inappropriately, the Star has learned. Gerry St. Germain, a retired Conservative senator for British Columbia, believes there was nothing inappropriate about the contracts, gifts and travel for both him and his staff that auditor general Michael Ferguson flagged in the report on his exhaustive investigation last year. ""Mr. St. Germain has informed Senate administration that he does not intend to provide reimbursement for the claimed expenses,"" his spokesman, Bob Ransford, wrote in an email statement Friday. ""It is Mr. St. Germain's position that the expenses were properly incurred in the conduct of his business as a senator. Mr. St. Germain will vigorously defend any proceedings that may be commended to recover those amounts,"" the statement said. The Senate says he still owes $67,120 after having repaid $468 - the amount he had claimed for a dinner meeting St. Germain had said was to wrap up parliamentary business, but other information indicated it was a family dinner, according to the audit report. Thirty senators - both former and sitting - had until Thursday evening to reimburse the Senate for expenses Ferguson identified in his politically explosive June 2015 report on the Senate expenses scandal. On Friday, seven former senators had not yet repaid a total of $527,788.54, which prompted the Senate to warn it would begin taking steps to get it back. ""The Senate has been clear about its intention to take legal action in order to recoup any monies owing by non- sitting Senators,"" said a statement issued by Conservative Sen. Leo Housakos and independent Liberal Sen. Jane Cordy, the chair and deputy chair of the Senate standing committee on internal economy, budgets and administration. ""To that end, the Senate Law Clerk has been instructed to seek outside legal counsel to initiate such action,"" the statement said. him to pay The other six former senators are: Manitoba Liberal Sharon Carstairs ($7,528), Ontario Liberal Marie-P. Charette- Poulin ($125,828), New Brunswick Liberal Rose-Marie Losier-Cool ($110,051), Nova Scotia Conservative Don Oliver ($23,955.54), Manitoba Liberal Rod Zimmer ($176,014) and Newfoundland Liberal Bill Rompkey ($17,292) None of the seven on the list chose to challenge the findings of the auditor general by participating in a binding arbitration process overseen by retired Supreme Court justice Ian Binnie, who delivered his conclusions last month. Many of the expenses they claimed are similar in nature to those that got Sen. Mike Duffy into trouble and landed him in court. The former broadcast journalist turned senator for Prince Edward Island was acquitted Thursday afternoon on all 31 charges of fraud, breach of trust and bribery, with Ontario Court Justice Charles Vaillancourt saying many of his expenses were allowed by the Senate administrative rules - now being updated - that were in place at the time. Don Bayne, his defence lawyer, said he does not think the acquittal sets a ""sweeping precedent for parliamentarians,"" but it does send a message to the Senate. ""The Senate has to create clear rules, educate senators on what they can and can't do in the public interest,"" Bayne told reporters gathered outside the Ottawa courthouse Thursday. In his findings on St. Germain, who retired in 2012, the auditor general said he could not conclude whether all of his expenses reviewed had been incurred primarily for parliamentary business. In his response, published in the report, St. Germain vigorously defended the expenses and his reputation. ""The presentation and tone of your general observations insinuate that I misappropriated my office resources in a nefarious manner. I find these apparent accusations to be a defamatory affront to my personal integrity,"" said St. Germain, a former Progressive Conservative cabinet minister who was appointed to the Senate on the advice of Brian Mulroney in 1993.

title: RETIRING THE SENATE: Newest senators sitting prettier than others
body: The cost of retiring Canada's 99 senators can be calculated this way: take the number of years a senator has left before retirement, and multiply it by the annual base salary of $ 64,400. Indexed, the figure rises. Under the scheme -- one of the several, including a lump sum calculation, being contemplated -- not all senators would benefit equally. The youngest senator would draw the most: more than $ 2 million. As it happens, interior decorator Nancy Teed, 43, comes from one of the country's poorest provinces, New Brunswick. A defeated provincial Tory cabinet minister, she was one of 23 senators Prime Minister Brian Mulroney named to the red room in 1990. Mandatory retirement could be sweet for Teed. With 32 years left before she reaches age 75, she is entitled to a total salary of $ 2,060,800 -- more, once the salary is indexed -- to be paid by the year 2,024. If she opts for early ""retirement,"" she will be entitled to three-quarters of her salary. Will she collect it? In an interview this week from her Saint John business office, Teed suggested she'd take a pass. She said she hasn't sought a lawyer's advice on what she's entitled to, nor has the issue come up in Tory caucus in the Senate and House of Commons. ""My interest is really what's in the best interest of the country. I can't say to you that I'm one of those self-serving politicians who are there in their best interests only."" But surely she'll want some compensation? Teed put it this way: ""I didn't accept my appointment on the premise that I would definitely be there until age 75, nor did I accept it on the basis that I would be gone in two years."" For now, until the government and the country decides, the money is hers. And her colleagues are sitting only a little less pretty. Of the 99 senators now in office, 20 have another two to three decades to go before retirement. Their time as senators is worth between $ 1.3 million and $ 1.9 million each. They include: Gerald Comeau, 46, a Nova Scotia Tory appointed under Mulroney on the same date as Teed: $ 1,867,600. Janis Johnson, 46, a national Tory organizer from Winnipeg (Mulroney, 1990): $ 1,867,600. Colin Kenny, 48, of Ottawa; a former Dome Petroleum executive appointed under Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau in 1985: $ 1,738,800. Michel Cogger, 53, a Montreal lawyer named to the Senate by Mulroney in 1986, now facing influence-peddling charges for helping a Japanese businessman get government grants: $ 1,481,200. Michael Pitfield, 55, of Ottawa; a former clerk of the Privy Council and close friend of Trudeau, who named him to the Senate in 1982: $ 1,288,000. Another 39 senators have between 10 and 19 years before reaching age 75. If they were retired tomorrow, they would be owed between $ 644,000 and $ 1.2 million each. They include: Peter Stollery, 56, a Toronto businessman and former MP who was pulled from his Spadina seat and named to the Senate in 1981, allowing Jim Coutts, Trudeau's principal secretary, to run for office: $ 1,223,600. Former Tory cabinet minister Pat Carney, 57 (Mulroney, 1990): $ 1,159,200. Willie Adams, 58, an Inuit electrician from the Northwest Territories (Trudeau, 1977): $ 1,094,800. Norm Atkins, 58, of Toronto, an important federal Tory strategist: $ 1,094,800. Mira Spivak, 58, an educator and wife of former Manitoba Tory party leader Sidney Spivak (Mulroney, 1986): $ 1,094,800. Jack Austin, 60, former legislator and Bank of British Columbia president (Trudeau, 1975): $ 966,000. Gerald Beaudoin, 63, known most recently to Canadians for co-chairing two constitutional renewal committees (Mulroney, 1988): $ 772,800. Claude Castonguay, 63, a Montreal banking executive and former Quebec cabinet minister (Mulroney, 1990): $ 772,800. Leo Kolber, 64, chairman of Claridge Inc., the Montreal holding company for the hefty investments of Charles Bronfman and his family: (Trudeau, 1983): $ 708,400. Senators with less than 10 years to retirement will be owed between $ 128,800 and $ 579,600. They include: Keith Davey, 66, the federal Liberal fund-raiser nicknamed the Rainmaker (named to the Senate in 1966 by Prime Minister Lester Pearson): $ 579,600. William Kelly, 67, chairman of Rothmans Inc. (Trudeau, 1982): $ 515,200. Royce Frith, 68, leader of the Liberal opposition in the Senate (Trudeau, 1977): $ 450,800. Finlay MacDonald, 68, a federal Tory organizer (Mulroney, 1984): $ 450,800. Richard Doyle, 69, former editor-in-chief of the Globe and Mail (Mulroney, 1985): $ 386,400. Jacques Hebert, 69, Katimavik founder and onetime hunger-striker, now the Liberal whip in the Senate (Trudeau, 1983): $ 386,400. Allan MacEachen, 71, former Liberal cabinet minister (Trudeau, 1984): $ 257,600. Paul David, 72, a heart surgeon, now ill and unable to talk, whose father and grandfather were also senators: $ 193,200. Col. Jack Marshall, 72, a former Newfoundland Tory MP, now an ardent campaigner for Canada's war veterans and defender of controversial war heroes such as Billy Bishop (Trudeau, 1978): $ 193,200. The oldest senators of the 99 -- former Nova Scotia Tory legislator John Michael Macdonald, 86, and Montrealer Hartland deMontarville Molson, 85 -- will earn full salary until they die. They were appointed for life before 1965, when the retirement age of 75 was set.
