title: The Tories say Carney is being 'sneaky' about his assets. What do the rules say?
body: OTTAWA - In a series of press conferences in recent weeks, the federal Conservatives have demanded that Liberal leadership candidate Mark Carney comply with the conflict of interest rules that apply to members of Parliament and cabinet ministers. Carney, who is neither an MP nor a member of cabinet, has said he will comply with the rules when they apply to him. Here is what the rules say. What are the rules for members of Parliament? MPs are subject to the Conflict of Interest Code for Members of the House of Commons, which came into force in 2004 and has been updated five times, most recently in March 2023. The code includes a process to disclose private interests to the ethics commissioner and procedures to make some of that information public. It also sets out rules to help MPs avoid conflicts of interest. It only applies to sitting members of Parliament, so it's not in force during an election. What are the rules for the government? Cabinet ministers and the prime minister are subject to the Conflict of Interest Act and must make disclosures to the ethics commissioner. Some of the information disclosed to the commissioner has to be made public. What are the rules for candidates in a party leadership race? Elected MPs are subject to the House of Commons conflict of interest code. That code applies to two candidates in the current Liberal leadership race: Chrystia Freeland and Karina Gould. Cabinet ministers and parliamentary secretaries also have to comply with the Conflict of Interest Act, but Freeland and Gould both stepped down from their cabinet roles before the leadership race began. Frank Baylis, who was an MP from 2015 to 2019, would have made disclosures at that time. Right now, he and Carney are not subject to either set of rules. Why don't the rules apply to Carney? Rob Shepherd, a professor of public policy and administration at Carleton University, said the rules are ""meant for protecting the interests of the Canadian public once they're in office."" ""No candidate is required to disclose their personal assets,"" he said, adding that asking candidates to disclose assets early could run afoul of privacy laws. This is an unusual situation, since Carney could become prime minister before becoming an MP. Shepherd said that's led to questions about whether the rules need to be changed. ""It may be a very legitimate question to ask,"" he said. Shepherd said that while changes could be made to the laws that govern elections, it's up to political parties to set the rules for their own leadership races. What happens when the leadership race is over? The winner of the Liberal leadership race will be appointed prime minister by the governor-in-council and will then have to comply with the Conflict of Interest Act. That law says public office holders have 120 days to complete an initial compliance process. They must divest controlled assets — assets like stocks or bonds that could rise or fall in value as a result of government actions. Those assets must be sold in an arm's-length transaction or placed in a blind trust. Within 60 days of taking office, a cabinet minister, minister of state or parliamentary secretary must submit a confidential report to the ethics commissioner's office. According to the wording on the ethics commissioner's website, they must ""make reasonable efforts to include a similar description for (their) spouse or common-law partner and dependent children."" That report is reviewed by the commissioner's office, which provides a summary statement and advice on any public declarations required. Those must be signed and handed to the commissioner within 120 days of the initial appointment to office. What are the Conservatives saying? Conservative MPs say Carney is exploiting a ""loophole"" in the laws. MP Michelle Rempel Garner said last week that because Carney could win the Liberal leadership and quickly call a federal election, ""it's conceivable that he wouldn't have to disclose his financial interests … until after an election."" She argued the law did not anticipate ""an unelected person who had significant corporate board interests becoming prime minister"" and called on Carney to disclose all his corporate interests now. ""I firmly think that anybody seeking to lead this country needs to live above the letter of the law,"" she said. Conservative MP Michael Barrett pointed out that Carney was Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's ""senior economic adviser"" for years. Carney became an informal adviser to the federal government on economic matters during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. In late 2024, the Liberals announced he would chair a task force to help the party develop ideas on spurring economic growth. ""It's very clear that we have a problem with the rules as they exist because Mark Carney can be sneaky about what his business dealings are,"" Barrett said Tuesday. He did not answer when asked whether party leadership races should be restricted to sitting MPs. He also didn't say which rules should be changed. Dennis Matthews, president of advertising agency Creative Currency and a Conservative strategist, said the Liberals and the Conservatives are both racing to brand Carney, who is a relative unknown on the political stage. ""All of the best attacks in politics have to have a kernel of truth to them. So when you look at Conservatives going after Carney on financial disclosures, or business dealings from the past … these can be answered with a little bit of sunshine from Mark Carney,"" he said. ""If he's not willing to answer, you can see that brings into (play) questions of, 'What's being hidden?'"" But Shepherd said the attacks are a ""false flag."" ""What's sneaky about this, exactly? The (Conflict of Interest Act) doesn't capture (Carney),"" he said. He said he thinks the Conservatives are ""doing whatever they can to slow down a speeding train, that is, their decline in the polls."" ""You throw as much as you can out there and see what sticks,"" he said. What is Carney saying about all this? When he announced his intention to run for the Liberal leadership, Carney said he resigned as UN special envoy for climate action and finance and left his executive role at Brookfield Asset Management and the boards of Stripe and PIMCO. His campaign team said in an emailed statement on Monday that he has resigned from all professional or advisory roles. ""He will work hard to earn a seat in the House of Commons, where he is committed to complying with all applicable ethics rules and guidelines relating to these roles,"" said campaign spokesperson Emily Williams. ""It's clear that Pierre Poilievre is afraid to face Mark Carney in the coming election campaign."" This report by The Canadian Press was first published Feb. 26, 2025.

title: THE UNOFFICIAL RACE IS ON; Here's a look at the field of top contenders - and a few wild cards - to take over as party leader
body: Let the political games begin. With Justin Trudeau's decision to step down, the unofficial race to replace him is on. By convention in Canada's parliamentary system of democracy, whoever leads the party that holds the confidence of the House of Commons becomes prime minister. So the stakes couldn't be higher. Polls show the Liberals far behind the Conservatives at the moment. Although a federal election is not scheduled in law until the fall of 2025, a vote of non-confidence whenever the minority Parliament resumes could trigger one immediately. Still, senior Conservatives know the power of the Liberal political brand in Canada, and a new leader could motivate Liberal voters in a way Trudeau no longer could, and give them a way to snub Pierre Poilievre. Poilievre is already rolling out the nicknames to frame would-be opponents, like ""carbon tax Carney."" Here, in alphabetical order, are the top likely contenders for the job of Liberal leader: Anita Anand, 57 Born and raised in Nova Scotia, the former law professor was first elected as MP for Oakville in 2019. As minister of procurement during the COVID-19 pandemic, she led Canada's scramble for medical equipment and vaccines during the global race. Anand (whose name rhymes with almond) became defence minister after the 2021 election after her predecessor, Harjit Sajjan, fumbled sexual misconduct allegations and the Canadian evacuation from Afghanistan. In 2023, Anand was shifted into Treasury Board, the government agency that sends out the cheques, and a job that took her and her leadership ambitions out of the limelight. Mark Carney, 59 Chair of Brookfield Asset Management and special UN envoy on climate action and finance, Carney is a Harvard- and Oxford-educated economist and former central banker for Canada and the United Kingdom. Early gigs over as party leader included working for Goldman Sachs and the Canadian finance department. Now affiliated with Canada 2020, a think tank closely aligned with Liberal politics, Carney declared allegiance to the Liberal party of Canada in 2021, but chose not to run in any of several safe Liberal seats he was encouraged to contest. Carney is believed to want the top job, and giving up his blue-chip salary to become a backbench MP was never on his bingo card. François-Philippe Champagne, 54 A former corporate lawyer, the MP for Shawinigan speaks fluent English, French and Italian and his nicknames - Frankie Bubbles and Energizer Bunny - speak to his reputation as an energetic pitchman in a range of cabinet jobs: international trade, infrastructure, foreign affairs and now industry. He led Ottawa's efforts to draw international investment into building an electric vehicle manufacturing supply chain in Canada. One of three Trudeau officials charged with leading the latest Canada-U.S. charm offensive ahead of the U.S. election, Champagne is also a skilled retail politician, enthusiastically shaking hands and kissing babies, but it's unclear if he has a political organization to galvanize. Christy Clark, 59 Senior adviser at the law firm of Bennett Jones, Clark served as B.C. Liberal premier from 2011 to 2017. Clark called openly for Trudeau to step down after the Toronto-St. Paul's byelection loss, saying she wanted to see the return of the Liberal party she used to work and vote for. National youth campaign director for Jean Chrétien in 1993 and later a staffer for senior cabinet minister Doug Young, Clark returned to B.C. in 1996, where she was elected and sat first in opposition under B.C. Liberal leader Gordon Campbell. She served in his government as deputy premier. Clark left politics in 2005, but returned to replace Campbell in 2011, and won a come-from-behind victory in the 2013 provincial election. Under her, the party narrowly won the 2017 election, with one seat shy of a majority, but did not hold onto power after the NDP and Greens struck a deal to govern. Sean Fraser, 40 Fraser is a bagpipe-skirling Nova Scotian from Pictou County, a lawyer, member of the tight-knit Saint-FX alumni, and father of two. Fraser quit Trudeau's cabinet mid-December, the day Chrystia Freeland did too, to go spend time with his family in Nova Scotia. But he should not be ruled out. Fraser learned French since arriving in Ottawa. Trudeau called on Fraser's formidable communication skills and moved him from the immigration portfolio into the hot seat of housing as Liberal polling numbers began to go into free fall. Conservatives see that as his political pain point: he led when numbers of international students and temporary foreign workers soared way beyond the housing and rental supply in Canada. Chrystia Freeland, 56 Trudeau's erstwhile minister of everything who quit suddenly on Dec. 16, Freeland led Canada's side in the 2016- 18 NAFTA renegotiation, deftly handling Donald Trump's tantrums and trade advisers. She became Canada's first female finance minister when Trudeau tapped her to replace Bill Morneau and bestowed on her the title of deputy prime minister. A former journalist and author, the Alberta native is the daughter of Ukrainian immigrant parents and was long ago declared persona non grata by Russia for her opposition to its authoritarian regime. Fluent in Ukrainian, she was a key figure in Canada's response to the war in Ukraine. But her global Rolodex doesn't translate to an ease in retail domestic politics. Freeland is not a caucus favourite, and - like many of her cabinet peers - may struggle to differentiate herself from Trudeau's record. But she gained a lot of new supporters when she quit on a point of principle, throwing flames Trudeau's way. Mélanie Joly, 45 Foreign affairs minister since 2021, Joly has led Canada's response to the war in Ukraine and to the Israel-Hamas war in the Middle East. A savvy political organizer and former candidate for the Montreal mayoralty, Joly joined Trudeau's team and won a federal seat in 2015. Though she stumbled as a rookie heritage minister, Joly proved a hard worker and made her way back into the prime minister's circle of trust and up the cabinet ladder. Her job has over as party leader kept her on the road a lot, but Joly still has built up political contacts beyond Quebec in a range of diaspora voting communities. Dominic LeBlanc, 57 LeBlanc was Trudeau's fixer-in-chief through the intergovernmental travails of the pandemic and health-care negotiations, the toxic reign of former governor general Julie Payette and, now, foreign interference. The New Brunswick MP is a partisan animal whose been targeted for favouring relatives and connections, but has an ability to use humour to defuse nasty attacks from rivals or from unfriendly premiers. Son of Romeo LeBlanc, a former Pierre Trudeau cabinet minister who became governor general, LeBlanc grew up in Ottawa, once babysat Trudeau, but was not a childhood friend per se. He, too, harboured leadership ambitions in 2013, but bowed out when Trudeau ran. A cancer survivor, LeBlanc is not seen as a details person, but he was a trusted confidante among the few who could lighten Trudeau's mood in a flash. Wild cards, in alphabetical order Frank Baylis, 62. A businessman and executive chair of Baylis Medical Technologies, Baylis was a one-term Liberal MP for Pierrefonds-Dollard. He ran under Trudeau's banner in 2015, but did not run again in 2019. He confirmed Monday night he intends to run for the leadership. Andrew Furey, 49. Liberal premier Furey heads the government in Newfoundland and Labrador. An early ally of Trudeau's, he ran party efforts in his province to get Trudeau elected leader and prime minister in 2015 and 2019. Son of George Furey, a former Liberal organizer and Senate speaker whom Chrétien named to the red chamber, Furey is an orthopedic surgeon and founder of Team Broken Earth charity, which delivered surgical services to post-earthquake Haiti and now to other needy countries. Tensions arose between him and the prime minister over Trudeau's carbon price plan, which hit the provincial economy and Furey's political fortunes hard. He recently renegotiated a hydro deal with Quebec that many doubted possible. Ahmed Hussen, 48. Born in Mogadishu, Hussen arrived in Canada as a young refugee, became a lawyer and head of the Canadian Somali Congress. Trudeau named Hussen to the immigration portfolio in 2015. Later as families minister, he struck most of the federal-provincial $10-a-day child-care deals. As housing minister, he was put in place to develop housing and homelessness strategies. But when it became the toughest political file, Trudeau shifted Hussen to the lower-profile job of international development where he leads Ottawa's attempts to get aid into Gaza. Hussen is an ambitious and capable political organizer, but privately said he wouldn't run for Trudeau's job. That was before it was clear the field is wide open. Jane Philpott, 64. Physician, Queen's University health sciences dean and former Trudeau minister for health, Indigenous services and, briefly, Treasury Board, Philpott was ousted as a Liberal alongside Jody Wilson-Raybould. She lost when she vied for her old seat as an Independent. She has called around to Liberals to seek organizers for a potential bid, sources say. Jody Wilson-Raybould, 53. A former regional chief of the B.C. Assembly of First Nations, Wilson-Raybould was Canada's first Indigenous justice minister. Title: THE UNOFFICIAL RACE IS ON; Here's a look at the field of top contenders - and a few wild cards - to take over as party leader
Body: Let the political games begin. With Justin Trudeau's decision to step down, the unofficial race to replace him is on. By convention in Canada's parliamentary system of democracy, whoever leads the party that holds the confidence of the House of Commons becomes prime minister. So the stakes couldn't be higher. Polls show the Liberals far behind the Conservatives at the moment. Although a federal election is not scheduled in law until the fall of 2025, a vote of non-confidence whenever the minority Parliament resumes could trigger one immediately. Still, senior Conservatives know the power of the Liberal political brand in Canada, and a new leader could motivate Liberal voters in a way Trudeau no longer could, and give them a way to snub Pierre Poilievre. Poilievre is already rolling out the nicknames to frame would-be opponents, like ""carbon tax Carney."" Here, in alphabetical order, are the top likely contenders for the job of Liberal leader: Anita Anand, 57 Born and raised in Nova Scotia, the former law professor was first elected as MP for Oakville in 2019. As minister of procurement during the COVID-19 pandemic, she led Canada's scramble for medical equipment and vaccines during the global race. Anand (whose name rhymes with almond) became defence minister after the 2021 election after her predecessor, Harjit Sajjan, fumbled sexual misconduct allegations and the Canadian evacuation from Afghanistan. In 2023, Anand was shifted into Treasury Board, the government agency that sends out the cheques, and a job that took her and her leadership ambitions out of the limelight. Mark Carney, 59 Chair of Brookfield Asset Management and special UN envoy on climate action and finance, Carney is a Harvard- and Oxford-educated economist and former central banker for Canada and the United Kingdom. Early gigs over as party leader included working for Goldman Sachs and the Canadian finance department. Now affiliated with Canada 2020, a think tank closely aligned with Liberal politics, Carney declared allegiance to the Liberal party of Canada in 2021, but chose not to run in any of several safe Liberal seats he was encouraged to contest. Carney is believed to want the top job, and giving up his blue-chip salary to become a backbench MP was never on his bingo card. François-Philippe Champagne, 54 A former corporate lawyer, the MP for Shawinigan speaks fluent English, French and Italian and his nicknames - Frankie Bubbles and Energizer Bunny - speak to his reputation as an energetic pitchman in a range of cabinet jobs: international trade, infrastructure, foreign affairs and now industry. He led Ottawa's efforts to draw international investment into building an electric vehicle manufacturing supply chain in Canada. One of three Trudeau officials charged with leading the latest Canada-U.S. charm offensive ahead of the U.S. election, Champagne is also a skilled retail politician, enthusiastically shaking hands and kissing babies, but it's unclear if he has a political organization to galvanize. Christy Clark, 59 Senior adviser at the law firm of Bennett Jones, Clark served as B.C. Liberal premier from 2011 to 2017. Clark called openly for Trudeau to step down after the Toronto-St. Paul's byelection loss, saying she wanted to see the return of the Liberal party she used to work and vote for. National youth campaign director for Jean Chrétien in 1993 and later a staffer for senior cabinet minister Doug Young, Clark returned to B.C. in 1996, where she was elected and sat first in opposition under B.C. Liberal leader Gordon Campbell. She served in his government as deputy premier. Clark left politics in 2005, but returned to replace Campbell in 2011, and won a come-from-behind victory in the 2013 provincial election. Under her, the party narrowly won the 2017 election, with one seat shy of a majority, but did not hold onto power after the NDP and Greens struck a deal to govern. Sean Fraser, 40 Fraser is a bagpipe-skirling Nova Scotian from Pictou County, a lawyer, member of the tight-knit Saint-FX alumni, and father of two. Fraser quit Trudeau's cabinet mid-December, the day Chrystia Freeland did too, to go spend time with his family in Nova Scotia. But he should not be ruled out. Fraser learned French since arriving in Ottawa. Trudeau called on Fraser's formidable communication skills and moved him from the immigration portfolio into the hot seat of housing as Liberal polling numbers began to go into free fall. Conservatives see that as his political pain point: he led when numbers of international students and temporary foreign workers soared way beyond the housing and rental supply in Canada. Chrystia Freeland, 56 Trudeau's erstwhile minister of everything who quit suddenly on Dec. 16, Freeland led Canada's side in the 2016- 18 NAFTA renegotiation, deftly handling Donald Trump's tantrums and trade advisers. She became Canada's first female finance minister when Trudeau tapped her to replace Bill Morneau and bestowed on her the title of deputy prime minister. A former journalist and author, the Alberta native is the daughter of Ukrainian immigrant parents and was long ago declared persona non grata by Russia for her opposition to its authoritarian regime. Fluent in Ukrainian, she was a key figure in Canada's response to the war in Ukraine. But her global Rolodex doesn't translate to an ease in retail domestic politics. Freeland is not a caucus favourite, and - like many of her cabinet peers - may struggle to differentiate herself from Trudeau's record. But she gained a lot of new supporters when she quit on a point of principle, throwing flames Trudeau's way. Mélanie Joly, 45 Foreign affairs minister since 2021, Joly has led Canada's response to the war in Ukraine and to the Israel-Hamas war in the Middle East. A savvy political organizer and former candidate for the Montreal mayoralty, Joly joined Trudeau's team and won a federal seat in 2015. Though she stumbled as a rookie heritage minister, Joly proved a hard worker and made her way back into the prime minister's circle of trust and up the cabinet ladder. Her job has over as party leader kept her on the road a lot, but Joly still has built up political contacts beyond Quebec in a range of diaspora voting communities. Dominic LeBlanc, 57 LeBlanc was Trudeau's fixer-in-chief through the intergovernmental travails of the pandemic and health-care negotiations, the toxic reign of former governor general Julie Payette and, now, foreign interference. The New Brunswick MP is a partisan animal whose been targeted for favouring relatives and connections, but has an ability to use humour to defuse nasty attacks from rivals or from unfriendly premiers. Son of Romeo LeBlanc, a former Pierre Trudeau cabinet minister who became governor general, LeBlanc grew up in Ottawa, once babysat Trudeau, but was not a childhood friend per se. He, too, harboured leadership ambitions in 2013, but bowed out when Trudeau ran. A cancer survivor, LeBlanc is not seen as a details person, but he was a trusted confidante among the few who could lighten Trudeau's mood in a flash. Wild cards, in alphabetical order Frank Baylis, 62. A businessman and executive chair of Baylis Medical Technologies, Baylis was a one-term Liberal MP for Pierrefonds-Dollard. title: The year that was a look back at 2025; Just like that, another year has come and gone. This is Part 2 of Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back at the significant events at home and abroad that defined 2025
body: JULY 1: The Trump administration says it's withholding once-promised precision arms for Ukraine including air defence weaponry. 2: The UCP government announces the creation of a new provincial police force - the Alberta Sheriff's Police Service - to fill in law enforcement gaps and offer an alternative for municipalities. 2: One-time superstar rapper Sean (Diddy) Combs is acquitted on sex trafficking and racketeering charges but convicted of prostitution-related offences. He's sentenced to four years in prison in October. 4: A massive flash flood in central Texas fatally sweeps away about 140 people, many of them children. The tragedy unleashes a political firestorm over federal efforts to notify and help those affected. 7: U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi insists a client list linked to the late convicted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein doesn't exist, walking back her previous insistence she was preparing to release it. Kennedy and that an agency operative had stonewalled access to documents on the case. 14: In an apparent reversal of his loyalties in the conflict, U.S. President Donald Trump vows to continue arming Ukraine and threatens Russia with sanctions unless it agrees to a ceasefire within 50 days. 15: Calgary police Const. Craig Stothard is charged with second-degree murder in the shooting deaths of Levon Wildman and Wesley Davidson during a May 2023 incident in the city's northeast. Canada follows suit days later. OCTOBER 1: Premier Danielle Smith says she'll lead a technical advisory committee pushing for a new energy pipeline from Alberta to the west coast by promoting the project to Ottawa as one of national significance. 1: Legendary primate researcher and animal rights/environmental activist Jane Goodall dies at the age of 91. But the violence continues. 14: Voters in Newfoundland and Labrador oust John Hogan's Liberals after a 10-year reign, handing a slim majority government to Tony Wakeham's Progressive Conservatives. 17: While a report into medical procurement in Alberta doesn't directly implicate top UCP officials of wrongdoing, it concludes the process was deeply flawed. 18: Millions of Americans throughout the U.S. turn out for No Kings protests against the Trump administration. 19: A brazen heist at Paris's Louvre nets thieves crown jewels worth at least US$102 million. Several suspects are later arrested. 20: Calgary voters oust Mayor Jyoti Gondek in favour of former city councillor Jeromy Farkas while also ensuring 11 new faces on council. 24: A TV ad produced by the Ontario government using former U.S. president Ronald Reagan's comments attacking tariffs inflames U.S. President Donald Trump, who drops trade talks with Canada and increases duties on its products. 27: The UCP government tables back-to-work legislation for striking Alberta teachers under a contract conditions teachers had twice reject and with an intent to invoke the notwithstanding clause of the Charter to end the threeweek labour action. 30: King Charles revokes his brother Prince Andrew's royal titles and evicts him from his royal residence as fallout from Andrew's links to convicted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein continue. NOVEMBER 4: The federal Liberal government tables a 2025-26 budget leaning heavily on infrastructure project investments in response to the trade war with the U.S., while nearly doubling the deficit from the previous year. 4: Conservative MP Chris D'Entremont defects to the Liberals, decrying Pierre Poilievre's leadership style. Edmonton Conservative MP Matt Jeneroux resigns from the party a few days later, citing disappointment with the political status quo. 9: Flight cancellations at U.S. airports expand as the nation's federal government shutdown results in unpaid air traffic controllers being absent from work. 9: Several Democratic senators vote with Republican counterparts for a spending deal to end a six-month government shutdown. 10: U.S. President Donald Trump pardons his former personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani and others who took part in efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election they falsely claimed was fraudulent. 12: Emails emerge seeming to more closely link Donald Trump to convicted and deceased pedophile Jeffrey Epstein, increasing the pressure on the U.S. president. 13: Following a drawn-out roller-coaster ride, Cenovus Energy Inc.'s $8.6-billion acquisition of MEG Energy Corp. is finally closed to create a new oilsands giant. 13: The federal Liberal government unveils its first list of major economic infrastructure projects it's prioritizing, none of them involving Alberta-related initiatives. 18: Alberta's UCP government invokes the notwithstanding clause to push through a contentious three-pronged package of legislation affecting trans children and their parents. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... 18: Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives dramatically break ranks with President Donald Trump in voting en masse for the Department of Justice to release the so-called Epstein files. 19: Alberta's auditor general reports that the UCP government's failed attempt to privatize the province's medical lab services by hiring DynaLIFE cost taxpayers more than $109 million, and that the government wasn't fully transparent in assisting the investigation. 20: A 28-point plan to end the war in Ukraine allegedly drafted by Washington surfaces, pushing major territorial, military and political concessions from Kyiv. Allegations the plan was crafted solely by Russia also emerge. 21: U.S. President Donald Trump calls for the arrest and death of Democratic congress members after they implore the U.S. military to disobey illegal orders. 21: Longtime MAGA warrior Marjorie Taylor Greene says she's quitting the House of Representatives after breaking with President Donald Trump over his handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case and health care. 26: A massive fire sweeps through a Hong Kong highrise complex, leaving at least 160 dead and leading to multiple arrests over alleged corruption in renovation work. 26: Two National Guard soldiers deployed to Washington, D.C., by the country's Republican administration are shot, one of them fatally. An Afghan emigre who'd worked with the U.S. during that country's war is charged with first-degree murder. 27: Ottawa and the Alberta government ink a memorandum of understanding promoting a potential oil pipeline from Alberta's oilsands to the northwest B.C. coast by granting environmental exemptions. It's predicated on industry meeting environmental benchmarks but the deal prompts the wrath of some First Nations and the B.C. government. Their son Nick is charged. 16: Skate Canada said it is prohibiting national and international competition in Alberta, in response to the province's ban on transgender participation in female sports. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... 18: Canada's cannabis industry gets a boost after U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order reclassifies marijuana as a painkiller. 19: The report from the Alberta Next panel recommends an Alberta police force and referendums on leaving the Canada Pension Plan and taking more control over immigration. 20: Despite a congressional mandate to release all of the so-called Epstein files, many key documents are missing or redacted following a dump by the U.S. Department of Justice. 21: In a move widely seen as political, CBS pulls a 60 Minutes story critical of the Trump administration on human rights violations at an El Salvadoran prison hours before it was to air. 23: Elections Alberta sanctions a referendum question presented by the group Alberta Prosperity Project asking if respondents want a province independent from Canada. 25: In a Christmas Day setback for Russian forces in the nearly fouryear-long all-out war, Ukrainian troops complete their recapture of Kupyansk in the Kharkiv region. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2025 Postmedia Network Inc. But following public backlash, Kimmel returns six days later. 21: As Israeli pressure mounts on Gaza and the West Bank, Canada says it's recognizing a Palestinian state. 22: A news report alleges U.S. border czar Tom Homan accepted a $50,000 bribe in September, 2024 in exchange for securing contracts in a future Trump administration. 25: The federal government announces plans for money- hemorrhaging Canada Post, including moving almost exclusively to a community mailbox model. Postal workers walk off the job in response in a full strike that lasts until Oct. 10, when it becomes a rotating strike. 26: Former FBI chief James Comey is indicted, accused of lying of lying to Congress in a move widely condemned as a political assault by President Donald Trump who pronounces him guilty on social media. 26: Alberta's highest court rejects a bid for more freedom for Matthew de Grood, who killed five young people at a house party in the northwest community of Brentwood in 2014. De Grood had sought a conditional discharge or less stringent conditions, arguing he no longer posed a public threat. 29: Calgary-based Imperial Oil reveals it's pulling out of the city and eliminating 900 jobs. 30: Hundreds of senior U.S. military officials gathered in Quantico, Va., are told by President Donald Trump to prepare to wage war against people in America, whom he calls ""the enemy within."" OCTOBER 1: Premier Danielle Smith says she'll lead a technical advisory committee pushing for a new energy pipeline from Alberta to the west coast by promoting the project to Ottawa as one of national significance. 1: Legendary primate researcher and animal rights/environmental activist Jane Goodall dies at the age of 91. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... 3: Bishop of London Sarah Mullally is chosen as the next Archbishop of Canterbury, the first female spiritual leader in the Church of England in 1,400 years. 6: In the largest strike in the province's history, 51,000 Alberta teachers walk off the job in a dispute centring on class size, support and pay. 9: After two years of death and destruction, the first phase of a peace deal in Gaza between Israel and Hamas that includes an exchange of captives goes into effect. But the violence continues. 14: Voters in Newfoundland and Labrador oust John Hogan's Liberals after a 10-year reign, handing a slim majority government to Tony Wakeham's Progressive Conservatives. 17: While a report into medical procurement in Alberta doesn't directly implicate top UCP officials of wrongdoing, it concludes the process was deeply flawed. 18: Millions of Americans throughout the U.S. turn out for No Kings protests against the Trump administration. 19: A brazen heist at Paris's Louvre nets thieves crown jewels worth at least US$102 million. Several suspects are later arrested. 20: Calgary voters oust Mayor Jyoti Gondek in favour of former city councillor Jeromy Farkas while also ensuring 11 new faces on council. 24: A TV ad produced by the Ontario government using former U.S. president Ronald Reagan's comments attacking tariffs inflames U.S. President Donald Trump, who drops trade talks with Canada and increases duties on its products. 27: The UCP government tables back-to-work legislation for striking Alberta teachers under a contract conditions teachers had twice reject and with an intent to invoke the notwithstanding clause of the Charter to end the threeweek labour action. 30: King Charles revokes his brother Prince Andrew's royal titles and evicts him from his royal residence as fallout from Andrew's links to convicted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein continue. NOVEMBER 4: The federal Liberal government tables a 2025-26 budget leaning heavily on infrastructure project investments in response to the trade war with the U.S., while nearly doubling the deficit from the previous year. 4: Conservative MP Chris D'Entremont defects to the Liberals, decrying Pierre Poilievre's leadership style. Edmonton Conservative MP Matt Jeneroux resigns from the party a few days later, citing disappointment with the political status quo. 9: Flight cancellations at U.S. airports expand as the nation's federal government shutdown results in unpaid air traffic controllers being absent from work. 9: Several Democratic senators vote with Republican counterparts for a spending deal to end a six-month government shutdown. 10: U.S. President Donald Trump pardons his former personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani and others who took part in efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election they falsely claimed was fraudulent. 12: Emails emerge seeming to more closely link Donald Trump to convicted and deceased pedophile Jeffrey Epstein, increasing the pressure on the U.S. president. 13: Following a drawn-out roller-coaster ride, Cenovus Energy Inc.'s $8.6-billion acquisition of MEG Energy Corp. is finally closed to create a new oilsands giant. 13: The federal Liberal government unveils its first list of major economic infrastructure projects it's prioritizing, none of them involving Alberta-related initiatives. 18: Alberta's UCP government invokes the notwithstanding clause to push through a contentious three-pronged package of legislation affecting trans children and their parents. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... 18: Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives dramatically break ranks with President Donald Trump in voting en masse for the Department of Justice to release the so-called Epstein files. 19: Alberta's auditor general reports that the UCP government's failed attempt to privatize the province's medical lab services by hiring DynaLIFE cost taxpayers more than $109 million, and that the government wasn't fully transparent in assisting the investigation. 20: A 28-point plan to end the war in Ukraine allegedly drafted by Washington surfaces, pushing major territorial, military and political concessions from Kyiv. Allegations the plan was crafted solely by Russia also emerge. 21: U.S. President Donald Trump calls for the arrest and death of Democratic congress members after they implore the U.S. military to disobey illegal orders. 21: Longtime MAGA warrior Marjorie Taylor Greene says she's quitting the House of Representatives after breaking with President Donald Trump over his handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case and health care. 26: A massive fire sweeps through a Hong Kong highrise complex, leaving at least 160 dead and leading to multiple arrests over alleged corruption in renovation work. 26: Two National Guard soldiers deployed to Washington, D.C., by the country's Republican administration are shot, one of them fatally. An Afghan emigre who'd worked with the U.S. during that country's war is charged with first-degree murder. 27: Ottawa and the Alberta government ink a memorandum of understanding promoting a potential oil pipeline from Alberta's oilsands to the northwest B.C. coast by granting environmental exemptions. It's predicated on industry meeting environmental benchmarks but the deal prompts the wrath of some First Nations and the B.C. government. Their son Nick is charged. 16: Skate Canada said it is prohibiting national and international competition in Alberta, in response to the province's ban on transgender participation in female sports. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... 18: Canada's cannabis industry gets a boost after U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order reclassifies marijuana as a painkiller. 19: The report from the Alberta Next panel recommends an Alberta police force and referendums on leaving the Canada Pension Plan and taking more control over immigration. 20: Despite a congressional mandate to release all of the so-called Epstein files, many key documents are missing or redacted following a dump by the U.S. Department of Justice. 21: In a move widely seen as political, CBS pulls a 60 Minutes story critical of the Trump administration on human rights violations at an El Salvadoran prison hours before it was to air. 23: Elections Alberta sanctions a referendum question presented by the group Alberta Prosperity Project asking if respondents want a province independent from Canada. 25: In a Christmas Day setback for Russian forces in the nearly fouryear-long all-out war, Ukrainian troops complete their recapture of Kupyansk in the Kharkiv region. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2025 Postmedia Network Inc. title: The year that was a look back at 2025; Just like that, another year has come and gone. This is Part 1 of Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back at the significant events at home and abroad that defined 2025
body: JANUARY 1: Ten people are killed and three dozen injured when a pickup truck plows through New Year's revellers on New Orleans' Bourbon Street. A Texas native and U.S. military veteran is fatally shot in a shootout with police moments later. 1: Ukraine halts the transit of Russian natural gas through its territory when a 2019 agreement expires. Kyiv claims it's a major setback for Russia in its nearly three-yearlong war. 3: Former Calgary mayor Rod Sykes dies peacefully at home at the age of 95. Sykes is credited with laying the groundwork for Calgary's light rail transit system and was also mayor when the first section of Deerfoot Trail opened in 1975. 6: Embattled Prime Minister Justin Trudeau says he'll step down following a Liberal leadership race and prorogues Parliament until March 24. 6: A 65-year-old hospitalized Louisiana man becomes the first person in the U.S. to die from avian flu. 7: Social media giant Meta announces it's eliminating independent fact-checking on its platforms, citing concerns over increasing partisanship and censorship. 7: U.S. president-elect Donald Trump declares he'll use economic force to bring Canada under the American flag and refuses to rule out force to absorb Danish-controlled Greenland and reclaim the Panama Canal. 7-8: Tens of thousands chaotically flee from massive wildfires spread by powerful winds in the Los Angeles area. By the time they were contained nearly a month later, about 30 people had been killed and tens of thousands of buildings destroyed. 9: Newfoundland and Labrador approves a massive $227-billion hydroelectric deal to supply neighbouring Quebec with power, a pact five decades in the making. 10: President-elect Donald Trump is sentenced to a conditional discharge for his 2024 hush money case conviction. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... 12: Premier Danielle Smith attends an unannounced meeting with U.S. president-elect Donald Trump at his Mar-A- Largo, Fla., compound to discuss trade issues. 13: A freshly released U.S. Department of Justice report states president-elect Donald Trump would have been convicted of charges stemming from his alleged interference in the 2020 election aftermath. 15: Premier Danielle Smith is an outlier at a first ministers' conference whose other participants sign on to an agreement to fend off U.S. president-elect Donald Trump's threat of 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian imports. She cites opposition to including oil and gas exports as a possible weapon in that trade war. 15: A letter sent by Alberta Energy Minister Brian Jean to the Alberta Energy Regulator states a moratorium on coal mining in the Eastern Slopes has been lifted. The UCP government says the move was made to head off potential lawsuits from the mining industry. 19: A ceasefire between Israeli forces and Hamas goes into effect in Gaza after 15 months of devastation and the reported deaths of at least 47,000 Palestinians. Hostages held by Israel and Hamas are swapped. 20: In an indoor ceremony, Donald Trump is inaugurated as U.S. president for the second time in eight years. 20-21: States across the U.S. Deep South receive heavy snowfalls amid record cold temperatures caused by a displacement of the polar vortex. 21: A fire at a Turkish ski resort kills about 70 people. 27: Former Calgary city councillor Joe Magliocca is convicted of fraud but acquitted of breach of trust years after he filed multiple bogus expense claims for hotels, alcohol and meals. 28: A report from the public inquiry into foreign election interference concludes while Canada needs to strengthen its defences, the 2019 and 2021 federal votes weren't significantly affected by the phenomenon and that there's no evidence lawmakers acted in a consciously treasonous manner. 28: Calgary city council grudgingly approves a Green Line LRT plan for the city's southeast that would ultimately include controversial elevated rail in the downtown. 29: Sixty-seven people are killed when a U.S. army Black Hawk helicopter collides with an American Airlines passenger plane, sending both crashing into the Potomac River in Washington D.C. 31: The UCP government announces it has dismissed the Alberta Health Services board of directors and replaced them with a single administrator, citing the need to complete its restructuring of the province's health-care system. It's the second time since November 2022 that the board has been disbanded. FEBRUARY 3: Pushback mounts against billionaire Donald Trump confidante and so-called special government employee Elon Musk's efforts to close U.S. government agencies, fire civil servants and access federal databases. 4: In the worst mass shooting in the country's history, a massacre at an adult education centre in Orebro, Sweden, leaves 10 people dead. 4: The Aga Khan, spiritual leader of Ismaili Muslims, dies in Portugal at the age of 88. 5: During a visit to Washington by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, U.S. President Donald Trump proposes a U.S.-takeover and redevelopment of the devastated Gaza Strip and the displacement of its Palestinian population. 5: Right-wing Alberta lobby group Take Back Alberta, which was instrumental in ousting UCP premier Jason Kenney and in the rise of his successor, is fined more than $100,000 for breaking the province's electoral law. 5: It's reported the UCP government's dismissal of AHS CEO Athana Mentzelopoulos on Jan. 8 occurred two days before she was to bring her findings about concerns over provincial contracts being awarded to private surgical firms to Alberta's auditor general. 12: After speaking with Russian leader Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump says negotiations to end the war in Ukraine have begun, with the expectation Kyiv will have to cede some of its territory to Moscow and that American troops won't be included in any peacekeeping contingent. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... 13: A $200 tax on the registration of electric vehicles goes into effect in Alberta. 13: WestJet and Lufthansa Technik announce an agreement to build a $120-million aircraft engine maintenance facility at the Calgary airport. Construction will begin this year, with operation in 2027. 15: In an apparent further break between Europe and America, U.S. Vice-President JD Vance condemns the continent's governments for their alleged backsliding on civil rights, which draws a sharp rebuke. 17: European leaders hold an emergency meeting in response to the U.S. distancing itself from the NATO alliance, with some members vowing a more resolute approach to issues, including the war in Ukraine. 17: A Delta Air Lines flight out of Minneapolis crash-lands and flips over at Toronto's Pearson International Airport, leaving 21 people injured. 19: In an escalating war of words between the two leaders, U.S. President Donald Trump questions the legitimacy of his Ukrainian counterpart, referring to Volodymyr Zelenskyy as a ""dictator."" The previous day, Trump had claimed Ukraine had started the war against invading Russian forces. 24: Thousands of school support workers, including custodians, walk off the job in Calgary and other Alberta centres as they primarily seek higher wages. 24: On the third anniversary of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine, the U.S. breaks with its traditional allies in refusing to blame Moscow for the war during UN votes on resolutions aimed at ending the conflict. 25: Alberta Infrastructure Minister Peter Guthrie says he's leaving cabinet, citing frustration over what he calls the UCP government's unwillingness to address concerns over its procurement process. 25: In a move that breaks with decades of precedence, the Trump administration says it will hand pick members of the White House press pool. 26: Amid an emotionally and politically charged movement to search a Winnipeg area landfill for evidence of two murdered Indigenous women - Morgan Harris and Marcades Myran - human remains are found at the site. 27: Doug Ford's Progressive Conservatives win their third consecutive majority victory in Ontario's provincial election. 27: Alberta's UCP government delivers a budget with a $5.2-billion deficit, along with a long-promised tax cut. 28: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy finds himself in a very public Oval Office verbal clash with American counterpart Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance over Russia's invasion and a rare earth procurement deal. Zelenskyy is ejected from the White House and no deal is signed. MARCH 2: Washington says it will investigate Canadian softwood lumber imports that could lead to further duties on top of incoming general tariffs. 3: The UCP government announces Raymond Wyant, former Chief Judge of the Provincial Court of Manitoba, will lead a third-party investigation into alleged wrongdoing in AHS procurement practises. Critics say the process lacks teeth and accountability and call for a public inquiry. 4: Stock markets tumble as U.S. tariffs of 25 per cent on most goods and 10 per cent on energy products kick in against Canada and Mexico, which levy retaliatory duties. 4: The U.S. suspends military aid to Ukraine after supporting it for more than three years of full-scale Russian invasion. Around the same time, the Americans also cease providing military intelligence to Kyiv. 9: Former central bank chief Mark Carney handily wins the federal Liberal leadership race to succeed Justin Trudeau as prime minister. 10: Ontario slaps a 25 per cent duty on electricity exports to the U.S. in response to Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... American tariffs and threats against Canadian sovereignty. Premier Doug Ford relents after the U.S. reduces its steel and aluminum tariffs the following day but the trade war between the two countries continues. 10: Calgary-based oil and gas producers Whitecap Resources and Veren Energy announce a $15-billion merger. 13: A U.S. federal judge orders the reinstatement with back pay of thousands of probationary government workers fired by the Trump administration. 14: Canada's oldest company, long-beleaguered Hudson's Bay, says it will liquidate its stores but insists it's still searching for a way to refinance its operations. 14: A U.S. federal government shutdown is averted after a small group of senate Democrats led by majority leader Chuck Schumer agree to a GOP stop-gap spending bill. Many Democrats are furious over what they see as Schumer's appeasement of the Trump administration. 15-16: Massive storms sweep across multiple U.S. states, killing about 40 people and leaving hundreds of thousands without power. 17: Israeli air assaults shatter a January ceasefire in Gaza over a dispute regarding the release of Israeli hostages held by Hamas. Hundreds of Palestinians, including many women and children, are reported killed in the initial strikes. 18: Calgary school boards reach agreements with the Canadian Union of Public Employees, ending a three-week strike by more than 1,000 mostly custodial and maintenance employees. 23: Israeli troops kill 15 rescue workers in Gaza and bury their bodies with their ambulances, first insisting their vehicles weren't visible until videos show otherwise. 24: It's revealed top U.S. defence and security officials leaked details of air strikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen to the editor of the Atlantic on online chat site Signal. 26: Canadian country music star Shania Twain is named the 2025 Calgary Stampede parade marshal. 28: A 7.7 magnitude earthquake rocks central Myanmar, leaving more than 5,000 people dead. 28: An ice storm downs power lines and throws transportation into chaos across southern Ontario. APRIL 1: Canada's consumer carbon tax dies following a decision by new Prime Minister Mark Carney to kill it. 2: U.S. President Donald Trump's wide-ranging global tariffs regime kicks in, sparking fears of economic carnage. Canada is largely exempt from the latest round of duties that nonetheless send global stock indexes plummeting. 3: Chris Barber and Tamara Lich, leaders of the so-called 2022 Freedom Convoy protest in Ottawa, are convicted of mischief for their roles. 5: Hundreds of thousands in the U.S. and other countries gather to condemn the policies of U.S. President Donald Trump and his billionaire adviser Elon Musk. 6: The Washington Capitals' Alexander Ovechkin scores his 985th NHL goal in a game against the New York Islanders to break Wayne Gretzky's record. 8: More than 120 people are killed when a nightclub roof collapses in the Dominican Republic capital of Santo Domingo. 9: Amid a global market meltdown, the Trump White House pauses most of its reciprocal tariffs for 90 days, sending stock indexes soaring. 15: The Trump administration freezes nearly $3 billion in multiyear funding and contracts for Harvard University after the elite institution refuses to agree to White House demands it drop diversity, equity and inclusion measures. 15: Canada's Federal Court of Appeal dismisses a challenge of the Liberal government's ban on guns it says are at risk of being used in mass shootings. 15: Despite court orders to return permanent resident Kilmar Abrego Garcia from a notorious mega-prison in El Salvador to where he was deported by the U.S. government, the Trump administration continues in its refusal to do so. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... 21: An ailing Pope Francis dies at the age of 88. He was the first Latin American pontiff and had visited Canada in 2022, where he apologized for the Catholic Church's role in residential schools. 23: Fueling Minds Inc. pleads guilty to four bylaw offences linked to a massive E. coli outbreak at Calgary daycares that sickened hundreds of children in fall 2023. The commercial kitchen was later fined $10,000 for operating without a business licence at the time. 25: Gunmen massacre 28 people in an attack on tourists in India's restive Kashmir region. 26: Eleven people are killed and dozens injured when an SUV plows into a Filipino street festival in Vancouver. Kai- Ji Adam Lo, 30, who police say has had numerous mental-health encounters with them, is charged with multiple murder counts. 28: Canadians elect a minority Parliament, returning a Liberal government under new Prime Minister Mark Carney to power in a federal election coloured by U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs and threats to annex the country. 30: The U.S. and Ukraine sign a deal that will grant the Americans access to the war-torn country's rare earth minerals in exchange for continued U.S. military support in its war with Russia. MAY 2: Five-year Calgary police Chief Mark Neufeld abruptly and immediately resigns from his post, though his contract wasn't supposed to end until 2027. He's succeeded by deputy chief Katie McLellan. 2: Damien Kurek, Conservative MP-elect for Battle River-Crowfoot, says he's resigning his seat to allow Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre - who lost the Ottawa-area riding of Carleton last month - to run in a byelection in the riding. 5: In a provincewide address, Premier Danielle Smith says her government is creating a new panel to discuss the province's future within Canada along with a special negotiating team to confront Ottawa ahead of an anticipated citizen-led referendum on independence in 2026. 6: Prime Minister Mark Carney meets with U.S. President Donald Trump in the Oval Office for the first time since being elected prime minister, telling his American counterpart his country will never become America's 51st state. 8: American-born missionary Robert Prevost is chosen new pope for the world's 1.4 billion Roman Catholics and takes the name Leo XIV. 9: Onex Corp. announces the sale of a 25 per cent stake in WestJet to two large international airlinesU.S. giant Delta Air Lines and Korean Air. 11: Calgary Wild FC take to the new turf of McMahon Stadium for the professional women's team's first home game in the Northern Super League. 12: Alberta says it's indefinitely freezing its industrial carbon tax for heavy emitters at $95 a tonne. 13: A UN body concludes Russia bears responsibility for the 2014 shoot-down of Malaysia Airline Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine that killed 298 people. 16: In a contentious decision, the Alberta Energy Regulator green lights Australian coal mining firm Northback Holdings' application to conduct exploratory work at its Grassy Mountain site in the Crowsnest Pass. 16: Tornadoes begin sweeping through parts of the U.S. Midwest and south, leaving nearly 30 people dead. 18: Calgary Canucks defeat the Melfort Mustangs 7-2 at a packed Max Bell Centre to win the 2025 Centennial Cup. 19: Five years after Brexit took effect, the U.K. and EU sign a pact easing economic relations and travel barriers. 19: In an unusually strongly worded statement, Canada joins the U.K. and France in condemning Israel's blockade and renewed offensive in Gaza and threatening sanctions. 21: Alberta's k.d. lang is inducted into Canada's Country Music Hall of Fame during a ceremony at the National Music Centre. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... 22: Former Calgary city councillor Joe Magliocca apologizes for filing false expense claims before being given a six-month conditional sentence for his January fraud conviction. 26: Alberta's education minister vows to create provincewide stan- dards for school library material, stating dozens of books containing ""explicit sexual content"" were found in Calgary and Edmonton schools. 27: King Charles III reads the speech from the throne to open Canada's Parliament, the first time a monarch has done so since his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, performed the task in 1977. 28: A U.S. federal trade court strikes down the Trump administration's use of emergency powers to justify its sweeping international tariffs. JUNE 1: Audacious Ukrainian drone strikes from trucks driven far into Russia destroy more than 40 of the Kremlin's nuclear-capable bombers on military airfields. 2: A first ministers' conference in Saskatoon described by some participants as the best in memory yields vows to fast-track vital infrastructure projects throughout the country. 4: Washington's doubling of steel and aluminum tariffs to 50 per cent come into effect, severely impacting Canadian producers. 7: U.S. President Donald Trump orders California National Guard troops to deal with protests against federal government immigrant roundups in Los Angeles, contrary to the wishes of the state's governor. Two days later, he orders U.S. Marines to the area. 9: Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will move quickly to boost the country's defence spending to two per cent of Canada's GDP to meet NATO expectations. 10: Calgary Flames goaltender Dustin Wolf finishes second - behind Montreal's Lane Hutson - in voting for the NHL's rookie of the year award. 11: The much-revered and influential leader of the Beach Boys, Brian Wilson, dies at the age of 82. 11: Ex- Hollywood movie producer Harvey Weinstein is convicted of one criminal sex act but acquitted of another by a jury in his retrial. 12: The crash of an Air India Dreamliner during take off in Ahmedabad kills 241 people. 12: Alberta posts its highest number of measles cases in nearly 40 years, with 868 confirmed infections reported. The number of cases would near 2,000 by November. 13: Israel launches a massive wave of air strikes against Iran's nuclear infrastructure, scientists and military leaders that kills scores of them and provokes retaliation from the Islamic state. 14: A US$45-million parade is held in Washington, D.C., to mark the U.S. army's 250th anniversary but many see it co-opted by President Donald Trump to celebrate his 79th birthday. 14: Minnesota state Rep. Melissa Hortman and her husband are killed and another Democratic lawmaker injured in separate targeted shootings in the midwestern state. 15-17: G7 leaders and their invited guests gather in Kananaskis to discuss peace, war, AI, the economy and climate change. But due to a recalcitrant U.S. President Donald Trump who exits early, the event finishes without a final joint communique. 17: Florida Panthers repeat as Stanley Cup champions after defeating the Edmonton Oilers 5-1 in Game 6 of the finals. 18: After a 21-month wait, the UCP government releases survey results on Albertans' view of a provincial pension plan which shows 63 per cent of respondents opposed to the concept while 10 per cent approve. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann's look back .... 19: A rockslide at Bow Glacier Falls in Banff National Park kills two people, including a Calgary senior, and injures several others. 21: American warplanes bomb three Iranian nuclear sites, backing up Israeli's air campaign against the Islamic Republic. 23: In three Alberta provincial byelections, the NDP wins two races with Leader Naheed Nenshi becoming an MLA in Edmonton, while separatist parties show poorly. 24: Parkland Corp. shareholders vote in favour of $12.6 billion takeover by U.S.-based Sunoco. 27: Alberta Court of King's Bench grants an injunction against the UCP government's bid to ban gender-affirming care for minors, concluding it risks harming young people. 27: In a significant victory for U.S. President Donald Trump, the country's supreme court constrains the powers of individual judges to halt executive actions. 30: Fourteen years after it was removed, fluoride re-enters Calgary's water supply. 30: Canada becomes a liquid natural gas exporter with the departure of the first LNG cargo ship from the northern B.C. port of Kitimat, bound for Asia. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2025 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Third ex-cabinet minister pays fine for breaking Manitoba's conflict law
body: WINNIPEG - All three former Manitoba Progressive Conservative cabinet ministers fined for breaking the province's conflict of interest law have now paid up. Legislature Speaker Tom Lindsey says Cliff Cullen, who served as deputy premier, has paid his $12,000 fine. Former premier Heather Stefanson paid her $18,000 fine last month, and former economic development minister Jeff Wharton paid his $10,000 fine last month as well. The three were found by the province's ethics commissioner to have tried to get a mining project approved after the Progressive Conservatives lost the October 2023 election and before the incoming NDP government was sworn in. The commissioner said the three violated the caretaker convention — a long-standing parliamentary principle that forbids outgoing governments from making major decisions after losing an election. The commissioner ruled that, in doing so, the three improperly furthered the private interests of other people, contrary to the conflict law. Members of the legislature voted unanimously in favour of the fines last month, and all fines were paid within a 30- day deadline. Stefanson and Cullen have left politics. Wharton still holds a legislature seat. The controversy stemmed from a proposal by Calgary-based Sio Silica to drill thousands of wells over 24 years across a large swath of southeastern Manitoba, although only an initial phase was being considered for an environmental licence. The company planned to extract more than 30 million tonnes of high-purity quartz silica, used in semiconductors, solar panels, fibre optics and other products. The NDP government rejected the proposal a few months after being elected, partly due to concerns over the potential effect on water. Sio Silica recently submitted a new plan to drill fewer wells in a smaller area. Extraction would be phased in, reaching up to 500,000 tonnes annually by the fourth year, and water brought to the surface would undergo filtration and UV treatment before being returned down the wells, the company said in a recent submission to Manitoba's Clean Environment Commission. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2025.

title: This lawyer's not just battling prorogation. He's battling 'corrupt' Justin Trudeau
body: Liberals are magicians. Through sleights of hand and by proroguing Parliament, the Liberals could yet win another election with a new leader. Not so fast, shout defenders of democracy. David MacKinnon and Aris Lavranos - both living in Nova Scotia, both lawyers - have asked the Federal Court to weigh in on whether Trudeau's proroguing of Parliament was legal. Calgary-based Justice Centre for Constitutional Freedoms, a non-profit founded by John Carpay, offered up a legal team from Charter Advocates Canada. And on Feb. 13 and 14, Chief Justice Paul Crampton heard arguments for and against prorogation, and committed to rendering a swift decision before the issue becomes moot. Asking a court to reverse prorogation at a time like this; why bother? There's a government in place, with all its executive branch tools, pragmatists argue. Plus, proroguing Parliament - hitting the reset button - is a tactic that's been deployed by a host of prime ministers, including Sir John A. Macdonald, Brian Mulroney, Jean Chretien, Stephen Harper and now Justin Trudeau. Never has a governor general said no to a prime minister's request. In 2020, then Gov. Gen. Julie Payette agreed to prorogue Parliament on flimsier grounds in the aftermath of the WE Charity scandal and a Liberal government cabinet shuffle. The applicants' glimmer of hope lies in the 2019 decision of the Supreme Court of the U.K., which ruled then-prime minister Boris Johnson had prorogued unlawfully to avoid parliamentary scrutiny of the government's Brexit negotiations. If the Federal Court in Canada decides in a similar fashion, not only would Parliament resume immediately but future prime ministers might not be so cavalier in reaching for the prorogation button. In a recent Zoom conversation with MacKinnon, I asked him about the application and what propelled him to act. He's just driven from Montreal to his home in Amherst, N.S., through a ferocious snowstorm. Understandably, he's weary and from time to time in our conversation, he reaches up to rub the stubble on his jaw. This 70-year-old man has seen the dark side of humanity; he translated for criminal tribunals related to Rwanda, the Hague and Yugoslavia. He's not angry, but he is offended by a junior government lawyer's offhand suggestion: ""Citizens have a solution"" - complain to the federal ombudsman via your acting MP. MacKinnon strikes me as a caring man, with compassion for ""regular folks""- he speaks fondly of his work, decades ago, as a roughneck in Alberta's oil patch, as a longshoreman, even a morgue attendant. In a blog post shared online a few weeks ago, he describes life in his hometown of Amherst, ""a town that has fallen on hard times, as have many small communities in outlying areas during the reign of Justin Trudeau."" The place evokes JD Vance's ""Hillbilly Elegy,"" he writes. ""The men sport chest beards, the houses are often as not in disrepair and you can lease space for a dollar a foot in the 'downtown,' also visible from our home. It's not unusual to see a flaming-red, oversized SUV, with the ""FU Trudeau"" flag proudly flying from the box."" A lawyer, registered in two law societies in Canada, MacKinnon's reticent to talk about the merits of the application. ""I fully trust the Chief Justice to the extent that if he rules against us, he's right, not me,"" he assures me. ""This is a question of law and if we're interested in the rule of law, let the courts do their job."" With some prodding, MacKinnon frames the legal questions being debated before the Federal Court in terms that can be understood by non-lawyers. The prime minister gives the advice to prorogue, and the governor general acquiesces, MacKinnon explains. ""If the prime minister gives his advice, he has one duty but he wears two hats,"" MacKinnon continues. ""And one of them is as head of the Liberal party. So he must act as the head of the government when he gives that advice. If not, one line of reasoning might say that is a simulacrum of prorogation ... a deliberate attempt to subvert the will of Parliament."" MacKinnon is chagrined to learn I've read his blog post. In fact, it's the reason I've reached out to him. His words speak to a frustration I hear from others, workers and builders who gave the Liberals their proxy, thinking the party would have their back. Jody Wilson-Raybould took the bait too, as have many other smart folks. ""There is no shortage of reasons to hold Justin Trudeau in contempt,"" MacKinnon writes, ""but two of them come to mind as I write these words. Coincidentally, both concern Indigenous Canadians. ""The first is my recollection of Trudeau's comments in Rolling Stone magazine in the wake of the Patrick Brazeau charity boxing match staged between the senator and the prime minister... for Trudeau to say the following words bespoke a man lacking a fundamental quality as a human being, never mind a future prime minister. 'I wanted someone who would be a good foil, and we stumbled upon the scrappy tough-guy senator from an indigenous community. I saw it as the right kind of narrative, the right story to tell.'"" The second incident, MacKinnon writes, occurred behind closed doors. In the Jody Wilson-Raybould book ""Indian in the Cabinet: Speaking Truth to Power,"" the former justice minister described how she experienced ""a consistent and sustained effort"" by many people within the government to seek to politically interfere in the exercise of prosecutorial discretion in my role as the attorney general of Canada in an inappropriate effort to secure a Deferred Prosecution Agreement (DPA) with SNC-Lavalin. And, then she related that during a late 2018 meeting, Trudeau asked her ""to lie to protect a Crown government acting badly; a political party; a leader who was not taking responsibility."" MacKinnon concludes: ""Those two anecdotes exemplify for me two of the overarching qualities of this man that render him unfit for purpose: a lack of empathy, and a contempt for the rule of law, ironically the same two labels affixed to the reputation of his political enemy, Donald Trump."" It's maybe 90 minutes' drive from Amherst, N.S., to Charlottetown, P.E.I., the place where Confederation was set in motion by our founding fathers in 1864. This small town was the birthplace of Canada's sixth prime minister, as well as the father of Dwayne ""The Rock"" Johnson. It's a good place to contemplate the past and the future of our country, MacKinnon writes. ""A good place to plan a battle to bring down a corrupt prime minister and a corrupt Liberal party, steeped in hubris and disdain for the ordinary suffering of citizens getting by as best they can."" As fellow lawyers, we share a faith in the power and authority of the courts to protect democracy. But we know full well, to quote MacKinnon, not everyone is pleased when ""the court becomes our last refuge against a scoundrel."" B.C.'s free-drugs 'experiment' has left many dead.
