title: What's at stake in the four federal byelections on Monday, and what to expect
body: OTTAWA - Four federal byelections will be taking place on Monday, June 19, filling seats left vacant by the death of former Liberal minister Jim Carr as well as the departure of veteran MPs Marc Garneau (Liberal), Candice Bergen (Conservative) and Dave MacKenzie (Conservative). Two of these seats are considered safe for the Liberals and the two others would usually be guaranteed wins for the Conservatives. But political watchers will also be looking to see if the People's Party of Canada's Maxime Bernier manages to increase his party's results in Portage-Lisgar in Manitoba, and if the Conservatives can hang onto their seat in Oxford in southwestern Ontario. Here are some of the politics at play in the ridings that are set to elect brand-new MPs come Monday evening, and what the results could mean for the main parties at play. Portage-Lisgar (Manitoba) The Manitoba riding that belonged to former interim Conservative leader Candice Bergen has been in the national spotlight ever since People's Party of Canada leader Maxime Bernier decided to jump into the byelection. He's been fighting hard to establish himself as the stronger populist, over Conservative Branden Leslie, a former campaign director for Bergen. Bernier lashed out against his former party( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/maxime-bernier-lashes-out-at- conservative-party ) for promoting ""gender ideology, mass immigration, climate hysteria, the cult of diversity."" Leslie has fought back, accusing Bernier of being an ""opportunist from Quebec who will say or do anything he thinks people want to hear."" More recently, Leslie has been attacking Bernier for attending the World Economic Forum( https://nationalpost.com/opinion/by-election-descends-into-argument-over-whos-the-bigger-wef- sellout?utm_term=Autofeed&;utm_medium=Social&;utm_source=Twitter#Echobox=1686925757 ) in 2008 when Bernier was foreign affairs minister in Stephen Harper's government. ""It's becoming clearer and clearer to people that the strategy for the Conservatives... is to take the opportunity to absolutely crush the PPC and to crush Bernier,"" said Royce Koop, professor of political studies at the University of Manitoba. The main reason behind Bernier's decision to run in Portage-Lisgar is the fact that, Solomon Wiebe, the PPC candidate there in 2021, was the strongest performer in his party in the most recent election, with nearly 22 per cent of the vote. Bergen still easily won with 53 per cent of the votes. Recent polling by Mainstreet Research in the riding shows that the PPC may have gained some ground, with 27 per cent of voters saying they're leaning to Bernier's party, but Mainstreet's data analyst Robert Martin admits that the riding was ""extremely hard to poll"" and one should proceed with caution with these results. Martin pointed to the high number of Mennonites in the riding, who either do not own a cell phone or have a ""general distrust of technology, which is not good for a telephone pollster."" ""It's good to do a survey to see what people are thinking in the riding. But at the end of the day, if the PPC got 15 per cent or if the PPC won, I wouldn't be particularly surprised. It's good to have a benchmark but I think anything could kind of happen in this riding."" Koop said he thinks there is no question the Conservatives will win in Portage-Lisgar but still cautioned against placing too much significance on byelection results. ""If the PPC gets a respectful vote, sure, it's going to be embarrassing for the (Conservative) party. Will it hugely affect its strategy going forward? I'm not so sure about that... I don't think we should overstate the significance of these things, to be honest,"" he said. Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre stands beside candidate Arpan Khanna as he speaks at a rally in Woodstock, Ont., May 6, 2023. Oxford (Ontario) The real nail-biter on Monday could be the riding of Oxford in southwestern Ontario, where Conservative voters have been put off by internal battles over the nomination process. Mainstreet Research is polling the Liberal and Conservative candidates as neck-to-neck, at 38 per cent among decided voters in a recent survey. ""Days ago, I was a skeptic. Before we did this poll, I thought this was going to be the most boring one, literally. I'm surprised by it,"" said Martin, the data analyst. It all started when the Christian evangelicals' candidate of choice, Gerrit Van Dorland, a Conservative staffer who grew up in the riding, was disqualified from the nomination( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/conservative- party-disqualified-pro-life-nominee ) process by the party for failing to ""disclose required information during the candidate application process"". In the end, Arpan Khanna, who served as Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre's Ontario leadership campaign co- chair last year, won the nomination. Two Conservative riding association leaders then resigned, accusing the party of stacking the deck to help Khanna win the nomination. Former MP Dave MacKenzie, who held the riding between London and Hamilton, Ont. for the past 19 years, has since pledged to support Liberal candidate David Hilderley, a local real estate agent. MacKenzie has also been blasting Khanna for having strong roots elsewhere - in Brampton, Ont. not Oxford. ""He's burnt bridges. He's blown up the dam,"" said Peter Woolstencroft, a political science professor emeritus from the University of Waterloo, of MacKenzie's criticism. ""He has walked away 100 per cent, because nobody in Ottawa is going to thank him."" Liberals have been quietly saying that they do not expect to win Oxford, but they hope to get a better score than in previous elections, where their candidates were trailing behind MacKenzie by double digits. Martin pointed out that the Liberals have not only a local but also a relatively moderate candidate in David Hilderley, which could be an asset for them. ""This guy is not particularly controversial. It doesn't seem like he's a particularly left-wing Liberal, which definitely helps,"" he said. Winnipeg South Centre has long been considered a safe riding for the Liberals, but the Conservatives think they have a chance to change that in Monday's byelection. Winnipeg South Centre (Manitoba) Former Manitoba MP and Liberal cabinet minister Jim Carr passed away last December. His son Ben Carr announced he would run for his late father's Winnipeg South Centre seat less than two months later. The riding of Winnipeg South Centre is considered to be a safe seat for the Liberals, having held the riding for all but four years since it was created in 1988. The last time Conservatives represented it was during Stephen Harper's majority government, from 2011 to 2015. When visiting the riding at the start of June, Poilievre said he thought that Conservative candidate Damir Stipanovic, an air traffic controller and first-generation immigrant, had a shot at winning( https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/manitoba-byelection-federal-leaders-1.6863859 ). But it would be a long shot. ""We know that the Liberals' popularity has dipped in Manitoba. We know the Conservatives are popular. And so the question is, is that enough to actually elect the Conservative candidate? I'm not sure it is,"" said Royce Koop, professor of political studies at the University of Manitoba. ""If they (Conservatives) boost their vote share, they'll be happy with that. But if they win... that would mean that the Liberals are in pretty rough shape in Manitoba right now."" Koop however noted that voters could be swayed by positive feelings towards the late Jim Carr which could benefit his son. ""People will feel good about casting their ballots for him, I think, not necessarily for the Liberal Party right now,"" he said. Meanwhile, voters will have a challenge locating the checkbox for their preferred candidate among 48 candidates on the ballot, all running to be the next MP. That will set the record of the most names on a ballot( https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/winnipeg-south-centre-byelection-longest-ballot-48-1.6874926 ) of any federal election in Canadian history - thanks to a group called the Longest Ballot Committee, which deliberately sought to overwhelm the ballot to protest the first-past-the-post voting system. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau campaigns with Anna Gainey, the Liberal candidate in the Notre-Dame-de-Grâce- Westmount riding byelection, in Montreal on June 16, 2023. Notre-Dame-de-Grâce-Westmount (Quebec) There is little doubt former president of the Liberal Party of Canada Anna Gainey will be the next MP from Montreal: Notre-Dame-de-Grâce-Westmount is a riding that's as red as can be. ""Anna Gainey wears a lot of credentials within the Liberal party. She advised some ministers, she was with Canada 2000, which is a Liberal think tank, a major organization. So she is really a Liberal insider,"" said Daniel Béland, professor of political science at McGill University. In fact, she is so close to Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's inner circle that she and her husband, Tom Pitfield, accompanied the prime minister on his infamous Bahamas vacation to the Aga Khan's private island in 2016( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/liberal-mp-party-president-joined-trudeau-for-his-controversial-bahamas- vacation-with-the-aga-khan ), which led to the ethics commissioner concluding Trudeau violated the conflict of interest rules. The only question on Monday is how large Gainey's majority will be. Her rivals include the co-leader of the Green Party of Canada, Jonathan Pedneault, who is hoping to attract some votes from Liberal voters who feel frustrated that Trudeau's climate plan doesn't go far enough, fast enough. And once she is elected, there will be speculation to see if she makes it to Trudeau's cabinet amid rumours of a cabinet shuffle this summer. Beland said Gainey is ""certainly potential ministerial material"" and could make the cut ""at some point in the future"" if not right away. title: Where did 2025 go? A look back at the year that was
body: Just like that, another year has come and gone. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann looks back at significant events at home and abroad that defined 2025. JANUARY 1: Ten people are killed and three dozen injured when a pickup truck plows through New Year's revellers on New Orleans' Bourbon Street. A Texas native and U.S. military veteran is fatally shot in a shootout with police moments later. 1: Ukraine halts the transit of Russian natural gas through its territory when a 2019 agreement expires. Kyiv claims it's a major setback for Russia in its nearly three-year-long war. 3: Former Calgary mayor Rod Sykes dies peacefully at home at the age of 95. Sykes is credited with laying the groundwork for Calgary's light rail transit system and was also mayor when the first section of Deerfoot Trail opened in 1975. 6: Embattled Prime Minister Justin Trudeau says he'll step down following a Liberal leadership race and prorogues Parliament until March 24. 6: A 65-year-old hospitalized Louisiana man becomes the first person in the U.S. to die from avian flu. 7: Social media giant Meta announces it's eliminating independent fact-checking on its platforms, citing concerns over increasing partisanship and censorship. 7: U.S. president-elect Donald Trump declares he'll use economic force to bring Canada under the American flag and refuses to rule out force to absorb Danish-controlled Greenland and reclaim the Panama Canal. Flames overtake the intersection of Temescal Canyon and Pacific Coast Highway Fire at the Palisades Fire in California on January 7, 2025. 7-8: Tens of thousands chaotically flee from massive wildfires spread by powerful winds in the Los Angeles area. By the time they were contained nearly a month later, about 30 people had been killed and tens of thousands of buildings destroyed. 9: Newfoundland and Labrador approves a massive $227-billion hydroelectric deal to supply neighbouring Quebec with power, a pact five decades in the making. 10: President-elect Donald Trump is sentenced to a conditional discharge for his 2024 hush money case conviction. 12: Premier Danielle Smith attends an unannounced meeting with U.S. president-elect Donald Trump at his Mar-A- Largo, Fla., compound to discuss trade issues. 13: A freshly released U.S. Department of Justice report states president-elect Donald Trump would have been convicted of charges stemming from his alleged interference in the 2020 election aftermath. 15: Premier Danielle Smith is an outlier at a first ministers' conference whose other participants sign on to an agreement to fend off U.S. president-elect Donald Trump's threat of 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian imports. She cites opposition to including oil and gas exports as a possible weapon in that trade war. 15: A letter sent by Alberta Energy Minister Brian Jean to the Alberta Energy Regulator states a moratorium on coal mining in the eastern slopes has been lifted. The UCP government says the move was made to head off potential lawsuits from the mining industry. 19: A ceasefire between Israeli forces and Hamas goes into effect in Gaza after 15 months of devastation and the reported deaths of at least 47,000 Palestinians. Hostages held by Israel and Hamas are swapped. 20: In an indoor ceremony, Donald Trump is inaugurated as U.S. president for the second time in eight years. 20-21: States across the U.S. deep south receive heavy snowfalls amid record cold temperatures caused by a displacement of the polar vortex. 21: A fire at a Turkish ski resort kills about 70 people. Former Calgary city councillor Joe Magliocca walks to the Calgary Courts Centre for the verdict in his fraud and breach of trust trial on January 27, 2025. 27: Former Calgary city councillor Joe Magliocca is convicted of fraud but acquitted of breach of trust years after he filed multiple bogus expense claims for hotels, alcohol and meals. 28: A report from the public inquiry into foreign election interference concludes while Canada needs to strengthen its defences, the 2019 and 2021 federal votes weren't significantly impacted by the phenomenon and that there's no evidence lawmakers acted in a consciously treasonous manner. 28: Calgary city council grudgingly approves a Green Line LRT plan for the city's southeast that would ultimately include controversial elevated rail in the downtown. 29: Sixty-seven people are killed when a U.S. Army Blackhawk helicopter collides with an American Airlines passenger plane, sending both crashing into the Potomac River at Washington D.C. 31: The UCP government announces it's dismissed the Alberta Health Services board of directors and replaced them with a single administrator, citing the need to complete its restructuring of the province's health care system. It's the second time since November 2022 that the board has been disbanded. FEBRUARY 3: Pushback mounts against billionaire Donald Trump confidante and so-called special government employee Elon Musk's efforts to close U.S. government agencies, fire civil servants and access federal databases. 4: In the worst mass shooting in the country's history, a massacre at an adult education centre in Orebro, Sweden, leaves 10 people dead. 4: The Aga Khan, spiritual leader of Ismaili Muslims, dies in Portugal at the age of 88. 5: During a visit to Washington by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, U.S. President Donald Trump proposes a U.S.-takeover and redevelopment of the devastated Gaza Strip and the displacement of its Palestinian population. 5: Right-wing Alberta lobby group Take Back Alberta, which was instrumental in ousting UCP premier Jason Kenney and in the rise of his successor, is fined more than $100,000 for breaking the province's electoral law. 5: It's reported the UCP government's dismissal of AHS CEO Athana Mentzelopoulos on Jan. 8 occurred two days before she was to bring her findings about concerns over provincial contracts being awarded to private surgical firms to Alberta's auditor general. WestJet CEO Alexis von Hoensbroech and Lufthansa Technik Canada CEO Max Schramm chat on February 13, 2025, after WestJet and Lufthansa Technik announced a 15-year, multi-billion-dollar contract to build and operate a maintenance facility in Calgary to repair and maintain LEAP-1B aircraft engines. 12: After speaking with Russian leader Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump says negotiations to end the war in Ukraine have begun, with the expectation Kyiv will have to cede some of its territory to Moscow and that American troops won't be included in any peacekeeping contingent. 13: A $200 tax on the registration of electric vehicles goes into effect in Alberta. 13: WestJet and Lufthansa Technik announce an agreement to build a $120-million aircraft engine maintenance facility at the Calgary airport. A makeshift memorial of flowers, candles and a letter are seen on the Hollywood Walk of Fames Star of the late U.S. actor and director Rob Reiner on December 16, 2025, two days after he and his wife were found dead in the home in Brentwood, California. 16: Skate Canada said it is prohibiting national and international competition in Alberta, in response to the province's ban on transgender participation in female sports. 18: Canada's cannabis industry gets a boost after U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order reclassifies marijuana as a painkiller. 19: The report from the Alberta Next panel recommends an Alberta police force and referendums on leaving the Canada Pension Plan and taking more control over immigration. 20: Despite a congressional mandate to release all of the so-called Epstein files, many key documents are missing or redacted following a dump by the U.S. Department of Justice. 21: In a move widely seen as political, CBS pulls a 60 Minutes story critical of the Trump administration on human rights violations at an El Salvadoran prison hours before it was to air. 23: Elections Alberta sanctions a referendum question presented by the group Alberta Prosperity Project asking if respondents want a province independent from Canada. 25: In a Christmas Day setback for Russian forces in the nearly four-year-long all-out war, Ukrainian troops complete their recapture of the city of Kupyansk in the Kharkiv region. 30: A major water main break near 16th Avenue and Sarcee Trail N.W. disrupts service to hundreds of homes and businesses while also trapping motorists in a flood. Water usage restrictions were enacted the next day. The break is likely on the same feeder main that ruptured in 2024, officials said. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2025 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

Title: Where did 2025 go? A look back at the year that was
Body: Just like that, another year has come and gone. Postmedia Calgary journalist Bill Kaufmann looks back at significant events at home and abroad that defined 2025. JANUARY 1: Ten people are killed and three dozen injured when a pickup truck plows through New Year's revellers on New Orleans' Bourbon Street. A Texas native and U.S. military veteran is fatally shot in a shootout with police moments later. 1: Ukraine halts the transit of Russian natural gas through its territory when a 2019 agreement expires. Kyiv claims it's a major setback for Russia in its nearly three-year-long war. 3: Former Calgary mayor Rod Sykes dies peacefully at home at the age of 95. Sykes is credited with laying the groundwork for Calgary's light rail transit system and was also mayor when the first section of Deerfoot Trail opened in 1975. 6: Embattled Prime Minister Justin Trudeau says he'll step down following a Liberal leadership race and prorogues Parliament until March 24. 6: A 65-year-old hospitalized Louisiana man becomes the first person in the U.S. to die from avian flu. 7: Social media giant Meta announces it's eliminating independent fact-checking on its platforms, citing concerns over increasing partisanship and censorship. 7: U.S. president-elect Donald Trump declares he'll use economic force to bring Canada under the American flag and refuses to rule out force to absorb Danish-controlled Greenland and reclaim the Panama Canal. Flames overtake the intersection of Temescal Canyon and Pacific Coast Highway Fire at the Palisades Fire in California on January 7, 2025. 7-8: Tens of thousands chaotically flee from massive wildfires spread by powerful winds in the Los Angeles area. By the time they were contained nearly a month later, about 30 people had been killed and tens of thousands of buildings destroyed. 9: Newfoundland and Labrador approves a massive $227-billion hydroelectric deal to supply neighbouring Quebec with power, a pact five decades in the making. 10: President-elect Donald Trump is sentenced to a conditional discharge for his 2024 hush money case conviction. 12: Premier Danielle Smith attends an unannounced meeting with U.S. president-elect Donald Trump at his Mar-A- Largo, Fla., compound to discuss trade issues. 13: A freshly released U.S. Department of Justice report states president-elect Donald Trump would have been convicted of charges stemming from his alleged interference in the 2020 election aftermath. 15: Premier Danielle Smith is an outlier at a first ministers' conference whose other participants sign on to an agreement to fend off U.S. president-elect Donald Trump's threat of 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian imports. She cites opposition to including oil and gas exports as a possible weapon in that trade war. 15: A letter sent by Alberta Energy Minister Brian Jean to the Alberta Energy Regulator states a moratorium on coal mining in the eastern slopes has been lifted. The UCP government says the move was made to head off potential lawsuits from the mining industry. 19: A ceasefire between Israeli forces and Hamas goes into effect in Gaza after 15 months of devastation and the reported deaths of at least 47,000 Palestinians. Hostages held by Israel and Hamas are swapped. 20: In an indoor ceremony, Donald Trump is inaugurated as U.S. president for the second time in eight years. 20-21: States across the U.S. deep south receive heavy snowfalls amid record cold temperatures caused by a displacement of the polar vortex. 21: A fire at a Turkish ski resort kills about 70 people. Former Calgary city councillor Joe Magliocca walks to the Calgary Courts Centre for the verdict in his fraud and breach of trust trial on January 27, 2025. 27: Former Calgary city councillor Joe Magliocca is convicted of fraud but acquitted of breach of trust years after he filed multiple bogus expense claims for hotels, alcohol and meals. 28: A report from the public inquiry into foreign election interference concludes while Canada needs to strengthen its defences, the 2019 and 2021 federal votes weren't significantly impacted by the phenomenon and that there's no evidence lawmakers acted in a consciously treasonous manner. 28: Calgary city council grudgingly approves a Green Line LRT plan for the city's southeast that would ultimately include controversial elevated rail in the downtown. 29: Sixty-seven people are killed when a U.S. Army Blackhawk helicopter collides with an American Airlines passenger plane, sending both crashing into the Potomac River at Washington D.C. 31: The UCP government announces it's dismissed the Alberta Health Services board of directors and replaced them with a single administrator, citing the need to complete its restructuring of the province's health care system. It's the second time since November 2022 that the board has been disbanded. FEBRUARY 3: Pushback mounts against billionaire Donald Trump confidante and so-called special government employee Elon Musk's efforts to close U.S. government agencies, fire civil servants and access federal databases. 4: In the worst mass shooting in the country's history, a massacre at an adult education centre in Orebro, Sweden, leaves 10 people dead. 4: The Aga Khan, spiritual leader of Ismaili Muslims, dies in Portugal at the age of 88. 5: During a visit to Washington by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, U.S. President Donald Trump proposes a U.S.-takeover and redevelopment of the devastated Gaza Strip and the displacement of its Palestinian population. 5: Right-wing Alberta lobby group Take Back Alberta, which was instrumental in ousting UCP premier Jason Kenney and in the rise of his successor, is fined more than $100,000 for breaking the province's electoral law. 5: It's reported the UCP government's dismissal of AHS CEO Athana Mentzelopoulos on Jan. 8 occurred two days before she was to bring her findings about concerns over provincial contracts being awarded to private surgical firms to Alberta's auditor general. WestJet CEO Alexis von Hoensbroech and Lufthansa Technik Canada CEO Max Schramm chat on February 13, 2025, after WestJet and Lufthansa Technik announced a 15-year, multi-billion-dollar contract to build and operate a maintenance facility in Calgary to repair and maintain LEAP-1B aircraft engines. 12: After speaking with Russian leader Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump says negotiations to end the war in Ukraine have begun, with the expectation Kyiv will have to cede some of its territory to Moscow and that American troops won't be included in any peacekeeping contingent. 13: A $200 tax on the registration of electric vehicles goes into effect in Alberta. 13: WestJet and Lufthansa Technik announce an agreement to build a $120-million aircraft engine maintenance facility at the Calgary airport. Construction will begin this year, with operation in 2027. 15: In an apparent further break between Europe and America, U.S. Vice-President JD Vance condemns the continent's governments for their alleged backsliding on civil rights, which draws a sharp rebuke. 17: European leaders hold an emergency meeting in response to the U.S. distancing itself from the NATO alliance, with some members vowing a more resolute approach to issues, including the war in Ukraine. 17: A Delta Airlines flight out of Minneapolis crash-lands and flips over at Toronto's Pearson International Airport, leaving 21 people injured. 19: In an escalating war of words between the two leaders, U.S. President Donald Trump questions the legitimacy of his Ukrainian counterpart, referring to Volodymyr Zelensky as a ""dictator."" The previous day, Trump had claimed Ukraine had started the war against invading Russian forces. 24: Thousands of school support workers, including custodians, walk off the job in Calgary and other Alberta centres as they primarily seek higher wages. 24: On the third anniversary of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine, the U.S. breaks with its traditional allies in refusing to blame Moscow for the war during UN votes on resolutions aimed at ending the conflict. 25: Alberta Infrastructure Minister Peter Guthrie says he's leaving cabinet, citing frustration over what he calls the UCP government's unwillingness to address concerns over its procurement process. U.S. Vice-President JD Vance speaks during a meeting with President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office at the White House on February 28, 2025. 25: In a move that breaks with decades of precedence, the Trump administration says it will hand pick members of the White House press pool. 26: Amid an emotionally and politically charged movement to search a Winnipeg area landfill for evidence of two murdered Indigenous women - Morgan Harris and Marcades Myran - human remains are found at the site. 27: Doug Ford's Progressive Conservatives win their third consecutive majority victory in Ontario's provincial election. 27: Alberta's UCP government delivers a budget with a $5.2-billion deficit, along with a long-promised tax cut. 28: Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelensky verbally clash publicly in the Oval Office with American counterpart Donald Trump and vice-president JD Vance over Russia's invasion and a rare earth procurement deal. Zelensky is ejected from the White House and no deal is signed. MARCH 2: Washington says it will investigate Canadian softwood lumber imports that could lead to further duties on top of incoming general tariffs. 3: The UCP government announces Raymond Wyant, former Chief Judge of the Provincial Court of Manitoba, will lead a third-party investigation into alleged wrongdoing in AHS procurement practises. Critics say the process lacks teeth and accountability and call for a public inquiry. 4: Stock markets tumble as U.S. tariffs of 25 per cent on most goods and 10 per cent on energy products kick in against Canada and Mexico, which levy retaliatory duties. 4: The U.S. suspends military aid to Ukraine after supporting it for more than three years of full-scale Russian invasion. Around the same time, the Americans also cease providing military intelligence to Kyiv. 9: Former central bank chief Mark Carney handily wins the federal Liberal leadership race to succeed Justin Trudeau as prime minister. Sale signs fill the doors of the downtown Calgary Hudson's Bay Company store on Wednesday May 28, 2025. 10: Ontario slaps a 25 per cent duty on electricity exports to the U.S. in response to American tariffs and threats against Canadian sovereignty. Premier Doug Ford relents after the U.S. reduces its steel and aluminum tariffs the following day but the trade war between the two countries continues. 10: Calgary-based oil and gas producers Whitecap Resources and Veren Energy announce a $15-billion merger. 13: A U.S. federal judge orders the reinstatement with back pay of thousands of probationary government workers fired by the Trump administration. 14: Canada's oldest company, long-beleaguered Hudson's Bay, says it will liquidate its stores but insists it's still searching for a way to refinance its operations. 14: A U.S. federal government shutdown is averted after a small group of senate Democrats led by majority leader Chuck Schumer agree to a GOP stopgap spending bill. Many Democrats are furious over what they see as Schumer's appeasement of the Trump administration. 15-16: Massive storms sweep across multiple U.S. states, killing about 40 people and leaving hundreds of thousands without power. 17: Israeli air assaults shatter a January ceasefire in Gaza over a dispute over the release of Israeli hostages held by Hamas. Hundreds of Palestinians, including many women and children, are reported killed in the initial strikes. 18: Calgary school boards reach agreements with the Canadian Union of Public Employees, ending a three-week strike by more than 1,000 mostly custodial and maintenance employees. 23: Israeli troops kill 15 rescue workers in Gaza and bury their bodies with their ambulances, first insisting their vehicle weren't visible until videos show otherwise. 24: It's revealed top U.S. defence and security officials leaked details of airstrikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen to the editor of the Atlantic on online chat site Signal. Calgary Stampede parade marshal Shania Twain smiles as she prepares to lead the parade in downtown Calgary on Friday, July 4, 2025. 26: Canadian country music star Shania Twain is named the 2025 Calgary Stampede parade marshal. 28: A 7.7 magnitude earthquake rocks central Myanmar, leaving more than 5,000 people dead. 28: An ice storm downs power lines and throws transportation into chaos across southern Ontario. APRIL 1: Canada's consumer carbon tax dies following a decision by new Prime Minister Mark Carney to kill it. 2: U.S. President Donald Trump's wide-ranging global tariffs regime kicks in, sparking fears of economic carnage. Canada is largely exempt from the latest round of duties that nonetheless send global stock indexes plummeting. 3: Chris Barber and Tamara Lich, leaders of the so-called 2022 Freedom Convoy protest in Ottawa, are convicted of mischief for their roles. 5: Hundreds of thousands in the U.S. and other countries gather to condemn the policies of U.S. President Donald Trump and his billionaire adviser Elon Musk. Hockey legend Wayne Gretzky greets Washington Capitals left wing Alex Ovechkin during a ceremony after he scored his 895th career goal against New York Islanders in Elmont, N.Y., on April 6, 2025. 6: The Washington Capitals' Alex Ovechkin scores his 985th NHL goal in a game against the New York Islanders to break Wayne Gretzky's record. 8: More than 120 people are killed following a nightclub roof collapse in the Dominican Republic capital of Santo Domingo. 9: Amid a global market meltdown, the Trump White House pauses most of its reciprocal tariffs for 90 days, sending stock indexes soaring. 15: The Trump administration freezes nearly $3 billion in multi-year funding and contracts for Harvard University after the elite institution refuses to agree to White House demands it drop diversity, equity and inclusion measures. 15: Canada's Federal Court of Appeal dismisses a challenge of the Liberal government's ban on guns it says are at risk of being used in mass shootings. 15: Despite court orders to return permanent resident Kilmar Abrego Garcia from a notorious mega-prison in El Salvador to where he was deported by the U.S. government, the Trump administration continues in its refusal to do so. St. Mary's Cathedral mourns the passing of Pope Francis in Calgary on Monday, April 21, 2025. 21: An ailing Pope Francis dies at the age of 88. He was the first Latin American pontiff and had visited Canada in 2022, where he apologized for the Catholic Church's role in residential schools. 23: Fueling Minds Inc. pleads guilty to four bylaw offences linked to a massive E. coli outbreak at Calgary daycares that sickened hundreds of children in fall 2023. The commercial kitchen was later fined $10,000 for operating without a business licence at the time. 25: Gunmen massacre 28 people in an attack on tourists in India's restive Kashmir region. 26: Eleven people are killed and dozens injured when an SUV plows into a Filipino street festival in Vancouver. Kai- Ji Adam Lo, 30, who police say has had numerous mental-health encounters with them, is charged with multiple murder counts. Canada's Prime Minister and Liberal party Leader Mark Carney dances at a victory party in Ottawa on April 29, 2025. 28: Canadians elect a minority Parliament, returning a Liberal government under new Prime Minister Mark Carney to power in a federal election coloured by U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs and threats to annex the country. 30: The U.S. and Ukraine sign a deal that will grant the Americans access to the war-torn country's rare earth minerals in exchange for continued U.S. military support in its war with Russia. MAY 2: Five-year Calgary police Chief Mark Neufeld abruptly and immediately resigns from his post, though his contract wasn't supposed to end until 2027. He's succeeded by deputy chief Katie McLellan. 2: Damien Kurek, Conservative MP-elect for Battle River-Crowfoot, says he's resigning his seat to allow Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre - who lost the Ottawa-area riding of Carleton last month - to run in a byelection in the riding. 5: In a provincewide address, Premier Danielle Smith says her government is creating a new panel to discuss the province's future within Canada along with a special negotiating team to confront Ottawa ahead of an anticipated citizen-led referendum on independence in 2026. 6: Prime Minister Mark Carney meets with U.S. President Donald Trump in the Oval Office for the first time since being elected prime minister, telling his American counterpart his country will never become America's 51st state. 8: American-born missionary Robert Prevost is chosen new pope for the world's 1.4 billion Roman Catholics and takes the name Leo XIV. 9: Onex Corp. announces the sale of a 25 per cent stake in WestJet to two large international airlines - U.S. giant Delta Air Lines and Korean Air. Wild FC midfielder Farkhuna Muhtaj and team mascot Echo pose by her spot in the team's new locker room at McMahon Stadium on Friday, May 9, 2025. 11: Calgary Wild FC take to the new turf of McMahon Stadium for the professional women's team's first home game in the Northern Super League. 12: Alberta says it's indefinitely freezing its industrial carbon tax for heavy emitters at $95 a tonne. 13: A UN body concludes Russia bears responsibility for the 2014 shoot-down of Malaysia Airline Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine that killed 298 people. 16: In a contentious decision, the Alberta Energy Regulator green lights Australian coal mining firm Northback Holdings' application to conduct exploratory work at its Grassy Mountain site in the Crowsnest Pass. 16: Tornadoes begin sweeping through parts of the U.S. Midwest and south, leaving nearly 30 people dead. 18: Calgary Canucks defeat the Melfort Mustangs 7-2 at a packed Max Bell Centre to win the 2025 Centennial Cup. 19: Five years after Brexit took effect, the U.K. and EU sign a pact easing economic relations and travel barriers. 19: In an unusually strongly worded statement, Canada joins the U.K. and France in condemning Israel's blockade and renewed offensive in Gaza and threatening sanctions. Country music icon k.d. lang during the plaque ceremony for their induction into the Canadian Country Music Hall of Fame in Calgary on May 21, 2025. 21: Alberta's k.d. lang is inducted into Canada's Country Music Hall of Fame during a ceremony at the National Music Centre. 22: Former Calgary city councillor Joe Magliocca apologizes for filing false expense claims before being given a six-month conditional sentence for his January fraud conviction. 26: Alberta's education minister vows to create provincewide standards for school library material, stating dozens of books containing ""explicit sexual content"" were found in Calgary and Edmonton schools. 27: Kings Charles III reads the speech from the throne to open Canada's Parliament, the first time a monarch has done so since his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, performed the task in 1977. 28: A U.S. federal trade court strikes down the Trump administrations use of emergency powers to justify its sweeping international tariffs. JUNE 1: Audacious Ukrainian drone strikes from trucks driven far into Russia destroy more than 40 of the Kremlin's nuclear-capable bombers on military airfields. 2: A first ministers' conference in Saskatoon described by some participants as the best in memory yields vows to fast-track vital infrastructure projects throughout the country. 4: Washington's doubling of steel and aluminum tariffs to 50 per cent come into effect, severely impacting Canadian producers. 7: U.S. President Donald Trump orders California National Guard troops to deal with protests against federal government immigrant roundups in Los Angeles, contrary to the wishes of the state's governor. Two days later, he orders U.S. Marines to the area. 9: Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will move quickly to boost the country's defence spending to two per cent of Canada's GDP to meet NATO expectations. 10. Calgary Flames goaltender Dustin Wolf finishes second - behind Montreal's Lane Hutson - in voting for the NHL's rookie of the year award. Brian Wilson of The Beach Boys, pictured in 1976. 11: The much-revered and influential leader of the Beach Boys, Brian Wilson, dies at the age of 82. 11: Ex-Hollywood movie producer Harvey Weinstein is convicted of one criminal sex act but acquitted of another by a jury in his retrial. 12: The crash of an Air India Dreamliner during take off in Ahmedabad kills 241 people. 12: Alberta posts its highest number of measles cases in nearly 40 years, with 868 confirmed infections reported. The number of cases would near 2,000 by November. 13: Israel launches a massive wave of airstrikes against Iran's nuclear infrastructure, scientists and military leaders that kills scores of them and provokes retaliation from the Islamic state. 14: A US$45-million parade is held in Washington, D.C., to mark the U.S. Army's 250th anniversary but many see it co-opted by President Donald Trump to celebrate his 79th birthday. 14: Minnesota state Rep. Melissa Hortman and her husband are killed and another Democratic lawmaker injured in separate targeted shootings in the midwestern state. 15-17: G7 leaders and their invited guests gather in Kananaskis to discuss peace, war, AI, the economy and climate change. But due to a recalcitrant U.S. President Donald Trump who exits early, the event finishes without a final joint communique. 17. Florida Panthers repeat as Stanley Cup champions after defeating the Edmonton Oilers 5-1 in Game 6 of the finals. 18: After a 21-month wait, the UCP government releases survey results on Albertans' view of a provincial pension plan which shows 63 per cent of respondents opposed to the concept while 10 per cent approve. The site of a fatal rockslide at Bow Glacier Falls can be seen from the edge of the closure area on June 20, 2025, off the Icefields Parkway north of Banff. 19: A rockslide at Bow Glacier Falls in Banff National Park kills two people, including a Calgary senior, and injures several others. 21: American warplanes bomb three Iranian nuclear sites, backing up Israeli's air campaign against the Islamic Republic. 23: In three Alberta provincial byelections, the NDP wins two races with Leader Naheed Nenshi becoming an MLA in Edmonton, while separatist parties show poorly. 24: Parkland Corp. shareholders vote in favour of $12.6 billion takeover by U.S.-based Sunoco. 27: Alberta Court of King's Bench grants an injunction against the UCP government's bid to ban gender-affirming care for minors, concluding it risks harming young people. 27: In a significant victory for U.S. President Donald Trump, the country's supreme court constrains the powers of individual judges to halt executive actions. 30: Fourteen years after it was removed, fluoride re-enters Calgary's water supply. 30: Canada becomes a liquid natural gas exporter with the departure of the first LNG cargo ship from the northern B.C. port of Kitimat, bound for Asia. JULY 1: The Trump administration says it's withholding once-promised precision arms for Ukraine including air defence weaponry. 2: The UCP government announces the creation of a new provincial police force - the Alberta Sheriff's Police Service - to fill in law enforcement gaps and offer an alternative for municipalities. 2: One-time superstar rapper Sean (Diddy) Combs is acquitted on sex trafficking and racketeering charges but convicted of prostitution-related offences. He's sentenced to four years in prison in October. 3: After marathon haggling and debate, the U.S. Congress passes President Donald Trump's contentious spending bill that promises cuts to social benefits and axes taxes mainly for the wealthy, along with huge spending increases on immigration-related enforcement. A man looks at a damaged road after severe flash flooding that occured during the July 4 holiday weekend, in Hunt, Texas, on July 6, 2025. 4: A massive flash flood in central Texas fatally sweeps away about 140 people, many of them children. The tragedy unleashes a political firestorm over federal efforts to notify and help those impacted. 7: U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi insists a client list linked to the late convicted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein doesn't exist, walking back her previous insistence she was preparing to release it. The reversal sparks a firestorm, including a backlash among President Donald Trump's supporters and infighting within his cabinet. 8: It's revealed that four current and former members of the Canadian Armed Forces have been charged with offences related to allegedly organizing and training a violent far-right movement. 10: Even as the two countries talk about reaching a quick trade agreement, U.S. President Donald Trump announces Canada will be hit with 35 per cent tariffs as of Aug. 1. 14: Alberta surpasses the entire U.S. in total reported number of measles cases, at over 1,300. 14: It's revealed the CIA, despite six decades of denials, was aware of the activities of Lee Harvey Oswald in the months leading up the assassination of President John F. Kennedy and that an agency operative had stonewalled access to documents on the case. 14: In an apparent reversal of his loyalties in the conflict, U.S. President Donald Trump vows to continue arming Ukraine and threatens Russia with sanctions unless it agrees to a ceasefire within 50 days. 15: Calgary police Const. Craig Stothard is charged with second-degree murder in the shooting deaths of Levon Wildman and Wesley Davidson during a May 2023 incident in the city's northeast. Mourners and music fans line the streets to pay their respects ahead of the funeral cortege of Ozzy Osbourne, the late lead singer of Black Sabbath, in Birmingham, central England on July 30, 2025. 22: Legendary heavy metal rock figure and Black Sabbath front man Ozzy Osbourne dies at the age of 76. 23: In an advisory opinion, the UN's top court says countries could be in violation of international law if they fail to take efforts to reduce climate change. 24: All five hockey players including former NHL skaters who were accused of sexually assaulting a woman during a 2018 junior tournament in London, Ont., are acquitted. 24: Amid the Israel-Gaza conflict, France recognizes the state of Palestine. Canada follows suit days later. AUGUST 1: Canada is hit with American tariffs of 35 per cent that hit sectors outside the U.S.-Canada-Mexico trade agreement. 1: It's revealed notorious sex offender Ghislaine Maxwell was transferred to a minimum-security prison in Texas after a meeting between her lawyer and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, who'd been President Donald Trump's personal lawyer. 2: U.S. President Donald Trump fires the lead official with the country's Bureau of Labour Statistics following the release of numbers showing anemic job growth, which many link to his administration's tariff policies. 5: To ward off the threat of wildfires, Nova Scotia prohibits the public use of the province's tinder-dry forests, a move backed by steep fines. Other provinces enduring drought conditions soon follow suit. 7: Tariffs imposed by the U.S. are implemented against more than 60 countries and the European Union at levels not seen in nearly a century. Air Canada flight attendants picketed along the departures lane of Calgary International Airport on August 16, 2025. 11: Although Washington, D.C.'s crime rate has been falling, the Trump administration moves to federalize the police in the U.S. capital city while deploying the National Guard as well. 14: Canadian farmers are subjected to a nearly 75 per cent tariff on canola levied by China, a major purchaser of their crop. 15: Russian leader Vladimir Putin meets with his American counterpart Donald Trump in Anchorage, Alaska, in a bid to bring peace to Ukraine but no ceasefire agreement is reached. 16: About 10,000 Air Canada flight attendants set to strike are locked out, stranding tens of thousands of passengers. After defying a federal back-to-work order, a tentative agreement to end the dispute is reached three days later. 18: In a closely watched byelection in the Alberta riding of Battle River-Crowfoot, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wins with 80 per cent of the vote to earn a seat in Parliament nearly four months after losing in his previous Ottawa-area constituency. 22: Ottawa announces it's removing retaliatory tariffs on goods compliant with the U.S.-Canada-Mexico trade pact that had been put in place to respond to Washington's import levies. 22: In what's widely seen as an act of political vengeance against an outspoken critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, the FBI raids the home of his former national security adviser John Bolton, on the premise he's been improperly holding classified documents. 24: Calgary Surge fall just short in the Canadian Elite Basketball League finals, losing 79-73 to repeat champion Niagara River Lions. Chief executive officer of the Major Projects Office Dawn Farrell takes part in a press conference in Edmonton on Sept. 11, 2025. 26: Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada's defensive military deployment of 2,000 troops in Latvia will be extended to 2029. 27: A gunman fires into a Catholic school's church in Minneapolis, Minn., during mass, killing two children and injuring another 17 people before killing himself. 28: An Israeli airstrike kills Yemen's Houthi Prime Minister Minister Ahmed Ghaleb Nasser al-Rahawi as well as a number of cabinet ministers. 29: Ottawa announces Dawn Farrell, the former Trans Mountain and TransAlta CEO, will lead the federal government's major projects office, to be based in Calgary. 31: A landslide in Sudan's Darfur region leaves at least 1,000 people dead. SEPTEMBER 1: Alberta's Fairness in Sport Act, which bars transgender girls from competing in school sports designated for ""biological"" females, takes effect. The legislation requires parents of students aged 12 and older to confirm their child's gender assigned at birth before they can participate in female-only sports. 2: A federal court judge rules U.S. President Donald Trump's deployment of the National Guard and Marines in Los Angeles over the summer was illegal. 2: Alberta's UCP government pauses and vows to rewrite a ministerial order for schools to purge books with graphic sexual content after the Edmonton Public School Board insisted it followed the decree, banning 200 titles, some of them classics. 2: U.S. forces deployed in the southern Caribbean destroy a boat allegedly carrying drug smugglers, a strike critics call a form of extrajudicial killing. 3: Lisbon, Portugal's iconic Gloria funicular crashes, killing 16 and injuring 21. 5: Sophie, the Duchess of Edinburgh, attends Spruce Meadows for the 50th anniversary of its Masters tournament and meets with several charitable organizations during her visit to the city. Sophie, the Duchess of Edinburgh, pets Calgary Police Service victim assistance support dog Calibri while meeting dogs with the Pacific Assistance Dogs Society at Spruce Meadows on September 7, 2025. 6: Montreal Canadiens goaltending legend and one-time federal cabinet minister Ken Dryden dies from cancer at the age of 78. 8: U.S. Democrats release contents of a 50th anniversary book given to convicted sex predator Jeffrey Epstein including a lewd birthday card apparently signed by Donald Trump. 9: Israel launches an air strike against Hamas leaders gathered in Doha, Qatar, who were negotiating a possible ceasefire in Gaza. Several people are killed though the group's main leadership survives. 10: Raising fears of an expansion of the war in Ukraine, NATO fighter jets shoot down Russian drones that had invaded Polish airspace. 10: Far-right influencer Charlie Kirk is fatally shot during an outdoor public event at a university in Utah. 15: The UCP government says that beginning next year all new and renewed driver's licences will display Albertans' health card numbers and their citizenship status. 16: Legendary actor, director and activist Robert Redford dies. He was 89. 16: Federal Transport Minister Chrystia Freeland resigns her cabinet post to become a special envoy to Ukraine. 16: For the first time, a UN agency - its Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - declares Israel is committing genocide in its nearly two-year onslaught on Gaza. The move draws opposition from Israel, the United States, the United Kingdom and Germany, among others. 17: Following pressure from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission and commentary by the late-night comedian on the aftermath of the assassination of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk, Jimmy Kimmel's show is suspended indefinitely by ABC. But following public backlash, Kimmel returns six days later. 21: As Israeli pressure mounts on Gaza and the West Bank, Canada says it's recognizing a Palestinian state. Imperial Oil's Calgary campus was photographed on Tuesday, September 30, 2025. The company will shift many of its functions away from the Calgary office. 22: A news report alleges U.S. border czar Tom Homan accepted a $50,000 bribe in September, 2024 in exchange for securing contracts in a future Trump administration. 25: The federal government announces plans for money-hemorrhaging Canada Post, including moving almost exclusively to a community mailbox model. Postal workers walk off the job in response in a full strike that lasts until Oct. 10, when it becomes a rotating strike. 26: Former FBI chief James Comey is indicted, accused of lying of lying to Congress in a move widely condemned as a political assault by President Donald Trump who pronounces him guilty on social media. 26: Alberta's highest court rejects a bid for more freedom for Matthew de Grood, who killed five young people at a house party in the northwest community of Brentwood in 2014. De Grood had sought a conditional discharge or less stringent conditions, arguing he no longer posed a public threat. 29: Calgary-based Imperial Oil reveals it's pulling out of the city and eliminating 900 jobs as part of a cost-cutting effort. 30: Hundreds of senior U.S. military officials gathered in Quantico, Va., are told by President Donald Trump to prepare to wage war against people in America, who he calls them ""the enemy within."" title: WHERE THE TROUGH WAS
body: SINCE Brian Mulroney came to power in September 1984, 10 cabinet ministers have left office amid controversy; four subsequently came back to power. Here is a chronology: 1. Feb. 12, 1985: Robert Coates resigns as defence minister after the Ottawa Citizen reveals that he visited a bar and chatted with a nude dancer in West Germany while on a government trip. 2. Sept. 23, 1985: John Fraser quits as fisheries minister after CBC TV reveals that he allowed a New Brunswick firm to put tainted tuna on the market. Later, he cOmes back as speaker of the House of Commons. 3. Sept. 25, 1985: Communications Minister Marcel Masse resigns from the cabinet after being investigated by the RCMP for election overspending. No charges are laid and he returns to the cabinet as communications minister. (He left, as defence minister, in the January cabinet shuffle.) 4. Dec. 31, 1985: Junior Transport Minister Suzanne Blais-Grenier quits the cabinet amid reports of her lavish spending on foreign trips. 5. May 12, 1986: Sinclair Stevens resigns as industry minister after the Globe and Mail reveals that his wife, Noreen Stevens, arranged a $ 3.6-million loan for the family business from a firm that received federal aid. In 1987, a commission of inquiry rules that he broke cabinet conflict-of-interest rules 14 times and used his office for private advantage. 6. Jan. 17, 1987: Mulroney fires junior transport minister Andre Bissonnette after The Gazette reveals a complex land-flip scheme involving Oerlikon Aerospace, a firm with defence contracts, in the minister's riding, St. Jean sur Richelieu. He and his campaign manager, Normand Ouellette, are charged with fraud, breach of trust and conspiracy. Bissonnette is acquitted and later retires from politics. Ouellette is convicted, fined $ 100,000 and ordered to repay Oerlikon $ 1 million. 7. Feb. 19, 1987: Public Works Minister Roch LaSalle, the MP for Joliette, resigns amid allegations - which he denied - of influence- peddling. 8. Feb. 3, 1988: Mulroney fires Supply and Services Minister Michel Cote, a Quebec City MP, saying he failed to declare a $ 250,000 personal loan from a Quebec City businessman who had federal government contracts. No charges are laid. 9. Aug. 2, 1989: Consumer Affairs Minister Bernard Valcourt quits the cabinet after pleading guilty to drunk driving in a July motorcycle accident that cost him an eye. He returns as employment and immigration minister. WHERE THE TROUGH WAS 10. Jan. 24, 1990: Sports Minister Jean Charest quits the cabinet after revelations that he called a judge about a case involving a track coach. He returns as environment minister. At least four Tory backbenchers and two aides have been sentenced for wrongdoing in connection with their office: 1. Lotbiniere MP Maurice Tremblay was fined $ 12,000 last month for using $ 7,000 in federal funds to send political supporters on a trip to Mexico. Both sides are appealing the verdict. Tremblay says he is innocent; the Crown argues he should be jailed. 2. East-end Montreal backbencher Michel Gravel was sentenced to a year in jail and fined $ 50,000 in 1989 after pleading guilty to bribery and influence-peddling. He admitted receiving $ 97,000 from contractors and others looking for work on the Museum of Civilization in Hull. 3. Chambly MP Richard Grise resigned from Parliament in 1989 after pleading guilty to 11 counts of fraud and breach of trust in connection with kickbacks from builders. He was sentenced to a day in jail and fined $ 20,000. 4. Marie Letcher, an aide to Saskatchewan MP Jack Scowen, was convicted in 1989 of receiving $ 3,000 from a woman after offering to help bring her niece to Canada from India. 5. Marie Menard, a millionaire's daughter, was convicted in 1988 of stealing $ 88,000 from the office funds of her boss, Pat Carney, who was then trade minister. 6. Hochelaga-Maisonneuve backbencher Edouard Desrosiers pleaded guilty to breach of trust in 1989 and was fined $ 3,000 for pocketing $ 7,463 from his Parliament office budget. He did not seek re-election in 1988. One Tory senator and at least four Tory backbenchers are being tried now or face trials soon. 1. Saint-Maurice MP Denis Pronovost was charged in 1992 with sexual assault and paying boys for sex. His trial begins March 1 in Trois Rivieres. 2. Senator Michel Cogger, a lawyer, has pleaded not guilty to 1991 charges of influence-peddling in connection with $ 212,000 allegedly paid by businessman Guy Montpetit for help in obtaining a $ 45- million federal grant. The trial will continue in May. (Montpetit's trial on charges of buying influence begins March 22.) 3. Levis MP Gabriel Fontaine was charged in 1991 with 14 counts of fraud, breach of trust and conspiracy. Fontaine has challenged the legality of the charges, saying the RCMP has no authority to investigate how he spends his office budget. Two courts have ruled he should stand trial. Quebec's Court of Appeal will hear his case this spring. 4, 5. Beauce MP Gilles Bernier and Chambly MP Richard Grise were charged in 1990 with breach of trust for allegedly putting each other's children on their parliamentry office payrolls and paying them for work they never did. The Supreme Court of Canada refused to hear Bernier's appeal challenging the legality of the charges. A trial is pending. Graphic GAZETTE, AISLIN/ WHERE'S THE TROUGH? (1984) 'HEY! WHA'D'YA WANT?...INTEGRITY? WE GOT GUYS IN QUEBEC WHO'LL GIVE YOU TONS OF INTEGRITY… RIGHT OFF THE BACK OF A TRUCK (1989)(Illustration shows Mulroney as a gangster)

title: Who buys Christmas trees after Dec. 14? And other concerns about Trudeau's sales-tax break
body: OTTAWA - The Trudeau government took provinces, businesses and other Canadians by surprise Thursday by announcing a two-month GST/HST holiday to start before Christmas,( https://nationalpost.com/news/liberals-cut- gst-on-beer-christmas-trees ) to be followed by a $250 cheque to qualified Canadians next spring. The estimated cost: $6.28 billion. If it's passed by Parliament in time (more on that later), the sales-tax holiday is supposed to last from Dec. 14 to Feb. 15 and will apply to Christmas trees, alcohol, prepared food, children's clothing, diapers, toys, books, snacks and sweets. But the plan has retailers asking a lot of questions as they're already well into the holiday season. So are provinces, who find themselves on different sides of the sales-tax break. Here are some of the biggest issues: Unintended consequences for retailers Dan Kelly, President and CEO of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB), outlined on X many of the challenges( https://x.com/CFIB/status/1860012289899798782 ) posed by the upcoming tax break for many retailers. Kelly heard from many of them that the announcement did not give them enough advance notice to change their point-of-sale systems (aka cash registers) at the busiest time of the year and that the list of tax-exempt goods is too broad, leaving thousands of products in a grey area, bringing a risk of government tax penalties for getting it wrong. He also heard that the tax break is arriving very late in the Christmas shopping season and that customers will be tempted to return large purchases they've already got with the intention of buying them again after Dec. 14, tax- free. ""This will make it even tighter to make sales and serve customers,"" he wrote on X. Industry association Restaurants Canada, on the other hand, says it's members are rejoicing at the idea of offering a tax break to customers on prepared food after being hit hard by the pandemic and the inflation crisis. ""More Canadians will be able to celebrate with loved ones at a restaurant, have lunch with colleagues or treat themselves to a morning pastry on their way to work. We also appreciate that the relief will be extended over January, which is typically the lowest time of the year for our industry, and right through to Valentine's Day,"" read a statement from the association( https://www.restaurantscanada.org/restaurants-canada-statement-on-federal- governments-gst-holiday-for-restaurant-meals/ ) on Thursday. Sylvain Charlebois, a professor specializing in food distribution and security at Dalhousie University estimated on Friday( https://x.com/FoodProfessor/status/1859977485649313941/ ) that the average Canadian would save $4.51 in grocery taxes and $19.51 in restaurant taxes over the two-month period. Sorry retirees and homemakers, no cheque for you The $250 cheque the Liberals are promising some time ""early next spring"" will be for the 18.7 million Canadians who worked in 2023 and earned up to $150,000 individual net income. That means people who didn't have paid employment last year, including retirees and homemakers, won't be getting anything. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said Thursday his government had already provided targeted help to families and more vulnerable Canadians, but he said too many people who are struggling didn't qualify for those programs. ""As I travel across the country, I do regularly hear from working Canadians who are having trouble making ends meet, but saying, 'Look, I don't have kids. I'm not a senior yet, and I'm facing challenges,'"" he said. Trudeau mentioned his government's decision to increase Old Age Security for older seniors and the Canada Child Benefit for young families, but also investments in a national daycare program. The Liberals have also increased disability benefits in their last budget, even though many advocates have criticized the measure as being insufficient. The good news for people not struggling? Everyone gets the sales-tax break, even rich people. Will you be eligible to receive the newly promised $250 tax rebate from Ottawa?( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/will-you-be-eligible-to-receive-the-newly-promised-250-tax-rebate-from- ottawa ) Liberals to cut GST on beer, children's toys and Christmas trees( https://nationalpost.com/news/liberals-cut-gst-on- beer-christmas-trees ) Your provincial mileage will vary The sales-tax break will apply to all provincial and federal sales tax in the five provinces that have a harmonized tax: namely Ontario, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. But it will only apply to the GST - and not the separate provincial sales tax - in B.C, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Quebec (Alberta has no provincial sales tax). So depending on where you live, you'll get anywhere from a five- to 15-per- cent savings on qualifying goods. Some of the HST provinces were not thrilled to discover they're being roped in to the Liberals' tax break. New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said the measure will cost her province $62 million in lost revenue( https://tj.news/new-brunswick/federal-tax-holiday-will-cost-n-b-62-million-in-lost-revenue-holt ) and said she expects to be compensated by the federal government. It is unclear at the moment if she will be. P.E.I. Premier Dennis King said the measure would cost his province $14 million. ""There is no agreement that the federal government would come in and give us that money or make us whole in any way,"" King said in the provincial legislature Friday. ""We'll continue working with them and see what we can do, because it would drive a bit of a hole in our budget."" But Ontario Premier Doug Ford said his government had already eliminated the provincial portion of the HST for some of the items mentioned in the federal government's list, including children's essentials and books. ""I gotta give them kudos,"" Ford said. ""Any government - I don't care what political stripe - wants to put more money back in the people's pockets? Good for them."" Newfoundland and Labrador announced it would ""match"" the federal tax break( https://www.gov.nl.ca/releases/2024/exec/1121n07/ ) and framed it as an affordability measure meant to provide an extra $48 million in relief. Economist Trevor Tombe, at the University of Calgary, estimated Friday that it would cost the Liberal government about $1.4 billion to reimburse the HST provinces( https://x.com/trevortombe/status/1860049185082368161 ) for lost provincial tax revenue, on top of the $1.6 billion lost in federal GST revenues. Parliament isn't passing anything right now If the Liberals hoped that they could end two months of gridlock in the House of Commons by dangling more than $6 billion worth of holiday cheer, they may have miscalculated. The House has been paralyzed by a standoff over questions of privilege, as the government refuses to hand over documents related to the ""green slush fund"" scandal, and matters of privilege supersede all other House business. NDP Leader Jagmeet Singh said his party would agree to ""pause"" the current privilege debate for one day at a time. He said pausing the debate would leave enough time for MPs to adopt the temporary break on the GST/HST for two months before Dec. 14. But he agrees with the Conservatives that the government should provide the unredacted documents to the House. Trudeau said it ""boggles the mind that the NDP is crossing its arms"" and refusing to adopt the long list of legislation that has been on the back burner for weeks now. The government is also running out of time to review and pass the supplementary estimates before Dec. 10 to ensure that government spending can flow to fund critical programs. ""I'm really calling on the opposition parties to not let Conservatives continue to prove Parliament is broken and instead get busy delivering concretely for Canadians,"" he said. Freeland's deputy director of communications, Katherine Cuplinskas, said it would be a ""shame"" if opposition parties ""put partisan politics ahead of giving Canadians real relief."" That means that the next three weeks will be crucial in finding a path forward to pass not only the tax breaks but approve billions more in spending. The Speaker of the House of Commons, Greg Fergus, has already urged MPs to end the standoff( https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-speaker-warns-standoff-over-documents-risks- conflict-with-parliaments/ ) to make sure Parliament fulfills its duties and it is unclear whether the situation could force him to intervene. Who the heck buys a Christmas tree after December 14? According to a quick survey done in the National Post parliamentary bureau, no one. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said Thursday his government had already provided targeted help to families and more vulnerable Canadians, but he said too many people who are struggling didn't qualify for those programs. ""As I travel across the country, I do regularly hear from working Canadians who are having trouble making ends meet, but saying, 'Look, I don't have kids. I'm not a senior yet, and I'm facing challenges,'"" he said. Trudeau mentioned his government's decision to increase Old Age Security for older seniors and the Canada Child Benefit for young families, but also investments in a national daycare program. The Liberals have also increased disability benefits in their last budget, even though many advocates have criticized the measure as being insufficient. The good news for people not struggling? Everyone gets the sales-tax break, even rich people. Will you be eligible to receive the newly promised $250 tax rebate from Ottawa?( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/will-you-be-eligible-to-receive-the-newly-promised-250-tax-rebate-from- ottawa ) Liberals to cut GST on beer, children's toys and Christmas trees( https://nationalpost.com/news/liberals-cut-gst-on- beer-christmas-trees ) Your provincial mileage will vary The sales-tax break will apply to all provincial and federal sales tax in the five provinces that have a harmonized tax: namely Ontario, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. But it will only apply to the GST - and not the separate provincial sales tax - in B.C, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Quebec (Alberta has no provincial sales tax). So depending on where you live, you'll get anywhere from a five- to 15-per- cent savings on qualifying goods. Some of the HST provinces were not thrilled to discover they're being roped in to the Liberals' tax break. ""I'm really calling on the opposition parties to not let Conservatives continue to prove Parliament is broken and instead get busy delivering concretely for Canadians,"" he said. Freeland's deputy director of communications, Katherine Cuplinskas, said it would be a ""shame"" if opposition parties ""put partisan politics ahead of giving Canadians real relief."" That means that the next three weeks will be crucial in finding a path forward to pass not only the tax breaks but approve billions more in spending. The Speaker of the House of Commons, Greg Fergus, has already urged MPs to end the standoff( https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-speaker-warns-standoff-over-documents-risks- conflict-with-parliaments/ ) to make sure Parliament fulfills its duties and it is unclear whether the situation could force him to intervene. Who the heck buys a Christmas tree after December 14? According to a quick survey done in the National Post parliamentary bureau, no one. title: Who speaks for provinces? Cabinet ministers, premiers and senators lay claim to job
body: In conducting the nation's business, who could most effectively represent the provinces' interests - cabinet ministers, the premiers or senators? Traditionally, every province has at least one minister in the powerful federal cabinet, which formulates government policy. The current 36 cabinet ministers were elected in the provinces as follows: Newfoundland 1; Nova Scotia 1; Prince Edward Island 0; New Brunswick 2; Quebec 12; Ontario 11; Manitoba 2; Saskatchewan 1; Alberta 2; British Columbia 4. All four MPs from P.E.I. are Liberals and, therefore, ineligible for cabinet. That illustrates one difficulty a prime minister can encounter in trying to achieve all-province representation in cabinet. Some critics argue that when government policy, such as the goods and services tax, is in conflict with regional wishes, constituents' desires take a back seat to cabinet ministers' allegiance to the party or government. In the 1960s, when former Ontario premier John Robarts called a meeting of first ministers, he initiated a process that has become known as ""executive federalism."" Before that there were federal-provincial conferences to decide financial arrangements between Ottawa and the provinces, but first ministers' meetings now deal with constitutional, social and economic matters. The question of who represents the provinces is, in part, at the root of the present crisis over Meech Lake. In 1982 Quebec did not sign the patriated Constitution with its new Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Although the province is legally bound by the 1982 Constitution, many observers do not feel Quebec belongs to ""the constitutional fold."" It was to get Quebec onside that Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and the 10 provincial premiers negotiated the Meech Lake accord in 1987. Former prime minister Pierre Trudeau rejects that interpretation of events. He says that the Quebec separatist Parti Quebecois government in 1982 would never have signed the Constitution, but he contends that Quebec nevertheless approved the act because he and a substantial number of his ministers and caucus were elected in Quebec. If Meech Lake were to become law, there would have to be at least one first ministers' meeting each year. One bone of contention surrounding first ministers' meetings is whether they should be held in the open. Those who favor closed sessions say that with television cameras present, participants pander to their constituents and cannot be seen to be backing down. Others argue that it is undemocratic for the nation's business to be conducted behind closed doors. A major criticism of first ministers' meetings, particularly the current round, was voiced by former Manitoba premier Howard Pawley, who said that such meetings are often doomed because there is not sufficient public consultation by participants beforehand. Provinces that do not ratify agreements are then subject to the charge that they have repudiated their leaders' promises. The Fathers of Confederation intended the Senate, with its regional composition, to represent provincial interests, but because that chamber is unelected, it cannot effectively exercise its powers and discharge that function. The less populated provinces advocate an elected, effective Senate wherein all provinces would have equal representation. Supporters of the idea say the U.S. Senate should be our prototype. Opponents argue such a Senate would give undue power to sparsely populated provinces. In the U.S., where there are 50 states, it is difficult for any region to impose its will on the others. In Canada, with just 10 provinces, disproportionate regional power would be easier to attain, critics say. Last week, Senate reform was emerging as the most difficult problem to solve in the Meech Lake controversy. Discuss it Discuss this in class: Who could most effectively represent the provinces' interests in our nation's affairs - cabinet ministers, premiers or senators? Why? Watch for: * News of the Warsaw Pact summit meeting in Moscow Thursday. * Statistics Canada to release May unemployment figures Friday and last month's cost-of-living index data one week later. * Former White House aide John Poindexter, who was found guilty over the Iran-Contra scandal, to be sentenced next Monday. * Reports of the three-day visit to Canada of Nelson Mandela beginning June 17. * The outcome of the Liberal leadership convention in Calgary June 23. * Coverage of the Queen's visit to Canada June 27-July 1. She will stop in Quebec. Quick quiz Without rereading, test your knowledge of the news by labelling each numbered statement true or false. 1. There is at least one cabinet minister elected in each province now. 2. John Robarts was a former premier of Ontario. 3. Quebec did not sign the 1982 Constitution and, therefore, is not legally bound by its provisions. 4. If the Meech Lake accord becomes law, there will have to be at least one first ministers' meeting annually. 5. Howard Pawley is a former premier of Manitoba.
